Albares meets with British counterpart to strengthen bilateral relations
Spain
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
14:22:56 CEST
21:22:56 KST

The Minister for Foreign Affairs, the European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, welcomed his British counterpart, the new Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs, Edward Miliband, this Wednesday, at a time of renewed momentum in bilateral relations, the culmination of which has been the signing of the UK–European Union Treaty on Gibraltar, initialled on 14 July, and the removal of the fence.
“Our bilateral relations are very good, but the signing of the agreement on Gibraltar represents a historic opportunity to go further and deepen them. Furthermore, we have the Bilateral Strategic Framework signed in London in September 2025, and we wish to continue making progress on its implementation,” said Albares.
Climate emergency
During the meeting, the ministers signed a joint statement in which they recognised the need to prioritise the fight against the climate emergency in their foreign policy, in light of the record-breaking heatwaves and severe wildfires currently affecting Europe as a result of climate change.
They also agreed to jointly lead the green transition, convinced that decarbonisation, energy security and environmental protection are objectives that are inseparable from the prosperity and competitiveness of both countries’ economies.
The joint statement recognises that climate change is a global problem that must be addressed through effective multilateralism and respect for international law; it emphasises the need to adopt effective measures and to mobilise sustainable funding commensurate with the scale of the challenge we face.
Furthermore, Albares and Miliband have signed a cooperation agreement on gender equality to eradicate violence against women and girls, advance the Women, Peace and Security Agenda, and increase the presence of women in decision-making processes, particularly in the field of diplomacy.
Strategic relationship
Spain enjoys a privileged relationship with the United Kingdom, not only in economic terms – as the main market for Spanish exports outside the EU and the second most important destination for our direct investment abroad –; the United Kingdom is the fourth-largest investor in Spain.
“The ties that bind us are much deeper: one million Spaniards and Britons live in both countries, and 19 million British tourists visited Spain in 2025, making it the leading source market for tourists to our country. Spain and the UK are the two best-connected countries in the world by air, with around 400 daily flights in both directions,” Minister Albares pointed out.
Scientists, sportspeople, tourists, students, businesspeople and artists travel constantly between the two countries, bringing the number of British visitors to Spain in 2025 to 50 million. Furthermore, Spain is home to the largest British resident community in Europe, and one of the largest in the world.
International agenda
Albares and Miliband also discussed relations between the UK and the European Union, how to strengthen them and how to further enhance cooperation between the two regions – something essential for continuing to make progress on mutual support in the political, economic and security spheres.
In this regard, the Spanish minister noted that the United Kingdom’s return to the Erasmus programme is excellent news for young European university students.
Other topics discussed included European defence and the conclusions of the recent NATO summit in Ankara, as well as the need to remain united in supporting Ukraine, a sovereign and democratic State that has been the victim of an illegal act of aggression. Spain supports the UK’s participation in the military financial aid package for Ukraine and hopes that negotiations on this matter will conclude soon.
Finally, they also discussed the worrying situation in the Middle East, where it is clear that there is no alternative to diplomacy. “We must continue to demand respect for international law, including the Law of the Sea. The Strait of Hormuz must be reopened in accordance with international law and without any tolls or charges. And, for free transit to be viable, there must be a stable ceasefire and a return to the negotiating table by all parties,” insisted Albares.

British shipyards could build warships for America
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
13:20:58 BST
21:20:58 KST

President Trump has ordered the Pentagon to open American warship construction to foreign shipbuilders under a model that would allow the first two ships of a class to be built abroad, provided the builder establishes or buys a shipyard in the United States and builds everything after that on American soil, according to a presidential memorandum issued on 13 August.
The memorandum also directs the Secretary of War to produce a plan to strip the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System and the Advanced Weapons Elevators out of the aircraft carrier CVN-81 and replace them with steam catapults and hydraulic elevators, reverting to the arrangement used on the previous generation of carriers.
Addressed to the Secretary of War, the Director of the Office of Management and Budget and the National Security Adviser, the document states that the Navy “has experienced a series of shipbuilding setbacks stemming from overly complex designs and iterative design change procedures, which have resulted in cost growth, delays, and cancellations.” It says a lack of capacity and competition among shipbuilders has produced large backlogs across six major programmes and a commercial sector that is not globally competitive.
The Finland Model
The mechanism for bringing in foreign builders is described in the memorandum as the Finland Model, taking as its template a memorandum of understanding signed with Finland in October 2025 covering medium icebreaker construction. It can be applied to up to three ship classes.
Under the conditions set out, a foreign supplier must simultaneously build a new American shipyard or take ownership or a majority equity position in an existing one, and build all ships after the first two in the United States. It must hire and train an American workforce, license the proprietary shipbuilding techniques and technologies used at the parent yard to the American yards, and source an American supply chain for construction and maintenance.
Building warships in foreign yards is generally prohibited under United States law. The memorandum delegates to the Secretary of War the authority to make the national security determination that a contract qualifies for a waiver and to notify Congress of each determination, with no contract permitted until 30 days after Congress receives it.
A new frigate competition
Within 90 days the Secretary of War is to submit a plan for what the memorandum calls “a new competitive acquisition approach for surface combatants with sufficient inherent capabilities to perform anti-submarine warfare, surface warfare, and convoy escort duties”, explicitly allowing proposals based on the international procurement model.
That description covers the ground occupied by the British Type 26 and Type 31, both of which are already exported. BAE Systems has sold the Type 26 design to Australia, Canada and Norway, the last in a £10 billion deal signed in 2025, while Babcock’s Arrowhead 140, the parent design for the Type 31, has been selected by Poland and Indonesia. Both are mature designs in production, which is what the memorandum says it wants.
The insistence on design stability runs through the document. It states that the Navy “shall not impose iterative design changes upon the original mature parent designs” within the programmes concerned, and that no changes may be made without the approval of the Secretary of War in consultation with the Navy Secretary, OMB and the National Security Adviser.
The target of that instruction is not named, but the Constellation-class frigate offers the obvious precedent. Derived from the Italian FREMM design and intended as a low-risk buy of a proven ship, it accumulated so many American modifications that commonality with the parent design fell away, and the programme ran years late amid heavy criticism from the Government Accountability Office.
Yards and repair capacity
Within 120 days the department is to submit a plan to increase nuclear submarine and carrier readiness, including the establishment of a fifth public Navy yard. The United States currently operates four, at Portsmouth in Maine, Norfolk, Puget Sound and Pearl Harbor.
The plan is to address drydock capacity for the planned growth of the attack submarine fleet over the next two decades, with locations proximate to the Pacific Fleet including the continental United States, Alaska, Hawaii and American territories, and site options covering up to three new drydocks sized for every current and projected class of submarine. Public-private partnerships are named as a possible financing route.
A separate plan, due within 90 days, covers a Component Repair Center to receive new parts and refurbish old ones for the submarine repair industrial base, holding at least one ship set of spare equipment for the Los Angeles, Virginia, Seawolf, Ohio and Columbia classes.
Naval Sea Systems Command is also to be reviewed within 120 days, with recommendations for personnel, organisational and structural reform. The stated objectives include introducing results-based accountability for NAVSEA leadership measured by speed of delivery, reducing bureaucracy, eliminating competing priorities within the command, and preventing it from imposing redesigns on mature parent designs.
The memorandum builds on an executive order signed in April 2025 titled Restoring America’s Maritime Dominance. It notes that implementation is subject to the availability of appropriations, and creates no enforceable right or benefit.

Sydney library withdraws book on Gaza genocide critical of US media coverage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Amir Latif Arain
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
A Sydney library has withdrawn a book critical of US media coverage of Israel’s war on Gaza from its shelves for “review” following multiple complaints, including one from a survivor of the 2025 Bondi Beach attack, local media reported Tuesday.
How to Sell a Genocide: The Media's Complicity in the Destruction of Gaza, by American writer Adam Johnson, was removed from Waverley Library, The Sydney Morning Herald reported, citing Waverley Council.
The library serves Bondi and surrounding suburbs in Sydney’s east, home to one of Australia’s largest Jewish communities and close to the site of the December 2025 terrorist attack.
“The book has been removed from library shelves for review, and council will further consider processes to ensure closer oversight of book selection,” a council spokesperson said on Tuesday.
Waverley Council said it had received multiple complaints about the book, which remains listed in the library’s catalogue and is still available to reserve.
The council, however, declined to answer questions about how many complaints it had received, the criteria used to remove books from its collection, when the review would be completed or whether its findings would be made public.
Published in April by long-established British publisher Pluto Press, the book argues that Israel’s war on Gaza could not have continued without the “active, sustained complicity” of the US media.
It also says major news outlets “systematically sanitised Israel’s war crimes, hid the US’s central role, and dehumanized the Palestinian people”.
Johnson said the complaints appeared to be largely focused on the use of the word “genocide” in the title.
“But ‘genocide’ is not my word, or my finding. The fact of genocide in Gaza is the overwhelming consensus of the human rights world, and it is a wholly mainstream opinion among those tasked with studying and determining such matters," Johnson was quoted in The Guardian Australia.
"That it makes some people upset is unfortunate, but reality is often upsetting. This particular reality is especially upsetting … to the parents of the over 20,000 children killed by Israel in Gaza since October 2023. Do Sydney officials plan on removing pro-Israel books from their libraries because it potentially upsets these community members?” he further said.

Ukraine Reveals Patriot Missile Shortage to CNN as Launchers Sit Empty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:18:07 UTC
21:18:07 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Reveals Patriot Missile Shortage to CNN as Launchers Sit Empty
Ukraine faces a severe shortage of air defense interceptors, leaving advanced Patriot launcher units idling in rural fields.
Ukraine currently holds only 1% of US missile stockpiles, well short of the 5% requested by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to secure air coverage through the winter, according to CNN on August 17.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A system spotted near Kyiv has 16 tubes showing signs of past use, but its unit chief engineer, Dmytro, noted the launcher had not fired in six weeks.
This deficit follows heavy consumption of interceptor missiles in the Persian Gulf during March and April, where coalition forces used an average of 225 interceptors daily over a four-day period against low-cost Iranian drone attacks.
Meanwhile, manufacturer Lockheed Martin produced 620 interceptors in 2025 (roughly 1.7 per day), creating a usage-to-production gap of 132 to 1.
In response, the Pentagon signed a seven-year agreement in January to increase output to 2,000 units annually by 2030. The shortage of interceptor missiles leaves crews unable to stop incoming strikes aimed at civilian areas and infrastructure, as reported by CNN.
Dmytro recalled experiencing his first complete depletion of interceptor ammunition in December 2025. "It’s really a terrible sight when you have the equipment, but you can’t intercept a single missile," Dmytro said.
"Ballistic missiles fly over your head, and you can do nothing about them, while civilians are behind you." Dmytro described the experience: "It’s hard to describe—strong and bad feelings. It’s like you’re learning to walk, but you can’t walk. You know how to breathe, but you can’t breathe."
Operating the system involves complex tracking equipment, remote command centers, and tactical decision-making under intense pressure. A crew member named Heorhiy explained that deciding which target to engage relies heavily on experience.
"It’s complicated, because you see targets flying and threatening the civilian population, critical infrastructure, as well as the families of my comrades and my own family," Heorhiy stated, describing the moment of firing an interceptor as "something magical."
Ukrainian leadership forewarned that heavy usage of defense assets in Middle Eastern operations would impact supplies needed to counter ballistic missiles during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"We predicted that we would have problems. We were very shocked by how many missiles they launched at once... the same missiles that we could have used against Russian ballistic missiles," Dmytro noted.
To secure future supplies, President Zelenskyy proposed allowing US defense manufacturers Raytheon and Lockheed Martin to build interceptors directly in Ukraine under license, offering them full ownership and operational control.
"It will be your company," Zelenskyy recalled telling the defense companies. "It will be our minds, our hands, our engineers. And I will do everything possible to build a big company for them. Because I don’t need to sell interceptors to anyone else who I need for my country."
Addressing global inventory levels, Zelenskyy noted: "I know the production, facilities, military, and stockpiles of almost all countries in Europe, including the United States. Not everything, but a lot."
Following a NATO summit in Ankara in June, former US President Trump floated licensing options for local manufacturing, leading to executive visits to Kyiv.
However, subsequent statements cast doubt on licensing approvals. "I want to get this," Zelenskyy said. "I think his word is the word of the President of the United States. And I hope that I will get it."
A White House official clarified that no final decisions or guarantees regarding local manufacturing have been granted, pointing to strict security requirements for US technology.
Regarding whether localized production could begin quickly if restrictions were removed, Dmytro expressed skepticism: "No. Definitely no, because it is a very complex procedure, and it requires a lot of knowledge, a lot of technical information."
On August 9, 2026, The Atlantic reported that Ukraine’s efforts to manufacture Patriot air defense systems domestically faced resistance from US defense contractors Raytheon and Lockheed Martin.
While the companies officially cited concerns over intellectual property theft and technology security, a Republican congressional official disclosed that their primary fear was commercial—specifically, that Ukrainian manufacturers would streamline the system to produce it faster, better, and at a significantly lower cost.
This industrial friction unfolded as Ukraine faced severe interceptor shortages during intensified Russian missile strikes, leaving President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to pursue immediate missile deliveries alongside long-term domestic licensing agreements.

Russia Starts Fining People for Complaining About Gasoline Shortages
Russian authorities have begun issuing fines to residents who publicly complain about gasoline shortages, with courts in Volgograd and Perm penalizing people over attempts to draw attention to fuel supply problems.
On August 13, the Central District Court of Volgograd fined local resident Tatiana Smetanko 10,000 rubles (around $120) for participating in an unauthorized public gathering, according to Mediazona.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The case stems from an incident on July 16, when five Volgograd residents gathered near a gas station on Rokossovsky Street to record a joint video appeal to Investigative Committee Chairman Alexander Bastrykin over fuel shortages. The participants were subsequently detained.
According to Mediazona, one participant, speaking anonymously to local outlet V1.ru, said the group had sought to complain about what they described as unequal access to gasoline. According to the participant, local administration employees were able to fill their tanks using fuel cards, while ordinary residents were often refused fuel.
Police, however, treated the recording of the appeal as an unauthorized public event, the participant said.
A similar case was reported in Perm, where activist Lev Samolovskikh was also fined 10,000 rubles after submitting an application to local authorities to hold a rally over gasoline shortages.
The fines come as fuel shortages continue to affect several Russian regions following month-long series of Ukrainian strikes. After temporarily easing restrictions in late July, authorities have again introduced gasoline rationing as renewed disruptions at oil refineries put pressure on domestic supplies.
At least six Russian regions reintroduced or tightened restrictions on fuel sales between August 10 and 15, The Insider reported. The measures include caps on gasoline purchases, restrictions on filling portable fuel containers, and odd-even rationing based on vehicle license plate numbers.

Putin Squeezes $4.6 Billion From Businesses Through “Voluntary Contributions” to Plug Budget Deficit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:17:40 UTC
21:17:40 KST

- Category
- World
Putin Squeezes $4.6 Billion From Businesses Through “Voluntary Contributions” to Plug Budget Deficit
Large Russian businesses have been forced to transfer hundreds of billions of rubles to the federal budget following Vladimir Putin’s demand for so-called “voluntary contributions” as the country struggles with a record budget deficit.
AAccording to Vedomosti on August 18, as of mid-August, so-called gratuitous payments to the federal budget had reached 383.69 billion rubles (about $4.6 billion). Before Putin’s March meeting with representatives of major Russian businesses, contributions from non-governmental organizations stood at just 15.6 billion rubles (around $187 million).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Following Putin’s appeal, the volume of transfers increased tenfold within a month, reaching 159.7 billion rubles (almost $2 billion). Payments rose by another 45.5% in May and 27% in June, before increasing by a further 30% during July and the first half of August.
Alexander Shokhin, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs, confirmed that business owners had transferred funds to the state, saying the money came not only from corporate structures but also from family foundations.
The Russian government, meanwhile, expects to receive around 300 billion rubles (nearly $4 billion) in such payments by the end of the year.
The contributions come as Russia’s public finances face mounting pressure. Between January and July, the federal budget deficit reached 6.455 trillion rubles (approximately $77.5 billion), 1.4 times higher than during the same period last year and nearly twice the amount initially planned for the entire year.
According to The Moscow Times, Russia’s mounting fiscal pressures have coincided with the growing cost of its war against Ukraine. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, the Russian federal budget has spent nearly 50 trillion rubles (about $600 billion) on the war.
To cover military expenditures, Russian authorities have already used three-quarters of the liquid assets held in the National Wealth Fund and confiscated private assets worth 4 trillion rubles (arout $48 billion). The government has also raised corporate profit taxes, personal income taxes, value-added tax, and levies on small businesses.
Amid these mounting fiscal pressures, Russian authorities have also reduced public access to information about the country’s remaining financial reserves. The Moscow Times reported on August 13 that the government had stopped publishing official figures on cash reserves held in its single treasury account, a key financial cushion for unallocated budget funds.
Russia’s Federal Treasury removed daily operational data covering ruble deposits placed with commercial banks, money market transactions, and the total amount of cash available across different levels of the budget system.

Russia Has Started Supplying Explosives to Iran to Replenish Weapons Stocks
Russia has begun shipping explosives, ammunition, and drone parts across the Caspian Sea to help Iran replenish its missile and drone stocks following strikes by the US and Israel.
According to a European government document cited by NBC News on August 18, the maritime route allows both nations to transfer military cargo directly between Russian and Iranian ports.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The landlocked Caspian Sea is bordered by five countries: Russia, Iran, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and Azerbaijan. Because Western navies, including the US Navy, do not operate in these waters, they cannot interdict shipments moving between the two allies.
In late March, Israel targeted the Iranian port complex of Bandar Anzali on the Caspian coast. Israeli officials said the facility was used to transport weapons from Russia. Shipments through the port restarted shortly after the operation.
The reliance on this supply route highlights a growing strategic alliance between Moscow and Tehran. Iranian forces have used drones and missiles against US military bases in the Middle East, leading to the deaths of at least 18 American service members since the start of active hostilities.
During the early stages of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Tehran provided primary support to Moscow. Iran supplied ready-to-use Shahed strike drones alongside production technology. Russian engineers later upgraded the design and established mass production inside Russia.
Reports from Financial Times previously indicated that Russia began sending drones back to Iran while sharing satellite imagery, intelligence, and targeting data to hit US positions in the Middle East.
US and Iranian officials agreed to a 60-day ceasefire in mid-June, which was extended for another two months in August. Reports from The Wall Street Journal state that Tehran is using this pause in fighting to rebuild its military inventory. Iranian officials aim to inflict sufficient damage on US and Israeli forces to deter future large-scale strikes on Iranian territory.
On July 25, 2026, Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) launched long-range drone strikes against multiple Russian military and logistical targets, hitting air defense systems in Rostov-on-Don and naval assets in the Caspian Sea.
The SBU reported damaging a 92N6E radar tower, a Tor-M2 air defense system, an electronic warfare complex, and two FPV drone warehouses in Rostov-on-Don.
In the Caspian Sea, Ukrainian drones targeted the Filanovsky offshore oil platform alongside two sanctioned cargo ships, the Port Olya 2 and the Begey, which had been transporting Iranian military equipment and ammunition to Russia.
Additionally, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Project 12418 Molniya-class missile boat stationed in the region.
In March 2026, Russia openly declared its support for Iran amid escalating confrontations involving the United States and Israel, signaling that Moscow did not consider itself a neutral actor in the Middle East crisis.
Russian Ambassador to the United Kingdom Andrei Kelin confirmed that Moscow was siding with Tehran, criticizing Western governments for placing full blame on Iran while ignoring initial strikes by the US and Israel.
Pointing to the deepening strategic partnership between the two nations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Kelin called for an immediate end to hostilities and a return to political dialogue rather than military escalation.

Russian Frigate Armed With Nuclear-Capable Zircons Appears Off German Coast With Tracker Switched Off
Russia has deployed one of its most advanced warships, armed with nuclear-capable Zircon hypersonic missiles, close to a German island in the Baltic Sea amid escalating Kremlin threats against British and European shipping, The Telegraph reported on August 17.
The Admiral Kasatonov, a modern Russian frigate capable of long-range strikes and anti-submarine warfare, was spotted last week near Fehmarn, a German island and popular tourist destination in the Baltic.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Telegraph, the frigate was sailing with its location transponder switched off, making its subsequent movements difficult to track. It remained unclear as of August 17 whether the ship was still operating near the island.
Commissioned in 2020, Admiral Kasatonov is considered one of the Russian Navy’s most modern surface combatants. Among its weapons are 3M22 Zircon hypersonic missiles, which Russia says can strike targets at long range and can be equipped with conventional or nuclear warheads.
The Telegraph described the deployment as the latest escalation between Russia and NATO in the Baltic, one of Europe’s most important maritime corridors and an increasingly tense arena for Russian and allied military activity.
Admiral Kasatonov is also the second Russian warship to appear in the Baltic in recent weeks. The destroyer Admiral Levchenko arrived in the region in late July.
The deployments come as Moscow increasingly threatens retaliation over Western actions against Russia’s so-called shadow fleet—a sprawling network of aging tankers and commercial vessels used to move Russian oil and other goods despite international sanctions.
Britain and France have intercepted or seized vessels suspected of operating for Russia in recent months, increasing pressure on the network Moscow relies on to sustain energy exports.
During an inspection of a Russian warship last week, Russian leader Vladimir Putin threatened reciprocal action against British and European vessels if Russia-linked ships were seized.
“It’s nothing but piracy and robbery. If this is done, we will be forced to respond in kind… [Russia can retaliate] in any area where we see it as necessary and appropriate,” Putin said.
He specifically mentioned the Pacific Ocean, a major route for British and European commercial shipping, where Russian officials have also discussed plans to board and inspect vessels.
Former Russian leader and current Security Council deputy chairman Dmitry Medvedev has issued even broader threats.
“Russia has the right to attack any merchant ship belonging to an enemy state, whether in our or neutral waters, if there is sufficient suspicion that it is transporting cargo in the interest of the enemy,” Medvedev said, referring to NATO states supporting Ukraine.
The arrival of the Zircon-armed frigate near Germany adds a military dimension to those threats.
Earlier, reports emerged that British warships and helicopters spent significantly more time tracking Russian naval activity in July as Moscow maintained an elevated presence around UK waters and across the North Atlantic.
Royal Navy patrol ships and aircraft devoted 21 days to monitoring Russian vessels during the month, up 25% from July 2025, according to figures released by the British Navy.

Kushner's visit to Netanyahu deepens Gaza's frustration on deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:17:32 UTC
21:17:32 KST

Breadcrumb
Kushner's visit to Netanyahu deepens Gaza's frustration over deadlocked talks
The lengthy meeting between US envoy Jared Kushner and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday has deepened frustration in Gaza, where Palestinians see negotiations over the ceasefire's next phase as trapped in a cycle of disputes over Hamas's weapons, Israeli withdrawal and promises of reconstruction.
The meeting lasted about eight hours and included Israeli officials and representatives of the so-called "Board of Peace", Israeli media outlets reported.
Netanyahu's office claimed in a press statement that the talks ended with an agreement to establish two working groups, one focusing on the disarmament of Gaza and another on sanitation, water and public health.
While Netanyahu's office described the discussions as "constructive and in-depth", many Palestinians saw little to suggest that the meeting would resolve the issues preventing the transition to the next phase of the supposed ceasefire.
Kushner met a Hamas delegation in Cairo before traveling to Israel. He said Hamas leaders "said all the right things" but emphasised Washington would judge them by their actions, not words.
He said disarmament progress could start in 30 days, with the US aiming for weapon removal and tunnel destruction in 60-90 days. Washington will not allow Gaza to rebuild until disarmament is done, but Israel retains the right to self-defence against perceived threats.
For Gaza residents, such timelines are disconnected from the daily reality of displacement, destroyed homes and shortages of basic necessities.
Reconstruction remains hostage
The central concern for many Palestinians is no longer how Hamas's weapons will be handled, but whether the political process can deliver a permanent end to Israel's violence, remove an Israeli occupation, and begin meaningful reconstruction.
"Kushner's meeting with Netanyahu offered little hope to families still struggling to survive," Radi Abu Afash, a father of six from Gaza City, told The New Arab.
"People in Gaza want to see results on the ground, not another series of statements and promises," he said, adding that his priority was for his children to live safely and have access to food, water and healthcare.
Abu Afash said that Palestinians were following the negotiations with concern because Israeli demands appeared to be dominating the process, while the needs of Gaza's population were pushed aside.
Salah Abu Hasira, who lives in a tent on Gaza City's beach after losing all his brothers and three of his sons, told TNA that the political discussions had become increasingly disconnected from the reality facing Palestinians.
His family, he said, had already paid an enormous price during the war. Any political initiative would mean little unless it brought a tangible improvement to people's lives.
"What Palestinians need now is an end to their suffering, dignified shelter, rebuilt homes and a future for children who have lost their parents and relatives," he added.
He said that the absence of Palestinian voices from high-level discussions reinforced the feeling that decisions about Gaza's future were being made without its residents.
For Samira Ayoub, also from Gaza City, the political debate comes amid the burden of caring for around 15 grandchildren after losing four of her children during the war.
Ayoub told TNA that the loss of her children had transformed her life, leaving her responsible for her grandchildren while living through extremely difficult conditions.
"Gaza's families can no longer endure more waiting," she said. "People who have lost their children, homes and livelihoods need concrete steps to restore security and stability."
"Palestinians wanted more than an agreement on paper: they wanted children to return to school, families to secure food and water, and survivors to rebuild their lives," she added.
A wider crisis
Frustration has grown with each new round of meetings that produces fresh working groups and deadlines without visible changes in Gaza.
Taysir Abdullah, a Gaza-based political analyst, told TNA that the expectations that Hamas would surrender its weapons completely and immediately were unrealistic.
He argued that Hamas could manoeuvre, delay, and adjust its positions but unlikely to take a step that could undermine its political and organisational existence. As an ideological movement deriving strength from its resistance identity, publicly surrendering its weapons could be seen as an admission of defeat.
Abdullah said Hamas might accept a gradual disarmament if conditions protect its political and symbolic standing, such as avoiding footage of weapons handovers, extending the process, and using a non-Israeli or non-American mediator.
He believes Hamas is relying partly on time, Turkish and Qatari political support and possible changes in Israel's political landscape, particularly ahead of elections.
Mustafa Ibrahim, another political analyst, takes a more pessimistic view. He describes the current proposals as "cosmetic concessions" that could restore aspects of daily life in Gaza without addressing the underlying political crisis.
Allowing limited sanitation, water and infrastructure projects, Ibrahim says, could reflect Israel's concern over the humanitarian and health consequences of Gaza's devastation rather than a genuine move towards ending the blockade or occupation.
"The danger is that these concessions become a substitute for a political solution," he added, warning against treating Gaza merely as a humanitarian, health and security problem requiring containment.
Political analyst Esmat Mansour, meanwhile, believes Hamas's acceptance of a disarmament process, regardless of how it is ultimately implemented, represents a significant strategic shift.
He argues that Hamas's adherence to the agreement could serve its interests as the confrontation moves from the military arena to the political and diplomatic one.
With Palestinians lacking sufficient leverage to impose their demands by force, Mansour believes the movement must rely on Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, the United States and international pressure to push Israel towards implementing the agreement.
Israel blocks next phase
Amid the uncertainty, Palestinian factions met in Cairo on Monday, including Hamas, Islamic Jihad, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine and the Democratic Reform Movement.
Hamas said its political bureau chief, Khalil al-Hayya, briefed the factions on meetings with Egyptian officials, mediators and guarantors in El Alamein, as well as subsequent discussions on the roadmap for the second phase of the ceasefire agreement.
The factions noted Israel was obstructing the transition to the second phase, accusing the government of reneging on understandings reached during the first phase and continuing violations.
They also discussed efforts to halt what they described as escalating aggression and prevent Gaza from becoming a casualty of Israel's political and electoral struggles, while accelerating relief, recovery and reconstruction.
Israeli media, citing political sources, reported that Netanyahu insisted during his meeting with Kushner on maintaining the Israeli army's freedom of action in Gaza. The meeting reportedly included the Shin Bet chief and the head of Military Intelligence, who presented what Israel described as evidence of Hamas violations.
Trump, meanwhile, said it would be better if Israel did not attack Gaza again, remarks welcomed by Hamas, which urged the US president to pressure the Israeli government to honour the understandings reached for the second phase.
For Palestinians, however, the contradiction remains stark: Washington is pressing for progress while Israel continues to insist on security conditions and freedom of military action.

Russia Classifies Beer, Wines and Vapes as “Strategic Goods” Under New Law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:17:26 UTC
21:17:26 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Classifies Beer, Wines and Vapes as “Strategic Goods” Under New Law
The Russian government has added light alcoholic beverages—including still and sparkling wines, beer, and ciders—along with electronic cigarettes, vape liquids, and nicotine salts to its list of strategically important goods, as reported by The Moscow Times on August 18.
Under the newly effective updates to Article 226.1 of the Russian Criminal Code, individuals caught bringing these items across the Russian border or the Eurasian Economic Union without proper customs clearance face up to five years in prison if the shipment exceeds 100,000 rubles ($1,100).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Previously, undeclared transport of these specific products was treated as an administrative violation resulting in monetary fines or compulsory labor.
Prior to 2022, criminal charges for illegal alcohol and tobacco transport applied only to shipments worth over 250,000 rubles ($2,750), with prison sentences restricted to cases involving organized crime groups or officials abusing their positions.
Although hard spirits and traditional tobacco were added to the strategic goods list in 2022, other alcoholic drinks and electronic smoking devices were omitted, creating a legal gap that operated for over three years.
Under the new regulations, bringing just two bottles of premium vintage wine or high-end champagne without declaring them can trigger criminal penalties.
Illegal transport of high-value wine in personal luggage has remained common practice, with Federal Customs Service data showing attempted illegal alcohol imports reaching 413.5 million rubles ($4.5 million) last year, up from 266.7 million rubles ($2.9 million) the year prior.
Primary origin points include Georgia, Thailand, Estonia, and Turkey. In one recent incident on August 9, customs officers at Domodedovo Airport discovered 15 bottles of 2021 Sassicaia wine valued at 2 million rubles ($22,000)—roughly 133,000 rubles ($1,460) per bottle—in a flight attendant’s luggage from Vietnam.
The individual faced administrative fines equal to twice the goods' value alongside total confiscation. Legal personal imports into Russia remain strictly limited to five liters of alcohol above 0.5% ABV, with any amount over three liters requiring formal declaration and a duty of 10 euros ($10.80) per excess liter.
Direct exports of European wines priced above 300 euros ($325) are prohibited under international sanction measures, while standard import routes face elevated Russian protective tariffs, recently raised from 20% to 25% with a minimum charge of 2 euros ($2.15) per liter.
Former government economist Oleg Vyugin noted that due to complex transport routes and rising tariffs, "European wines in restaurants cost like an airplane wing," adding that "if you want to drink good wine, you have to spend everything you earned over the last two months, or be an oligarch."
Previously, it was reported that spirits company Bacardi launched full-scale commercial bottling of its Martini brand in Russia, significantly expanding its footprint while boosting revenues.
Its subsidiary, Bacardi Rus LLC, saw its annual revenue increase by 71.45%, rising from approximately $380.5 million in 2021 to $572.6 million in 2025.
Production was handled in Dagestan by Alvisa, which planned to produce approximately 10 million liters of vermouth annually for the Russian market to bypass elevated import duties.

OpenAI launches ChatGPT for Teens with new safety guardrails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:13:35 UTC
21:13:35 KST

The AI company is rolling out age-specific protections for 13- to 17-year-olds, as researchers and parents raise growing concerns over teenagers' emotional reliance on chatbots.
Teenagers, the first generation to grow up with artificial intelligence, are already using ChatGPT for schoolwork, questions about daily life and even companionship. Now OpenAI is launching a version of the chatbot designed specifically for them.
The San Francisco-based company says ChatGPT for Teens, which launches Tuesday, is tailored for those aged 13 to 17 and includes stronger protections including content restrictions around issues such as suicide, self-harm and romantic or sexual chats.
It also provides homework and study support designed to help students learn rather than simply produce answers and school essays for them.
The aim is to guide teenagers toward healthy AI use in an age-appropriate environment, the company said.
"We want to treat teens like teens, which means that we have to make sure that we're showing up with the right developmental stage when we're not either talking down to them or treating them like kids, said Ann O'Leary, vice president of global policy at OpenAI.
"But we're also making sure that they're not exposed to material that they shouldn't be exposed to," she continued.
Risks abound in widespread teen usage of AI chatbots
Parents, educators and child development experts have been sounding alarms over children's use of AI chatbots, which have been blamed for facilitating cheating on schoolwork and even suicide.
Even adults can fall victim to anthropomorphising AI and developing unhealthy relationships with it, but teenagers' brains are not yet fully developed, and they can be particularly vulnerable.
Last year, research from a watchdog group found that ChatGPT would tell 13-year-olds how to get drunk and high, instruct them on how to conceal eating disorders and even compose a heartbreaking suicide letter to their parents if asked.
In interactions with researchers posing as vulnerable teenagers, ChatGPT typically warned against risky activity but went on to deliver startlingly detailed and personalised plans for drug use, calorie-restricted diets or self-injury.
In the US, more than 70% of teenagers are turning to AI chatbots for companionship, and half use AI companions regularly, according to a 2025 study from Common Sense Media, a group that studies and advocates for the sensible use of digital media.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has said the company is trying to study "emotional overreliance" on the technology, describing it last year as a "really common thing" among young people.
For users of ChatGPT for Teens, the chatbot is prevented from suggesting it has personal feelings toward the user or implying that it is conscious or experiences emotions, according to OpenAI.
That is in addition to blocking romantic or sexual chats.
"We went through and identified what are the hypothetical cues that a model could give that might make a teenager kind of develop a relationship to it," said Allison Mishkin, head of child development at OpenAI.
A new version of the chatbot expands safety protections
OpenAI does not verify users' ages, but it already uses age assurance to estimate whether someone is under 18 based on factors such as their types of queries.
If someone is identified, or identifies themselves, as a minor, they are automatically placed into the teen version of the chatbot.
This is similar to Meta's approach to teen accounts on Instagram, which have stricter content, chat and privacy restrictions than regular accounts.
To use parental controls, both the teenage user and their parent or guardian have to opt in.
But O'Leary said the idea behind the teen chatbot is to "make sure that this is safe, even if you don't use parental controls."
Parents with linked teen accounts can set "quiet hours" when their teenager cannot access ChatGPT and receive safety notifications in limited high-risk situations, such as the possibility of a user harming themself.
"We are adding additional notifications related to eating disorders, while limiting what is shared and focusing on moments when offline support may matter most," OpenAI said.
For homework help, OpenAI said the teen chatbot is designed not to give easy answers, but to guide students toward finding answers on their own.
The company already offers a version of ChatGPT for teachers, and tailoring a model to help teenagers with studying and homework could give OpenAI more ways to bring its product into schools.
"We continue to also invest in expanding interactive learning, because research shows that people learn more effectively when they actively engage and struggle with concepts," Mishkin said.

America's Top Venture Capital Firms of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:13:33 UTC
21:13:33 KST

The U.S. venture capital industry is one of the most impressive economic growth engines this country has. Seven of the top ten companies by market capitalization today were VC-backed when they were young, innovative, and very risky. My research with Will Gornall shows that companies that received VC funding and subsequently went public now account for nearly half of the U.S. market capitalization and 94% of R&D spending among all public companies founded in the last 50 years. Today, global VC assets under management stand at nearly $3.5 trillion, spread across more than 11,000 institutional VC firms. Those firms have backed a quarter of a million companies, including almost 4,000 unicorns.
Yet the industry remains shrouded in mystery. Many capital allocators struggle to select fund managers and manage their VC portfolios, and many founders are uncertain which VCs are the best fit for them. In this light, TIME is publishing its second annual ranking of America’s 350 Top Venture Capital Firms.
The 2026 methodology is a weighted average of four factors, some quantitative, others more subjective: fundraising (30%—how much capital the firm attracted over a one- to ten-year span, and the trajectory of that growth); investments (20%—how much capital was put to work, including deal volume); performance (40%—the scale of outcomes, including IPOs and highly valued private companies, along with the consistency of follow-on investments, with early-stage bets weighted more heavily); and leadership (10%—leading rounds and winning board seats).
Each of these four factors is relevant, though how they are combined and measured of course matters and can dramatically affect which firms come out on top. The combined 50% weight given to fundraising and investments by the TIME methodology largely reflects size. Size matters: many investors have minimum check sizes and pass on smaller VC funds, and many funds have grown dramatically in recent years. But capital allocators have yet to see whether greater size delivers similarly attractive returns and profits. Academic work also is not conclusive. A larger firm can underperform on the performance metrics and still score well on sheer scale. Emerging managers who have raised smaller funds, or who are simply young, may lose ground on the size factor. Two caveats deserve mention: deal volume favors firms making a great many bets, and the follow-on measure again rewards firms that invest early and then continue to back their winners. Performance is the critical consideration; at the end of the day, it is the ability to back home runs repeatedly and at scale that separates the greatest VC firms from the rest.
Taken as a whole, the methodology rewards what can be observed from the outside. Capital raised, deals done, and marquee portfolio names are all visible; the money actually returned to limited partners, for the most part, is not. Firms that are big, busy, and prominent will therefore do well, and on the whole they deserve to. But the ranking is best read as a measure of franchise strength rather than of skill per dollar invested.
Every ranking methodology reflects the objectives of its creators. I also co-created a methodology for assessing VC firms, with an emphasis on the economically relevant portions of the net profits generated by individual VCs’ investments. What the two lists agree on is as informative as where they part. Both put the same handful of firms, which have been prominent for a decade or more, at the very top; firms such as Sequoia, a16z, and Lightspeed. That agreement is real: the elite of the American VC industry is very select, relatively stable, and well capitalized. Below that, of the roughly 110 firms in TIME's top 200 that do not appear in ours, only fifteen are ones we rule out by definition: accelerators such as Plug and Play, angel networks, corporate vehicles, asset managers. We include some VC firms that are ineligible for TIME’s ranking (Meritech, Dragoneer, Addition, and Inflection Ventures all place in our top 100). We agree on the other firms: we simply score them lower. In other words, the industry has reached consensus on its top performers but not on the tier beneath it. For a founder or an allocator, that is the practical lesson: past the first twenty names, "top firm" is a claim about which yardstick you picked.
What our rankings make plain is that VC no longer has clean edges. Capital comes from crossover funds, sovereign investors, corporations, and firms that would not have called themselves VC a decade ago, while the earliest support often comes from accelerators, angel networks, and solo investors. A list of top American VC firms is a useful map of the industry's core. The interesting question is how much of the action has moved to its edges.
See TIME's full ranking of America's Top Venture Capital Firms of 2026 below.

Why Europe will be the biggest loser as Türkiye ‘de-prioritises’ EU membership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:13:17 UTC
21:13:17 KST

When Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan recently said that seeking membership of the European Union was no longer a priority, it marked a striking shift in Ankara’s views on the political and economic group of 27 countries.
Over the years, Türkiye had framed EU membership as a strategic goal throughout on-again, off-again accession talks.
In unusually blunt comments, Erdogan said that Europe did not appear willing to admit Türkiye, and pointed out that it was EU, not Ankara, that would be the loser as a result of this rebuff.
Joining the EU gives a country enhanced market access and visa-free travel and work opportunities across member nations.
But Brussels has been dragging its feet over Ankara’s accession on frivolous grounds for more than two decades, even though Türkiye is one of the biggest economic and military powers in Europe.
Experts say that Erdogan’s statement about the de-prioritisation of EU membership is grounded in facts rather than rhetoric.
Ankara’s policy shift represents a rational response to two decades of EU double standards, they say. As a result, Europe stands to lose more from the de-prioritisation than Türkiye itself, they note.
Ali Murat Kursun, assistant professor at the Department of International Relations at Marmara University in Istanbul, says that Ankara’s decision is “highly rational and structural” rather than an emotional reaction.
“At the core of this rupture lie the chronic double standards directed at Türkiye,” he tells TRT World.
He says the EU never treated Türkiye as a peer. Instead, it sought to position the country “beneath its own hierarchy, treating it as a peripheral state” to which it could outsource Europe’s security and migration policies.
Over the same period, however, Türkiye built substantial military, diplomatic and technological capacities and achieved “tremendous strategic autonomy”.
For a country that has created “its own centre of gravity in the new multipolar global system”, the EU’s patronising relationship towards Türkiye became “inherently unsustainable”, Kursun says.
The EU’s failure to offer unconditional support during Türkiye’s confrontations with terror groups, such as the PKK, YPG, and FETO, further eroded that trust, he says.
When Ankara pursued its own priorities – in Syria, the Eastern Mediterranean or on the Palestinian issue – the EU often viewed these steps as competition rather than contributions to regional stability.
Türkiye found an “exclusionary club” before it, rather than a rational integration actor, he says.
“President Erdogan's statement is, in fact, the official and highest-level declaration of this de facto reality,” Kursun says.
Not merely a ‘technical process’
According to Muhammed Ali Ucar, foreign affairs expert and chairman of the Vienna-based PLUS Institute, Türkiye’s sustained efforts to get EU membership only encountered “shifting conditions, new political obstacles and moving goalposts”.
A fundamental problem arose when Ankara began to realise that fulfilling the criteria would not necessarily lead to EU membership.
“Conditionality can only work when the candidate believes that meeting the conditions will eventually produce the promised outcome,” he tells TRT World.
The issue of Greek-administered Cyprus stands out as particularly consequential for Ankara’s EU membership.
The EU admitted Greek-administered Cyprus, even though the island remained divided between Greek and Turkish Cypriots.
It created an “extraordinary political exception to its own enlargement logic”, says Ucar.
In the 2004 Annan Plan referenda, a clear majority of Turkish Cypriots supported settlement, while Greek Cypriots rejected it. Yet, the side that rejected the settlement gained EU membership and institutional leverage, Ucar notes.
In addition, repeated questioning of Türkiye’s ultimate membership by leaders in Germany and France and the floating of a “privileged partnership” alternative refuted the idea that accession was a technical process based on objective criteria.
Visa restrictions and the increasingly transactional character of relations around migration further weakened public enthusiasm, he says.
“Türkiye did not simply abandon Europe. Rather, the credibility of the accession mechanism gradually eroded,” he says.
Ankara charted its own path independently
Analysts say that Türkiye’s economic and geopolitical influence has expanded largely independently of the EU accession process.
Had Ankara confined itself to the EU’s bureaucratic boundaries, it would never have attained its current strategic autonomy, Kursun says.
Türkiye has developed an “agile, multidimensional diplomatic posture” in Libya, Syria, the South Caucasus, the Eastern Mediterranean, the Gulf, the Horn of Africa, and across Eurasia, he says.
Meanwhile, the EU has become increasingly paralysed by internal vetoes and maximalist member demands.
“European defence restrictions and arms embargoes backfired, compelling Türkiye to build a world-class indigenous defence industry that now drives its geopolitical influence across multiple continents,” Kursun says.
Economically, geographical diversification reduced Türkiye’s vulnerability to single-market shocks, while major pipeline networks and connectivity projects positioned the country as an indispensable Eurasian energy and transit hub, he notes.
Ucar says today’s Türkiye is “considerably different” from the one that began negotiations in 2005.
That’s because its diplomatic reach, infrastructure, defence industry and capacity for autonomous foreign policy have expanded substantially over the last two decades.
But strategic autonomy should not be confused with separation from Europe, he insists.
Türkiye’s deeper ties with the Gulf, Africa or Central Asia need not come at Europe’s expense.
“A stronger and more autonomous Türkiye can ultimately be a more valuable partner for Europe,” Ucar says.
Who is the net loser?
Erdogan’s assertion that the EU is the net loser for dilly-dallying on the accession issue resonates strongly with both analysts.
Kursun says that the EU has traded its own geopolitical relevance for internal bureaucratic comfort.
Europe faces high-intensity conventional warfare to its east and chronic instability to its south. Yet, it lacks the integrated military capacity and autonomy to manage these challenges effectively, especially under a reduced US security umbrella, he says.
In contrast, Türkiye possesses a battle-tested military, a booming defence industry, and the political will to project power – without which, Europe will become “highly exposed”.
In energy, Türkiye has become the indispensable transit hub for diversification after Europe cut off ties with Russia. On migration, Türkiye’s role as a geopolitical buffer protects Europe’s societal resilience, Kursun says.
“By alienating Türkiye, the EU did not isolate Türkiye. It isolated itself from the geopolitical realities of its own neighbourhood,” Kursun says.
Ucar interprets Erdogan’s statement as an argument about Europe’s opportunity cost.
The relationship remains interdependent, but Europe’s changing environment has increased Türkiye’s strategic value, he says.
Issues relating to security, energy, and migration illustrate mutual dependence, even though the asymmetry between Ankara and Brussels has widened.
“By keeping Türkiye permanently at arm’s length, Europe is not only denying Türkiye something. It may also be depriving itself of an important strategic asset,” Ucar says.

Veteran Italian film producer Fulvio Lucisano dies at 98
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
12:11:49 UTC
21:11:49 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
18 August 2026•Update: 18 August 2026
Veteran Italian film producer Fulvio Lucisano has died at the age of 98, Italian media reported Tuesday.
His daughter Paola confirmed his death on social media, writing, “Rest in peace, Dad,” according to Italian news agency ANSA.
Born in Rome in 1928, Lucisano began his career in the late 1940s at Istituto Luce, where he worked in documentary production.
He founded Italian International Film in 1958 and went on to become one of the leading figures in Italian cinema, producing more than 130 films over a career spanning more than seven decades.
His productions included Ricomincio da tre (I'm Starting from Three), Il grande cocomero (The Great Pumpkin), Fantozzi - Il ritorno, and Notte prima degli esami (Night Before the Exams).
Lucisano worked with several prominent names in Italian cinema, including Lina Wertmuller, Luigi Comencini, Alberto Sordi, Mario Bava, and Massimo Troisi.
He also served as president of Italy's national film industry association ANICA from 1998 to 2001.
During his career, Lucisano received five David di Donatello awards, including a lifetime achievement honor in 2009, as well as four Nastri d'Argento awards.
Italian Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli hailed Lucisano as “one of the great architects of Italian cinema,” praising his passion, intuition, and ability to recognize talent.

Harness-racing legend Varenne dies
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
14:07:56 CEST
21:07:56 KST

Varenne, the greatest harness-racer of all time, has died. The news, which is spreading on social media and the media, was confirmed to ANSA by the historic driver of the 'Captain', who celebrated his 31st birthday in May at the LJ stud farm in Eboli.
The trotter went to stud in 2004 after a glittering five-year career, and earned in the neighborhood of five million 
 
 Varenne was without a doubt the greatest trotter Italy has ever produced and some would argue the best the world has ever seen. 
 
He won 62 of the 73 races he ran in, raking in 6.3 million euro in prize money.
 
Varenne's final season was also a near-perfect one having won 13 races out of 14 races and setting new track records in six of them.
 
Varenne was born in Ferrara on May 19, 1995. He was the son of Waikiki Beach and Jalmaz and was named after the street in Paris where the Italian embassy is located.
 
The trotter quickly earned the nickname 'Il Capitano' (The Captain) for his commanding racing style.
 
He was bought in 1998 by enterprising Neapolitan stockbroker Enzo Giordano for 92,000 euro. 
 
Two years later, after emerging as a money-spinning phenomenon, Italian bookies' organisation SNAI paid almost 20 times that figure for a 50% share in the horse.
 
Varenne won the prestigious Prix D'Amerique three times and Italy's premier event, the Gran Premio Lotteria di Agnano, for three years.
 
His 2001 victory in America's Breeder's Crown, the richest harness-racing event in the world, was the first by an Italian horse in 24 years and netted his owners half a million dollars.
 
Varenne was valued at about 7.5 billion euro at the end of his career.
 
An example of the trotter's immense popularity came when a man from a town just outside Naples named his newly born son Varenne and refused to be budged despite threats of legal action from his wife.

Germany opens drone technology center for detection, neutralization tests

Germany on Tuesday opened a new drone technology center that will serve as a hub for developing advanced systems, testing the safe operation of drones, and detecting and neutralizing hostile unmanned aerial vehicles.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters at the opening ceremony at the eastern airfield of Cochstedt that the facility will research innovative technologies and drone security. He described the new center as one of the core components of Germany’s three-pillar strategy to counter unwanted or dangerous drones.
“We are seeing how they (foreign powers) are trying to harm us with drones, attempting to damage the most vulnerable points of our infrastructure — not just at airports, but also at other infrastructure sites,” Dobrindt said, referring to recent drone sightings at airports, military sites and energy facilities across Germany.
“Such scenarios can arise anywhere. That is why we must strengthen both our stationary drone defense systems at critical points and, above all, our mobile units, ensuring they can be deployed across Germany,” he said. The new technology center in Cochstedt, he added, will play a vital role in Germany’s drone security and defense, significantly bolstering the country’s capabilities and overall security architecture.
The conservative minister reiterated that Germany is a prime target of hybrid warfare, as hostile powers seek to undermine Europe’s political and economic stability by targeting the country. He added that authorities are stepping up efforts to counter these threats.
“We are the daily target of hybrid attacks — specifically as Germany — because we are a central pillar in the heart of Europe when it comes to economic, political, social and security stability across the continent,” he said.
“We fulfill a pivotal role, and that is precisely why we are a prime target for hybrid attacks. To target Germany is to strike at all of Europe. That is the calculation behind espionage, sabotage, destabilization attempts by foreign powers.”

Center Party backs Tiit Land for Estonia's presidency
At the joint meeting of the Center Party's board and its Riigikogu faction, it was decided to support the candidacy of Tallinn University of Technology rector Tiit Land in the presidential election.
The decision to support Land was not unanimous, because there were also supporters of Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise. "So we have two strong candidates, and we expect a substantive debate," said Center Party chairman Mihhail Kõlvart.
Kõlvart did not answer how the votes within the Center Party will be divided on September 2 election day. He said that the votes will come from the entire faction. "We proceed from the assumption that Tiit Land is our candidate in the Riigikogu and that he could become a dignified president," he said.
Kõlvart did also not say whether the Center Party would nominate Land in the second round of voting if necessary. He stated that Madise received many signatures, and in order for competition to emerge, support is needed for Land as well. "This is also one of the reasons why we are ready to support him," Kõlvart noted.
According to Kõlvart, Estonia needs a president who can unite society, stand up for Estonia's interests, and act in a politically independent manner.
"Tiit Land's strengths are his academic and international background as well as his long leadership experience. These qualities have brought recognition and public support also to the current president, Alar Karis," Kõlvart said. "I consider Tiit Land's political neutrality very important. The president should not be the representative of one party or political force, but the president of all Estonia."
The Center Party considers it important that real presidential elections take place, not the appointment of a head of state, and therefore the presence of at least two candidates is necessary from the standpoint of democracy, Kõlvart added.
"The meeting with Tiit Land showed that he is a person who can approach complex questions substantively and pragmatically. We talked about various topics important for Estonia — energy, demography, education, the economy and international relations. Tiit Land's readiness to discuss these issues in depth left a very good impression. He does not seek ideological confrontation, but solutions," the Center Party chairman said.
According to Kõlvart, one of the most important tasks of the next president will be to restore trust in Estonian society and to be a unifier of different worldviews and social groups. "Estonian society has in recent years become increasingly polarized. We need a president who can listen to different people, look for common ground, and bring to the same table even those whose views differ greatly. Tiit Land has the prerequisites for this," he noted.
Kõlvart said that Tiit Land's long experience in leading universities gives him good preparation for standing up for Estonia's science, education and innovation. "Estonia's competitiveness depends greatly on whether we can be innovative, educated and open to new solutions. Tiit Land understands these issues deeply, and as president he could be a strong advocate for these fields," Kõlvart said.
The Center Party's faction has seven MPs in the Riigikogu, and in addition they can count on Peeter Ernits, making a total of eight MPs. To nominate a presidential candidate, at least 21 MPs' support signatures are required. This means that to nominate Land, the Center Party would need support from Isamaa (eight in the faction, but 11 MPs in total) as well as from at least two independents.
Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise had 63 signatures as of Tuesday.
