100-SPECIES GREENHOUSE REDEFINES HOSPITALITY ON GEORGIA’S COAST
Located in Shekvetili along Georgia’s Black Sea coast, Hecate’s Garden opens as a distinct culinary destination set within an expansive glasshouse. Inspired by ancient Colchian mythology and Medea — priestess of Hecate credited with planting the world’s first botanical garden — the venue pairs an active greenhouse with an immersive dining environment. Designed to be touched, tasted, and explored, the space features nearly 100 plant varieties that directly feed the venue’s kitchen and bar. Here, guests can stroll through living flora, select live plants to take home, and taste fresh ingredients harvested on site, weaving the interactive garden directly into the dining journey.
Hecate’s Garden pairs an active greenhouse with a narrative-driven dining environment | all images courtesy of Hecate’s Garden
A COLLABORATION ON TACTILE BOTANICAL ARCHITECTURE
Realized within the ecosystem of — the country’s leader in live entertainment — Hecate’s Garden sets out to position Georgia’s ancient heritage on the global design stage. To bring this narrative into physical form, the project joined forces with Belgian design firm SEMPRE Design Build. Grounded in a material-first approach, Sempre paired natural materials, raw textures, and dense foliage to echo ancient Colchian visual forms. The interior atmosphere highlights organic shapes and artisanal details, establishing a continuous dialogue between the coastal landscape, contemporary interior design, and growing flora.
Belgian design firm SEMPRE Design Build incorporated natural materials, raw textures, and dense foliage to echo ancient Colchian visual culture
CONNECTING FLORA, CUSTOM CRAFTSMANSHIP, AND LOCAL GASTRONOMY
Considering that the mythical Kingdom of Colchis once spanned what is now western Georgia, Medea holds profound cultural resonance for the region. As a priestess of Hecate — the ancient goddess of nature, plants, thresholds, and transformation — Medea is mythologically celebrated as the cultivator of the world’s first botanical garden, from whose pioneering plant-healing traditions the word medicine itself is derived. This botanical legacy comes alive within a special dedicated nook filled with botanical references, plant studies, and historical references. The curated retail space presents custom teas, botanical candles, and specialized objects created specifically for the site.
Moving deeper into the greenhouse, mythology transforms into tangible design and modern craftsmanship. At the center stands a bespoke table adorned with individually hand-painted ceramic tiles, reinterpreting reconstructed ancient Colchian ornamental motifs through a contemporary lens. Here, surrounded by nearly 100 living plant species, guests can choose live botanical specimens to take home, extending the spatial experience beyond the site itself. Grounding the multi-sensory offering, the beverage program features regional wines from Guria, connecting the modern glasshouse to Georgia’s 8,000-year-old winemaking tradition and offering a fresh model for narrative-driven hospitality.

Can AI Help Us Connect With the Real World?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

By now, everyone is accustomed to the idea that technology has disconnected us from the world and one another. By design, smartphones, apps, and social media lure us in and capture our attention. These technologies consume as much of our time as we allow them. Technology has normalized taking our work home with us, answering emails and messages at all hours of the day. Teenagers and the elderly alike scroll infinitely, if on different platforms.
This situation is often lamented for its connection to addiction, disinformation, radicalization, and social disharmony—among other concerns. But as a technology critic who has written about toasters and slippers in addition to smartphones and the internet, I see another, more widespread effect of technological disconnection: It has robbed people of the small acts and moments of connection to the real, physical world.
No doubt, AI threatens to exacerbate this disconnection. But I would argue that AI also has the potential to offer a solution—to help people look away from their screens and reconnect with the physical world. It may sound ironic, but what if AI could make us more gratified?
Today, you don’t tear a paper towel from the airport restroom; you wave your hand under it hoping the thing will see you. You don’t feel the texture and narrow shape of the concert tickets in your pocket or hand; you scan a QR code instead. A consequence of this process of dematerialization is a loss of gratification—my name for the sensory enchantment of everyday life. All those tiny acts don’t always seem important, but they add up, offering an easy path to contentment.
Generative AI is also having a dematerializing effect on contemporary life. Services such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini promise to take over even more of daily life, replacing work and home tasks with automated, almost magical efficiency. Now even writing emails might be automated—and your recipient might automate reading them, too.
As a writer, a university professor, artist, and designer, I worry about the risk that generative AI might destroy the delightful, human experience of carrying out acts of creation, not to mention making careers in the pursuit of that creativity unviable. Whether or not AI will improve work or destroy jobs, it already distances people from some of the moment-to-moment acts that might have felt gratifying just a few years ago. If AI can write your emails, then you don’t need to feel the click of keys under your fingertips or hear the clack they produce when you type with them. If AI can generate a gift list for the holidays or a vacation plan for Spring Break, then you don’t need to swipe through catalogs or thumb through guidebooks. In this way, AI can amplify the same dematerializing effects of technology people have encountered for years.
But that’s not the whole story. As critical of AI as I sometimes am, I have also found that AI can direct people back toward the physical world and the gratifying feelings it offers. LLMs can be quite adept at helping people figure out how to plan and carry out real-world tasks, such as fixing a plumbing leak, repairing a car, or learning a new hobby.
Over the past year, I’ve found myself surprisingly delighted by how effective Claude or ChatGPT can be at synthesizing and explaining problems I have encountered in my ordinary life. Earlier this spring, a wayward sprinkler technician identified—but did not fix—a leak in my irrigation backflow, a mysterious mechanism meant to prevent contaminated outdoor water from mixing with indoor taps. The weather was getting hot, and I worried for my lawn’s fate. After feeding it a couple photographs of the device, ChatGPT was able to identify the model, the parts it needed, and the steps to attempt a repair—at least one good enough until I could get a licensed professional out to permanently fix and certify it. Unlike message boards or YouTube videos, AI was able to home in on the specifics of a situation (I used it again on a surprisingly complicated broken oven thermostat) and point me back toward particular parts, manuals, and guidelines.
Of course, AI services don’t always get the facts right, but they do strive to provide answers instead of luring people deeper into the attention-sink of social media. In this way, they have the potential to actually push people away from screens and back into the world. For example, AI-driven advice about diet or fitness can help people focus on those non-computer activities with greater purpose, inviting them to focus on what they are doing away from the machine instead of on it. Plus, AI’s efficiency and adeptness at processing information—such as a photo of a broken part—may also have the potential to reduce the distraction of smartphone life, inviting people to use it briefly and purposely and then return to their bodily, sensory life with other people and different apparatuses.
The future of AI is still murky and uncertain. It still risks devolving into more of the same, especially if AI services start using the same advertising- and attention-driven business models that cursed earlier internet technologies. But a path still exists for AI to repair some of the public’s lost physical connectivity with the world outside their phones, and to recapture some of the gratification lost from that era.

Is the World Getting Uglier?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

A few blocks from where I live, a quaint, mid-size home was recently razed and replaced by a house that seems to have eaten its own property. It stretches from one edge of the lot to the other, with barely enough room around it to suggest that land ever existed there before. It is large in the way so many new houses are large now: swollen, as though every available inch has been converted into interior space.
I have begun noticing the same impulse everywhere: things are getting bigger, louder and more visually insistent, as though occupying more space has itself become a form of value.
Cars have become taller, wider, and more aggressive, with grilles that look more weaponized than designed. The Tesla Cybertruck seems to have taken that impulse to the extreme: it is a vehicle so visually belligerent it appears constructed to win an argument no one knew they were having. In fashion, the appetite for exaggeration has taken a more deliberate form, as Gen Z embraces enormous silhouettes and awkward proportions that would have horrified generations raised to believe that looking “put together” was a virtue or a goal.
I have found myself wondering: Is the world getting uglier?
I know that suggesting something is ugly is deeply subjective, and every generation has looked at the one before it and wondered what they could possibly be thinking. Tastes evolve, standards change, and beauty is inherently vulnerable to nostalgia. But I don’t think what I am seeing is simply a matter of taste. I think it has more to do with proportion.
Good design relies on understanding context: how a building sits on its street, how a chair accommodates a body, how type works on the page and for the reader. What I am noticing now is how often these considerations seem to disappear, as if the object itself matters more than the environment or community it belongs to.
This matters because we are living in an attention economy, and attention rewards extremity. The more a design is rewarded for being instantly visible, recognizable, and shareable, the easier it becomes to lose sight of proportion, purpose, and the people who have to live alongside it. A house that dominates its lot, a cartoonishly oversized shoe, or a restaurant interior conceived to be posted online before the food arrives are all responding, in different ways, to the same pressure: to attract attention first and consider the consequences after.
Perhaps this is why so much contemporary design feels more bloviating than expressive, as though visual volume now matters more than beauty.
But the problem is not ugliness itself. Sometimes ugliness is the point.
In 1996, Miuccia Prada launched a spring collection titled Banal Eccentricity, which became better known as “Ugly Chic.” The line’s muddy browns, avocado greens and awkward proportions were intentional and used with precision to challenge more conventional ideas of beauty.
That lineage allows me to understand some of what I see in Gen Z fashion now. Oversized, mismatched clothes and deliberately awkward shoes can be knowing and self-aware; the person wearing the ugly shoe may know perfectly well that it is ugly, and that may be part of the pleasure. Fashion is also temporary. You can wear MSCHF’s enormous red boots today and take them off tonight.
A building is much harder to discard.
Years ago, in an interview I conducted with the Italian designer Massimo Vignelli, he declared that design’s responsibility was “to decrease the amount of vulgarity in the world.” He was explicit that he was not prescribing a style; what mattered was creating quality in everything that surrounds us.
The distinction between ugliness and vulgarity feels important now. Beauty often depends on proportion and on how well a building, an object, or an image relates to the world around it. Ugliness can challenge expectations and still be intelligent, deliberate, and even beautiful in its own way.
Vulgarity is different. It begins when scale, excess, or attention-seeking overwhelms context altogether.
Architecture, automobiles, and commercial environments make claims on people who have no part in choosing them. When houses squeeze into their lots, vehicles grow more imposing, and storefronts battle for attention, the problem is no longer simply whether something is beautiful or ugly. Vulgarity becomes consequential when it overwhelms the environment everyone shares.
The objects we design and consume reveal what we value, and more and more of them seem to reflect an increased appetite for more. Which leaves me wondering about one of design’s oldest and most human questions: How much is enough?

Press review: Iran war strains US global reach as Washington revives Gaza settlement talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, August 18. /TASS/. The US is scaling back its presence around the world, focusing its forces near Iran; Washington has resumed talks on Gaza; and Europe has run out of new options for an original sanctions package against Russia. These stories topped Tuesday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Vedomosti: How war with Iran reduces US presence around globe
The US is significantly reducing its participation in joint annual military exercises with South Korea, as they are costly and hinder the normalization of dialogue with North Korea, US President Donald Trump stated on August 17. He emphasized that one of the factors influencing his decision was his "very good relationship" with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Meanwhile, the US continues to bolster its military presence near Iran.
According to political scientist and US affairs expert Malek Dudakov, the reduction in joint exercises reflects a growing crisis in relations between Washington and Seoul. "We have been observing these crisis developments for more than a month now, but they are now reaching a point that is obvious to everyone," the expert told Vedomosti. He cited disagreements over South Korea’s promised investments in the US economy as one of the reasons: Seoul had previously announced plans to invest $350 billion. However, according to Dudakov, these plans were never carried out.
Another point of contention remains the cost of the US military presence. South Korea currently pays Washington about $1 billion a year, while Trump, according to Dudakov’s assessment, is insisting on increasing the amount to $3-5 billion. "So far, no agreement has been reached, and the issue remains unresolved," the expert pointed out.
The White House’s decision may also have been influenced by the Iranian factor, he stressed. US allies are in no hurry to support Washington in its actions against Iran, and American resources, including Patriot missile systems, are being shifted from Asia to the Middle East. Against this backdrop, "the Americans are gradually scaling back their military involvement on the Korean Peninsula," which the world may perceive as a sign of a declining US position, Dudakov emphasized.
The reduction in joint exercises with South Korea may reflect the US desire to restart negotiations with North Korea, Pavel Koshkin, a senior researcher at the US and Canadian Studies Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, said. According to the expert, this would signify a continuation of the diplomatic track that Trump attempted to establish during his first presidential term. At the same time, the US leader may have been reacting to Seoul’s refusal to support Washington in a military operation against Iran. "Trump is simply giving them a taste of their own medicine," Koshkin pointed out. He also noted that the US president is currently focused on the Middle East and does not want to "spread himself too thin" with military exercises until the Iranian issue is resolved. According to Trump, this approach fits into a broader policy of scaling back the US presence in lower-priority regions, the expert concluded.
Izvestia: US resumes Gaza settlement process
The situation in the Gaza Strip has gained new momentum: the US has reentered negotiations to promote the implementation of the second phase of the settlement. US special envoy Jared Kushner has coordinated efforts with all parties to the conflict. The process is underway, but achieving the complete disarmament of Hamas has not yet been achieved, and until then, Tel Aviv will not make concessions on the issue of troop withdrawal. Experts emphasize that achieving long-term peace in the Middle East is currently impossible: Washington is only attempting to settle the situation in the Gaza Strip, while completely ignoring the problem in the West Bank.
First and foremost, the parties disagree on the sequence of steps toward a settlement. Washington proposes withdrawing Israeli troops alongside the disarmament of Hamas. However, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insists that not a single soldier will leave the region until the Palestinian group’s arsenals have been completely destroyed. The new round of talks has not settled the issue. "Negotiations on the second phase are ongoing, but the main issue remains unresolved: Israel demands the actual disarmament of Hamas before any troop withdrawal," Netanyahu’s adviser Dmitry Gendelman told Izvestia. "No retreat from the ‘yellow line’ is anticipated or will occur until Hamas is genuinely disarmed," he noted.
However, the Gaza issue is not the only reason for Kushner’s visit to Israel, Konstantin Blokhin, a leading researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Center for Security Studies, stressed.
The parties will also discuss the confrontation with Iran. Trump cannot withdraw from the conflict without new agreements: the Republican politician was rash enough to publicly call ex-president Barack Obama’s previous nuclear deal the worst in history. As a result, the US administration has backed itself into a corner: Trump needs to conclude a new agreement with Tehran on more favorable terms. To do so, the White House needs the support of key Middle Eastern states, but Washington cannot fully rely on that support due to the unresolved crisis in Gaza, the expert stressed.
Meanwhile, the US congressional elections are drawing near, and there is nothing to show voters on the Middle East front. Any unfulfilled promises by the US leader, including a settlement in the enclave, will seriously hurt the Republican Party. In this regard, there is a slight chance of a "Trump-style" deal on Gaza, international relations expert Yelena Suponina pointed out. This would involve signing a framework document with general wording, which would be presented as a solid agreement but would not be implemented in practice and would lead to a new escalation. At the same time, a long-term peace agreement between Israel and Hamas is not to be expected. The problem is not being addressed at its core, since the current negotiations concern only the Gaza Strip, which constitutes only a small portion of the territory designated for a Palestinian state, the expert emphasized.
Izvestia: Europe exhausts new and original means of exerting pressure on Russia
The EU has exhausted all its options for exerting pressure on Russia. As a result, the most extensive expansion of sanctions lists since the start of the conflict in Ukraine is now underway. The draft of the 22nd sanctions package is scheduled to be unveiled in September. Ireland, which currently holds the EU Council presidency, hopes to adopt the package at the earliest opportunity. The bloc may step up pressure on the banking sector and maritime transport. In any case, Russia will adapt to the new restrictions.
Meanwhile, Western diplomats acknowledge that the list of sectors where new restrictions can be imposed is becoming shorter. In July, European media outlets reported, citing sources, that the EU had identified the "last potential areas" for new sanctions. Moreover, the adoption of new packages continues to face significant disagreements. However, the EU has fewer and fewer avenues for new restrictions. Simply expanding the sanctions lists no longer has a significant effect, Russian International Affairs Council program coordinator Polina Chupriyanova told Izvestia.
At the same time, the expert noted the EU still has some opportunities to exert pressure on Russia’s foreign trade and financial infrastructure. Restrictions could be expanded to cover regional financial institutions. Another area of focus is maritime transport. In the 21st sanctions package, the EU authorized the sale of confiscated Russian oil. It is unclear how this measure will work in practice, but it could ease the EU’s future tasks, Chupriyanova added.
The Russian president, however, warned that if such actions are taken, Moscow may respond and detain European vessels wherever it deems necessary. "Fears regarding potential incidents at sea are certainly justified, especially since the EU is stepping up its efforts to combat the so-called Russian shadow fleet," European Parliament member Diana Sosoaca stressed.
Ultimately, the new restrictions are unlikely to significantly alter the situation. In the case of maritime transport, they may at best make exports more expensive and more difficult, but they will not stop them entirely. The new measures against banks will also force Russian companies to use more lengthy chains of intermediaries. On the other hand, they will likely speed up the creation of alternative and independent payment channels.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Why shipping costs are rising and how Russia is seeking alternatives
Shipping costs along major maritime routes around the world have risen significantly due to the conflict in the Middle East and droughts in several countries. Experts believe that, like other countries, Russia will not be able to avoid the associated challenges but will be able to swiftly switch to alternative logistics routes.
"The cost of maritime shipping is rising because it reflects the risks posed by the choke points that currently exist in international trade flows," economic research expert Alexander Abramov told Rossiyskaya Gazeta. In this case, choke points are routes through the Panama Canal, the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea, and other passages.
The expert explained that ocean freight rates may include a surcharge for increased risk if armed conflicts break out at sea. Of course, in this case, the cost of transporting cargo will rise. "Yes, and Russian companies will pay a little more for shipping goods via dangerous routes or using alternative ones," Abramov noted.
The greatest challenge for Russia is not the higher tariffs but the EU’s sanctions that limit transit capacity. For example, tensions periodically arise between the EU and Russia over ship inspections. This creates difficulties in exporting Russian oil, grain, and other products through the Black Sea to the Mediterranean Sea. The expert stressed that transit capacity through the Baltic Sea is also partly limited for Russia. "On the other hand, new opportunities are emerging. These include, for example, growing demand for the Northern Sea Route," Abramov pointed out.
Other countries can also identify alternative shipping routes. Therefore, although the rising cost of transportation is an important factor, it is not a decisive one in terms of prices for fuel and other key commodities, the source concluded.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Future of Moroccan migrants stuck in Spain’s Ceuta
Officials in Madrid and Brussels are doing their utmost to resolve the crisis that arose in late July, when tens of thousands of Moroccans breached the Spanish and EU border near the city of Ceuta. The undocumented migrants who remained in this Spanish enclave in North Africa staged a protest. Their main demand is to be granted asylum instead of being deported to Morocco.
The migrants’ dreams of a more comfortable life will be shattered by the harsh reality: neither Spain nor Europe is ready to accept them. Meanwhile, the Spanish and EU authorities will have to decide what to do with the thousands of undocumented migrants still remaining in the city.
"The Spanish government is the most left-wing in all of Europe. It makes decisions based not only on economic expediency but also under the influence of ideological factors. [Prime Minister Pedro] Sanchez and his cabinet have a somewhat different approach to addressing the migration problem as a whole than most Western European governments," Yekaterina Cherkasova, a senior researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ World Economy and International Relations Institute, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta.
According to the expert, Spain posted the highest economic growth rate among all OECD (Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development) countries last year. "Sanchez believes that achieving such growth rates is impossible without attracting foreign labor," Cherkasova emphasized.
The expert pointed out that undocumented migrants from the enclave were not removed by police. Most of them left of their own accord. Ceuta is a very small territory with a population of about 80,000. After the influx, the number of people there nearly doubled. "The migrants had nothing to eat or drink and nowhere to sleep. They found that conditions in Ceuta were even worse than those they were trying to flee from," the analyst stressed.
"The Spanish government will have to deal with the aftermath of the crisis. Ceuta is unable to resolve them on its own and has already requested financial assistance from Madrid. And Madrid, in turn, will ask Brussels for funding," Cherkasova noted. Spain can count on EU assistance on the grounds that the remaining migrants are interested in settling in other European countries. They view Spain not as the final destination of their journey, but as a transit country on the way to Germany, Sweden, and other countries with more favorable reception conditions. "There are no camps in Ceuta that could accommodate such a large number of people. This means there is a possibility that the undocumented migrants will still have to be transported to the mainland and accommodated somewhere there," Cherkasova concluded.

The Cop Who Took On Flock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

On an early fall afternoon in 2023, midway through a shift in Pawtucket’s District Five, Rhode Island police officer Noel Pichardo noticed a strange camera perched on a utility pole over West Avenue.
Pichardo was 28, five years into the job, and alone in his cruiser during one of the brief lulls between responding to the typical churn of radio calls for domestic disputes, petty disturbances, and welfare checks. The camera was compact and solar-powered, angled down toward passing traffic. Pichardo made a U-turn and drove beneath it again, more slowly this time, to get a better look.
He then began searching for the cameras on roads near highway ramps, at major intersections, along the routes into and out of the city. He found them again and again. By the time Pichardo finished circling the district, he knew exactly where he had seen them before.
Two years earlier, officers had gathered on the second floor of a small police substation in Pawtucket for a presentation about a surveillance system made by Flock Safety. A high-ranking police official stood in front of a PowerPoint and explained that the company’s automatic license plate readers could identify passing vehicles not only by their license plates but by bumper stickers, roof racks, and other distinguishing features. Investigators could search for a particular car across jurisdictions and, camera by camera, reconstruct where it had been.
The system was presented as another tool of routine police work, a way to recover stolen cars, locate suspects, and find missing people. But as Pichardo listened, he found himself thinking less about the vehicles police wanted than about all the others. In a medium-size city like Pawtucket, where a handful of roads carried people nearly everywhere they needed to go, a record of a car’s movements amounted to a record of a person’s life—the places they visited, the people they saw, the routines they followed.
As Pichardo understood it, the Flock proposal had gone nowhere because the city could not afford a permanent installation. So he let it slip from his mind.
But now, on that afternoon on West Avenue, the cameras were all over his district.
Pawtucket’s cameras are one small piece of a sprawling vehicle-surveillance system that touches nearly every state in the country. Flock markets its platform as the nation’s largest fixed license-plate-reader network, processing billions of sightings each month. Because departments can open their records to agencies elsewhere, a camera installed by one municipality can become searchable by investigators hundreds or thousands of miles away.
In 2021, around the time of Pichardo’s training, Flock offered Pawtucket police a free 60-day pilot. Seventeen cameras went up around the city as part of a regional test that also included Cranston and Woonsocket, according to records reviewed by WIRED. The rollout quickly drew criticism. The ACLU of Rhode Island accused the department of installing the cameras surreptitiously, after the pilot began without prior public input or notice to the city council. Pawtucket chief of police Tina Goncalves later apologized, saying that the department would “work better in the future” to communicate with the city council.
The pilot ended later that year, and in May 2023 the local TV news reported that Pawtucket was not moving forward with the installation. Pichardo believed the idea was a dead letter.
It was not. In September 2023, records show, Pawtucket moved forward with a two-year deployment worth $128,000. Records show that the city planned to install 20 cameras along many of its busiest roads, including Newport Avenue, Main Street, Broadway, Smithfield Avenue, and West Avenue—where Pichardo first noticed one hanging over the road.
“Wait a minute,” Pichardo recalled thinking. “When did we make this decision to put these up?”
Within months, Pichardo’s questions would set off a chain of events that, he says, ended his career in law enforcement. They would also eventually place him, somewhat improbably, at the center of a backlash against Flock that unites large factions of the American left and right.
For a policeman, Pichardo contains more than his share of contradictions. He speaks with a thick Rhode Island accent that sounds like something lifted from a cop movie, but he peppers his conversation with occasional references to Nietzsche or obscure films. He describes himself as private by temperament but seems driven to stand out.
Having spent some of his childhood in a poor neighborhood where drugs and gangs were part of the landscape, Pichardo says he learned that it was safest to keep his opinions to himself and stay out of other people’s business. When he was 12 or 13, he learned that his father, who had returned to the Dominican Republic several years earlier, had done so because he had a criminal record and was told it would be best if he left the country. Becoming a police officer offered a way of drawing a line between his father’s path and his own. After studying in the criminal justice program at Salve Regina University in Newport, Pichardo entered the police academy and joined the Pawtucket department in 2018. To hear him describe it, he’s always been something of an outlier on the force. “I’m possibly the only cop who would voluntarily go to musicals,” he once told me.
In the weeks following that fall shift when he first noticed Flock cameras all over town, Pichardo kept picking at the question of how the cameras had returned. Detectives, he says he learned after asking around the department, were already using the system, though many patrol officers like himself appeared to know little about it.
Pichardo contacted his work district’s local city council rep and asked how the cameras had been approved—his first time speaking to a politician, he says—but didn’t emerge with a clear answer. (Records show that the department had notified the purchasing board that it planned to move forward, but there was no public vote before the cameras were installed. The question of approval surfaced only afterward, when a council member asked whether the deployment should have come before the council. Officials said no. Installing the cameras was, they explained, an “administrative prerogative.”)
Police officers swear oaths to uphold the law and report wrongdoing. Inside the department, Pichardo said, the unwritten rule was simpler: Don’t rat. He understood that speaking publicly could end his career. But he says he was inspired by whistleblowers like Frank Serpico and Edward Snowden, men of conviction who broke with powerful institutions and spent years living with the consequences. Pichardo has a pronounced sense of right and wrong and a tendency to treat compromise as betrayal. “You should never sell your integrity,” he says.
License plate readers are a routine investigative tool, useful for locating stolen cars or identifying suspect vehicles without stopping large numbers of motorists. Experts broadly agree that reducing unnecessary police encounters and high-speed pursuits is a good thing. But to Pichardo, that usefulness was beside the larger point. Pawtucket had created a new form of surveillance over public movement with no debate, helping to build a world in which the government could quietly record where ordinary people went. It was not a world he found acceptable. If the officers who understood the system would not raise that question, he wondered, who would?
Pichardo was still wrestling with whether to speak out about Flock when he brought it up with his wife, Emily. “Do what you believe is right,” she said; they would deal with whatever followed. After that, without notifying anyone in the department, Pichardo called a reporter at Pawtucket’s local newspaper.
The article in the Valley Breeze was published on October 11, 2023. Its headline was blunt: “Pawtucket Officer Has a Big Problem With New Cameras.”
In the article, Pichardo called Flock a “grave threat” to privacy and warned that the system was ripe for abuse. He said he had learned of the full deployment from the newspaper itself, not from his own department. If a patrol officer knew so little about the cameras going up around the city, he asked, how much could the public possibly know? The whole thing gave him, he said, “1984 vibes.”
This was not whistleblowing in the conventional sense. Pichardo did not reveal a secret program, leak internal documents, or expose a specific abuse. In some respects, the newspaper knew more about the deployment than he did. What he offered instead was the rare perspective of an active-duty police officer breaking ranks to publicly argue that his own department had adopted a powerful surveillance system without enough scrutiny.
When the article appeared, the first text Pichardo received came from another officer.
“I want to congratulate you on your testicular fortitude,” it read. The officer added that he was proud of Pichardo for doing what he believed was right. Then he warned him: The brass was furious.
Pichardo says many officers supported what he had said to the Valley Breeze. Others, mostly older officers, viewed him as a traitor. One officer asked how he still had a job. Around the station, he was told that officers were calling him “Valley Breeze” behind his back. One sergeant, he says, told him he should quit.
Within weeks, the warnings began to look prescient.
Police internal investigations are not criminal cases. Their purpose is generally narrower—to determine whether an officer has violated a policy, code of conduct, or general order. Investigators interview witnesses, review body-camera or surveillance footage, collect reports and emails, and question the officer at the center of the complaint. The interview is typically recorded, and the officer is often accompanied by a union representative.
The process generates paper. A complaint. A notice of investigation. Lists of possible policy violations. Interview recordings and investigators’ notes. Findings, disciplinary recommendations, and notices of punishment.
Before the Valley Breeze article appeared, Pichardo’s disciplinary record appears to have consisted of a single incident: In 2021, while working a police detail at a production of the musical Annie, he refused a vendor’s request that he wear a face mask, and he received a written reprimand and a two-week suspension. After Pichardo spoke out against Flock, he received notice of an internal investigation into his conduct on October 25, 2023. It would be the first of many.
The department’s complaint, which originated from Chief Tina Goncalves, stated flatly that Pichardo had spoken to a newspaper without prior authorization, had undermined the authority of the police department and its chief, and had suggested that information collected by Flock cameras could be used improperly. His comments, the notice said, were “liable to cause harm to the reputation of the department and affect the impact on the community.”
The potential violations included the department’s mission statement, code of ethics, media-relations policy, and a rule labeled “Criticism & Malicious Gossip.”
Pichardo was ordered to appear at the Office of Professional Standards, a basement-level room in the Pawtucket police headquarters. Across from him, he says, were a lieutenant and a sergeant. A union representative sat beside him but said little.
The interview lasted somewhere between 30 and 45 minutes, Pichardo recalls. The questions were straightforward at first. Had he spoken to the reporter? He had. Had he done so without authorization from the department? He had. Why?
Pichardo gave much the same answer he had given the newspaper: The cameras were tracking people across the city, and the public had a right to know how they were being used. Pichardo says the lieutenant disagreed. Not every police tactic, he told Pichardo, was the public’s business. Departments did not disclose every method they used or every form of surveillance available to them.
The investigators accused Pichardo of violating the public’s trust by speaking to the press.
“I think this department violated the public trust,” he says he retorted. Then they asked who, in his view, should be held responsible. “The chief,” Pichardo said.
WIRED could not review the underlying investigative file, including the recording that might confirm or contradict Pichardo’s account. The city declined to provide the file even when Pichardo requested records concerning his own case. Pawtucket officials did not respond to WIRED’s questions about the denial.
A disciplinary agreement signed in early 2024 does, however, state that Pichardo made “critical statements to the media” about Flock and the department’s leadership. Pichardo maintained that his comments were constitutionally protected speech. The department expressly denied that position in the agreement.
After consulting an attorney, the Pawtucket police union came to the conclusion that Pichardo’s comments were constitutionally protected and sent the city a letter warning that if it disciplined him, it would likely violate his rights. According to union lodge president Michael Cioe, the department initially sought a six-month suspension but reduced the proposed punishment after the union threatened litigation.
Rather than fight the case through disciplinary hearings and possible state or federal litigation, the two sides reached an agreement. Pichardo would serve a 30-day unpaid suspension for speaking to the paper.
Pichardo said he accepted the deal because he didn’t want his coworkers to see him as their enemy. “I wanted the war to end,” he says.
By then, the department had already opened another investigation into his conduct.
A month after investigators questioned Pichardo about speaking to the Valley Breeze, another internal investigation notice arrived. In December, the department opened an inquiry over Pichardo’s failure to appear for a municipal court hearing about a traffic citation, which resulted in an additional two-day suspension. Chief Goncalves was again listed as the complainant.
Then, in March, about a week after he returned to work from the suspension, yet another notice landed—this one concerning an encounter that had allegedly taken place nearly 15 months earlier.
The incident involved a man who was being taken to a hospital for a mental health evaluation. The complaint alleged that Pichardo grabbed the man’s arm, refused to let him retrieve a jacket, and would not allow him to feed his cat. When the man pointed out that the cat could not open a can of food on its own, Pichardo allegedly replied that “cats can take care of themselves” and laughed.
During his interview, Pichardo says he told investigators that the cat already had food and that other officers and mental health clinicians present could confirm that he had handled the encounter appropriately. Pichardo says the inquiry didn’t sustain the allegations, and he received no discipline.
By the spring, Pichardo felt sure that the department was trying to send a message with these three investigations. Inside the department, Pichardo says, there was an unspoken expectation that his disciplinary agreement with his superiors would end his public criticism. Nevertheless, in April he accepted an invitation to testify at a public hearing before the Rhode Island House Judiciary Committee, where lawmakers were considering legislation regulating automated license plate readers.
The hearing was carried live on the legislature’s Capitol Television network. Pichardo spoke off the cuff. He told lawmakers that the proposed legislation did not go far enough. Flock, he argued, was tracking people’s movements, and although he was “not a lawyer,” he believed the system raised serious Fourth Amendment concerns. He said the cameras had captured his own plate five times in a single day, cited an out-of-state officer who used Flock to track his ex-wife, and questioned whether police should possess technology with that kind of cross-jurisdictional reach.
At times, Pichardo’s confidence outran his precision. He asserted that officers’ use of Flock could not be monitored, although the system does in fact maintain user logs and performs regular audits. In interviews with WIRED, he acknowledged the distinction but argued that logs were only as meaningful as the people responsible for reviewing them. He pointed to cases in other jurisdictions where officers had used Flock to track romantic partners or conduct improper searches, sometimes without the misuse being caught until much later. His broader point, he said, was that “anybody’s capable of anything” when given a powerful tool without sufficient guardrails.
About a week later, in response to his testimony, the Rhode Island Police Chiefs’ Association sent a letter to the committee singling Pichardo out by name. It called his testimony “inaccurate at best” and, at worst, “inflammatory and patently false.” The association accused him of misunderstanding Flock’s capabilities, disputed his description of the system’s auditing, and suggested that he either lacked familiarity with the technology or had “an agenda where, in his mind, the truth is irrelevant.”
Back at work, Pichardo says, his union representatives were annoyed that he’d spoken up again. (The union disputes this characterization.) Other officers, even those who largely agreed with him about Flock, or at least respected what he was doing, started to express concerns. One sat Pichardo down and said that if he wasn’t careful, he might lose his job and never work as a police officer in Rhode Island again. “You’ve got to think about your family, dude,” Pichardo recalls him saying.
On May 10, 2024, a new incident set yet another internal investigation of Pichardo in motion: A delivery driver came to Pawtucket police headquarters to report that someone had thrown a bottle of soda at her vehicle during what she described as a road-rage encounter. Pichardo spoke with her, concluded that no crime had occurred, and declined to prepare a report.
The woman later spoke with a sergeant, asking for the incident to be documented, and Pichardo was directed to write a report. According to the department's records, the delivery driver was not initially asking to file a formal complaint against Pichardo, but she did return to the station later that day, recording portions of her exchanges with Pichardo on her cell phone.
Pichardo told her that Pawtucket is an urban environment where people argue and throw things, accused her of acting like a child and having a tantrum, and complained that she had “won” by persuading a supervisor to overrule him.
Several days later, the woman filed a formal complaint with the Office of Professional Standards.
Investigators reviewed the recordings and interviewed another officer on duty. The videos, investigators later wrote, showed the woman remaining largely calm as Pichardo became increasingly dismissive. They sustained more than a dozen allegations, including neglect of duty, insubordination, incivility, and conduct unbecoming.
Pichardo acknowledged to WIRED that his conduct was indefensible. “I should still be the bigger person,” he said.
What he disputed was the punishment: a 40-day unpaid suspension and removal from the detective eligibility list. He also says the union told him he was barred from taking the sergeant’s exam for two years. He was notified of the suspension on the day his second son was born, just as he was about to start paternity leave, meaning that his first 40 days at home with his baby were unpaid—a coincidence he alleges was deliberate.
By early 2025, Pichardo had come to believe the department was finished with him. He no longer trusted that, if a traffic stop, arrest, or routine encounter generated another complaint, anyone in command would give him the benefit of the doubt. He more or less began to avoid active patrolling, he says. Between calls, he often waited at the Fraternal Order of Police building, which he helped maintain, or remained inside his patrol car rather than looking for the next stop. “I was trying to stay off the radar,” he later recalled telling investigators.
Then two more investigations arrived.
The first grew out of a dispute over a snowbound Volkswagen. On February 10, Pichardo responded to what appeared to be an unregistered vehicle stranded in the snow, concluded it was already disabled and had been ticketed, and gave the owner until the following day to move it. A supervisor ordered him to return and have the car towed instead. Pichardo questioned the instruction over the radio before complying. The department concluded that he had essentially been insubordinate.
The second began less than two weeks later. Pichardo responded to a mother who wanted police to document her 13-year-old son as a wayward child after she suspected he had been burning paper inside their home. Pichardo declined to take a report, concluding that she lacked evidence and appeared more interested in having the state remove the boy than documenting a crime. Before leaving, he told her to go inside and “be a mother.”
The department combined the investigations. Rather than focus only on the underlying incidents, investigators reconstructed nearly an entire workday of Pichardo’s life in excruciating detail. Using dispatch records, time sheets, cruiser GPS, and location data transmitted by Pichardo's body camera, they mapped his movements throughout the day of the family call. (They didn’t use Flock data; they didn’t need to.) Their reconstruction concluded that he had spent approximately four hours and 57 minutes at police facilities or the Fraternal Order of Police building rather than on patrol.
Pichardo did not dispute where he had been. He explained that he helped maintain the union office and that officers routinely waited there between calls. From the department's perspective, the location data showed an officer spending much of his shift inside police or union buildings instead of policing the city. The department was recommending termination. The resulting complaint explaining the decision ran 25 pages. It contained 32 administrative charges—10 stemming from the tow dispute and 22 from the family call—and assembled nearly every disciplinary matter from Pichardo's career.
On the morning of July 16, 2025, after roll call, a major asked Pichardo to stay behind.
He knew what was coming.
Chief Goncalves had signed a complaint the day before recommending his termination. The major handed it to him and explained that he was being suspended with pay while he decided whether to request a hearing in accordance with Rhode Island's Law Enforcement Officers' Bill of Rights. He had five days.
Pichardo took the complaint home. But the more he thought about it, the less sense it made to fight. Even if he won, he believed, he would return to a department whose leadership had already decided it no longer wanted him.
Two days later, after seven years as a Pawtucket police officer, Pichardo resigned.
His letter was brief. Policing, he wrote, had meant a great deal to him and his family, but over the previous three years the department had made clear that he was no longer welcome because of his “philosophical convictions.” Remaining, he wrote, would only bring more grief to him and his family.
He did not apologize for speaking out.
"My only regret," he wrote, "is that I was not articulate and/or diplomatic enough in my attempts to explain my position." On the 18th, he walked the letter to the Office of Professional Standards, shook hands with his coworkers, turned in his badge, firearm, radio, and keys, and left police headquarters for the last time.
Pichardo alleges that the investigations and escalating discipline he was faced with were retaliation for speaking out about Flock. The reality may be more complicated. His union, which had backed him when the department sought to punish him for his comments to the Valley Breeze, says it saw no evidence that the later investigations were retaliatory. They believed another Pawtucket officer who engaged in comparable conduct would have faced similar discipline.
Whether that is true is difficult to establish. Pichardo does not deny that he broke department rules in several of the incidents. His argument is that the rules were enforced differently against him—that conduct that might have earned another officer a warning became an internal inquiry, and misconduct that might otherwise have brought lesser discipline resulted in lengthy unpaid suspensions. He claims he had seen other officers do worse and face less. There is no way to know what would have happened to the version of Pichardo who never called the Valley Breeze.
After resigning, Pichardo spent months trying to remain in law enforcement. He applied to other police departments, private-security jobs, and campus police positions, including one at his alma mater, Salve Regina University. Some never responded. Others interviewed him before deciding not to move forward. An acquaintance who works in campus security at a local college eventually asked around and offered an explanation: "You're blackballed."
He found work instead as a caregiver for a person with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
Pichardo tried to tell himself that he had done enough. But he couldn’t shake the feeling that he had left something unfinished. “My conscience was still haunting me,” he told me. “I just wanted to be able to say I tried.”
So he sat down with a friend who started a YouTube account for Pichardo, and they recorded a video.
Since I started speaking with Pichardo in April, the debate over Flock has spread far beyond Pawtucket. Across the country, cities have fought over whether to keep the cameras, some jurisdictions have canceled contracts or imposed new restrictions, and lawmakers in both Republican- and Democratic-led states have pushed for new limits on how the systems can be used. For Pichardo, there is something distinctly American about the backlash. The country has long attached dreams of freedom and self-determination to the car, a mythology reflected in advertising and even in the names of the vehicles themselves: Explorer, Expedition, Escape, Maverick, Liberty. Americans who agreed on little else could still recognize the promise of the open road—that, for a little while, a person might simply leave and be left alone. To Pichardo, Flock threatened that promise.
“That’s freedom,” Pichardo told me. “The ability to drive somewhere and no one knows where you’re going.”
The video opens with Pichardo sitting alone in a plain room, dressed in a crisp cream-colored shirt, daylight spilling through a nearby window. Looking directly into the camera, he tells viewers that speaking publicly is "one of the strangest things" he has ever done. But, he says, he feels obligated to warn them about a technology that has quietly spread into communities across the country.
"To put it bluntly," he says, "if you own a car, you are now being tracked."
He expected a few hundred people to watch. Hundreds of thousands did.
Within weeks, an email arrived from one of Tucker Carlson's bookers. Pichardo assumed it was a prank; he had never really sought a political audience. He had deleted his social media accounts years ago and had little interest in becoming a pundit. But in mid-July, there he was, spending nearly 20 minutes discussing license plate readers, surveillance, and the meaning of privacy with the former Fox News host. He was explaining Flock to one of the largest audiences in American media, in a video bombastically titled “Whistleblower Reveals the Largest Mass Surveillance Operation in History and the Coming Slave State.”
Podcasters started reaching out, followed by local reporters and The Washington Post. Strangers urged him to run for office. Others told him to build up his YouTube channel, lean into the moment, and turn the audience into a career.
The prospect was not without appeal. Pichardo was still rebuilding his life after losing his job; a large audience might offer money, security, even a new profession. But something about it felt dishonest. “The only reason people know who I am,” he told me, “is because I criticized something.”
He had watched enough people online to recognize what he thought of as a trap. You begin with sincere convictions about serving the public, then you begin tracking an audience, and in time, he says, “you become a parody of what you were before.”
His mind returned, he says, to a passage from the Gospel of Matthew. “What profit is it to a man,” the verse goes, “if he gains the whole world, but loses his own soul?”

In praise of zealotry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
25 minute listen
In 1706, an English woman visited her friend, Katherine. Katherine’s husband, Francis Atterbury, was a prominent politician and bishop. Upon hearing that Francis had just finished writing his sermon, Katherine’s friend asked if she could take it home to read it. Francis graciously agreed, no doubt expecting to receive some compliments from the lady. But his sermon was promptly returned to him by the woman with copious criticism and notes for its improvement. Francis was shocked: he complained to a friend that the lady lacked a ‘decent manner’ and that she was ‘offensive and shocking in her expressions’. He admitted: ‘I dread to engage her.’
This ‘indecent’ and ‘shocking’ woman was Mary Astell (1666-1731). Today, she is best known as England’s first feminist, whose paradoxical mix of conservative politics and pioneering feminism has long puzzled scholars. By 1706, Astell was no doubt used to being called offensive, irritating and impolite. She wrote most of her partisan pamphlets in the first decade of the 18th century, always studded with sharp attacks on men she disagreed with (often, but not exclusively, those on the side of the Whig liberals, the most famous of which was John Locke). One of the pamphleteers she attacked, James Owen, dismissed her as overly angry, zealous and ‘virulent’ – a dismissal that meant that he did not have to actually engage with her sharp and difficult arguments.
More than half a century later, another politically active woman received similar treatment. The historian and political theorist Catharine Macaulay (1731-91) had penned a sharp pamphlet attacking Edmund Burke, who remains widely received as the ‘father’ of modern conservatism and the first major proponent of organised political parties. Macaulay had taken issue with Burke’s now-famous defence of party, Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770). Instead of dealing with her critique head on, Burke wrote to his friend that ‘the Amazon is the greatest champion amongst them … no heroine in Billingsgate can go beyond the patriotick scolding of our republican Virago.’ Invoking the image of the fierce female warrior and of the loud, masculinised woman, he ridiculed Macaulay, but not without a sense of awe. Much like Atterbury, Burke admitted he was ‘afraid to answer her’.
But Burke’s dismissal of Macaulay was not just rudeness – it was entirely consistent with his broader vision of what partisanship should look like, and who should be allowed to practise it. In the very tract that sparked Macaulay’s attack, Burke argued that partisanship is best conceived of as a well-chosen, loyal friendship between polite, reasonable and like-minded men, who agreed with one another ‘at least nine times in ten’. Only in this way could partisanship exist ‘without violating concord’. By contrast, Macaulay’s pamphlet was impolite, fierce and zealous. In Burke’s eyes, then, Macaulay’s brand of partisanship certainly violated concord and harmony.
Burke was not the only 18th-century theorist to champion politeness, friendship, moderation and reasonableness. David Hume, too, stressed the importance of concord. A partisan shouldn’t be too principled; he should be able to ‘easily agree with his fellow-citizen’. Righteous partisans were ‘more zealous’ and ‘more furious and enraged’ than those who were reasonable and prone to compromise. Anthony Ashley-Cooper, the third Earl of Shaftesbury also thought it was crucial to safeguard concord. For this purpose, he recommended the cultivation of ‘serene, soft, and harmonious’ manners to combat angry, zealous political ‘warfare’. The message of these men was clear: partisans should be polite, reasonable, moderate and friendly. Only then could partisanship make politics better – that is, more harmonious. Only then could partisanship, as it were, be tamed. Impolite, zealous, angry, and righteous voices like those of Astell and Macaulay were threatening precisely because they disrupted concord.
What makes Astell and Macaulay’s shared experience all the more striking is that they came from opposite ends of the political spectrum. Where Astell was a Tory conservative defender of the Church of England, absolute monarchy and religious orthodoxy, Macaulay was a radical republican and Whig, championing popular sovereignty, religious toleration and revolution. But despite disagreeing on nearly everything, they arrived at remarkably similar views on how to do partisan politics. This suggests that their insight arose not from their partisan commitments but from their shared position on the margins. As women, neither could vote nor hold public office, and partisanship – writing pamphlets, joining political groups, intervening in public debates – was one of the few avenues of political participation available to them.
Their experience as women and partisans allowed them to see what the more fully politically included men around them couldn’t
We might expect Astell and Macaulay to have defended themselves against the likes of Atterbury, Owen and Burke by arguing that they were not in fact impolite or zealous or offensive. But, instead, they embraced these monikers. In her pamphlet Moderation Truly Stated (1704), Astell gladly admitted that she liberally ‘sprinkled’ her writing with ‘my inflaming Oratory, Satyr and Invective’. Unlike men such as Owen, Shaftesbury or Atterbury, she preferred the honest ‘Quintessence of Gall’ over the flattering, soothing ‘Extract of Honey’. Even if truths were hurtful or shocking, it was still preferable to dole them out rather than to hold back. ‘[I]f there appears any Bitterness in’ her own writings, Astell said, ‘it arises only from the Plainness and Force of Truth, which ill Men cannot bear.’ Macaulay similarly adopted an unapologetic attitude to men like Burke or Hume who found her shockingly honest and direct: the point of being a partisan was ‘to speak some bold offending truths’. Even if it caused one ‘to be very offensive’ and ‘obnoxious’, it was still preferable to dishonest politeness.
Why did Astell and Macaulay reject those ‘virtues’ that their male peers extolled? Their experience as women and partisans allowed them to see what the more fully politically included men around them couldn’t: that insisting that partisans be polite, moderate, reasonable and friendly would actually serve to exclude marginalised political voices. It could do so in two ways.
First, there was the problem of gatekeeping. As Astell put it: ‘Who shall be the Judge’ of what and who counted as (im)polite, (im)moderate, and (un)reasonable? It would be the powerful and fully politically included men like Shaftesbury who would be the judge. Paraphrasing Shaftesbury’s ‘Letter Concerning Enthusiasm’ (1708), Astell suggested he had argued that wit and ridicule were acceptable, provided ‘we treat it with Good Manners’. But while men like Shaftesbury might be able to dole out ridicule wherever they went and still be considered polite and well-mannered, women like Astell would, for the very same behaviour, be berated for their bad manners. In her last pamphlet, t (1709), Astell challenged Shaftesbury by asking whether women or servants would be allowed to ‘treat the Master of the Family in this Fashion?’ In other words, while powerful men would be allowed to behave however they liked and still be deemed well-mannered and reasonable, servants, women and other ‘Person[s] of No-Figure’ would not. In her book Mere Civility (2017), the political theorist Teresa Bejan shows that thick conceptions of early modern civility functioned in exactly this way – excluding dissenting voices by raising the threshold for civility so high that only insiders could meet it. But where Bejan proposes a thinner, more minimal form of civility, Astell and Macaulay went further.
Astell and Macaulay identified another problem: voices at the margins of politics had special cause to be righteous and zealous. On important issues – such as the equality of the sexes – it would not do to remain polite or seek a moderate compromise. Macaulay faced precisely this problem with Burke: he argued that only those involved in the daily practice of politics were qualified to make political judgments. By contrast, ‘speculative’ thinkers like Macaulay, who were not included in the thick of politics, were naive and unfit. They ‘soften[ed] into a credulity below the milkiness of infancy’. They could perhaps reason about the ‘ends of government’ but not with the practical means of it. Macaulay refused to accept this: she argued that her distance from power actually gave her superior insight vis-à-vis fully included partisans.
In her 1770 reply to Burke, Macaulay argued that ‘practical gentlemen’ like himself were too corrupted by self-interest and political power to make unbiased political judgments. But with some healthy distance, ‘speculative thinkers’ like Macaulay could think more clearly and were better equipped to spot the ‘sinister views’ of those in the thick of politics. A ‘moderate’ response to Burke would have been to concede that both sides have some important political insight – indeed, this was what he himself gestured at. But Macaulay refused to meet Burke on the middle ground, because the middle ground would still effectively silence her political voice. When it came to arguments about who was included and who excluded, it would not do to be polite, reasonable and moderate. For someone in Macaulay’s position, zeal and righteousness were not character flaws, but the only adequate response to a system that defined her out of legitimate political speech.
Astell agreed. Whereas, throughout the 18th century, people tended to define zeal as ‘excessive or immoderate enthusiasm’, she praised the ‘Zealot’, who was ‘warm and assiduous’ and ‘stiff and narrow-Spirited’. Astell’s subversive point was that inflexibility in one’s principles and beliefs was admirable – on important matters, from religion to women’s position in society, it was wrong to be quickly dissuaded, or to change one’s mind too readily: ‘an Honest Man’ had an ‘Inflexible Conscience’ and did not ‘Veer with the Times’. When it came to politics, it was important to take sides. And if the ‘Honest man’ thought the other side had a good point, then ‘he ought to go over to them.’ Macaulay, too, praised partisans with ‘inflexible attachment to the cause’, and who were ‘actuated by so warm and honest a zeal’. Righteous zeal meant taking a decided stance, not looking for middle ground, and zealously arguing one’s cause. It was directly opposed to the political virtues their male peers recommended.
Far from destroying political debate, righteous, zealous partisans in fact sustained it
To Astell and Macaulay, it was obvious that, in political debate, righteous zeal was preferable. First of all because partisans on the margins had most to lose from moderate, polite reasonableness. If they politely conceded that their opponents had a point, nothing ever changed. These virtues would only maintain the status quo, whereas Astell and Macaulay sought to challenge and change it. Astell wanted to combat the pernicious and ill-grounded ‘customs’ – a term that closely resembles our present-day idea of ‘social norms’ – that painted women as inferior creatures, incapable of political argument and devoid of intellect. ‘Custom, that merciless torrent that carries all before it’ needed to be checked. Macaulay likewise worried that ‘the generality of mankind are too fond of accustomed establishments’, and therefore ‘interested to reject every part of reformation’. Partisanship was a powerful means available to those on the margins – those who could never belong to Burke’s ‘practical gentlemen’ involved in daily politics – seeking to challenge the prejudices and norms that tried to keep them out. The philosopher Myisha Cherry makes a parallel argument in her book The Case for Rage (2021), writing that righteous anger was a driving force in the civil rights movement – a context where polite, moderate appeals for equality had long failed to produce change.
Accepting righteous zeal instead of polite, moderate reasonableness was more inclusive: it allowed for a greater number of people to make their voices heard and be taken seriously. But Astell and Macaulay also argued that, far from destroying political debate, righteous, zealous partisans in fact sustained it. After all, these ‘warm’ and ‘inflexible’ people kept arguing with their opponents even when it was unwelcome. As a righteous, zealous partisan herself, Astell envisioned meeting her ‘enemies in heaven hereafter’ where ‘they shall be sensible that their admission is in some measure owing to our own importunate intercessions for them’. In other words, it was only due to her constant arguments and persuasions that her opponents would improve themselves and their views. ‘This,’ she mused in her magnum opus The Christian Religion (1705), ‘will be no doubt a sweet revenge.’ Macaulay seems to have been a persistent political interlocutor too. An acquaintance of hers said that ‘though she plays at cards and talks of different subjects,’ she ‘always returns’ to politics, even at parties – ‘an odd character for a lady’.
Since righteous, zealous partisans favoured honesty over politeness, they were also happy to risk causing offence in pursuit of persuasion. Macaulay argued that, just as tyranny stood opposed to liberty, so zeal stood opposed to formality, or ‘outward appearance or semblance’ and ‘conformity to established rule’. For Macaulay, zeal thus implied a disregard of outward appearance or conformity. To be zealous often meant being bold, truthful, even impolite. As Astell put it, it involved ‘speaking truths which no man would say’, in other words, speaking ‘the Truth that wounds’.
At this point, the image of zealous, righteous partisans trying to persuade one another might conjure up worrying images of shouting without any genuine dialogue taking place. Even if such partisans would keep talking, would they really listen to one another? Astell and Macaulay’s writings show that they did in fact always take their opponents’ views seriously. Their most partisan and zealous works often targeted one or two men they disagreed with: they went through their arguments, one by one, including references to page numbers and quotations, and explained why they were wrong on all counts. In her pamphlet Moderation Truly Stated, Astell gave Owen this treatment – whereas Owen, the proponent of moderation and reasonableness, dismissed Astell’s entire work in one sentence. Macaulay’s two responses to Burke also engaged with his arguments in depth, whereas Burke ridiculed her but never deigned to respond to her arguments. This wasn’t a coincidence. A righteous, zealous partisan who wanted to persuade her opponents had to take their arguments seriously; whereas a polite, moderate partisan who valued concord over truth could afford to dismiss an uncomfortable, controversial voice and move on.
Today, righteous, zealous partisans seem as unreasonable as they are incapable of changing their minds. And what is the point of political debate if no one ever changes their mind? But to Astell and Macaulay, righteous zeal was compatible with a degree of open-mindedness and critical thinking. They certainly did not consider all standpoints as equally valid, but nonetheless took them seriously. Both Astell and Macaulay praised inflexibility and were wary of partisans whose views swayed with the wind. As the philosopher Lea Ypi points out, not being quick to change one’s mind can actually bolster political commitment and can ensure that partisan projects persist over time. In other words, it can ensure that partisans don’t give up too easily.
But even if partisans should be somewhat inflexible, would righteous zeal not foreclose the very possibility of open-mindedness? If we define it as taking every other standpoint as equally valid, then righteous, zealous partisans would indeed not be open-minded. But if we define it, as the philosopher Jeremy Fantl does in The Limitations of the Open Mind (2018), as the willingness ‘to pull back on your confidence if I offer an argument each step of which you find compelling and in which you cannot, by your own admission, find a flaw,’ then righteous zeal is certainly compatible with open-mindedness. Astell believed that, if a member of the Church of England did not think that dissenters were mistaken, ‘he ought to go over to them’. A partisan’s righteousness should never prevent them from looking critically at their own beliefs, nor preclude a change of mind: Astell advised her readers to ‘receive no man’s opinion on his bare word, nor to swallow his arguments without examining them.’
It is affective polarisation, not disagreement itself, that actually threatens political debate
What’s more, Astell and Macaulay’s rejection of partisanship as friendship actually protects against echo chambers. It is the moderate, friendship-based model that we find in Burke that risks groupthink, because loyalty to one’s friends and a desire to avoid offence prevents frank disagreement. Astell wrote that these friends ‘expect to be followed right or wrong in their principles, party, and passions’, and wished to ‘be flattered’. They would not ‘tell you of your Faults for fear of disobliging you’. By contrast, Astell and Macaulay were not only critical to partisans of opposing sides, but also criticised their co-partisans: Astell critiqued the Tory Charles Davenant in Moderation Truly Stated, and Macaulay had a disagreement with the fellow radical John Wilkes. Both women had a decided preference for open, honest enemies over ‘concealed enemies’ in the guise of friends. In other words, if you surround yourself with polite, loyal friends who flatter you and avoid offence, your views never get tested; if you engage honestly with your opponents who challenge you in turn, they do.
That this vindication of righteous zeal came from two women, not from the men who dominated partisan theory, is no accident. To forgo righteousness and zeal in the face of deep disagreement is a luxury not available to all – least of all to those positioned at the margins of politics. Likewise, to insist that partisans should dispense with righteousness and zeal in favour of reasonableness, politeness and moderation is itself a privilege. As Astell and Macaulay pointed out, it risks excluding or persecuting those who are most oppressed in politics, and who have most need of, and cause for, righteous zeal.
Astell and Macaulay’s diagnosis is especially urgent today, when we hear calls for more moderate, reasonable, polite debate from all sides of the political spectrum as the cure for polarisation. But the terms of what counts as reasonable political speech are still set by insiders, and voices expressing righteousness, zeal or anger are still viewed as threats to democratic life rather than as contributions to it. Just as in the 18th century, today this also works to silence partisan voices on the margins – those with most need of righteous zeal. It is certainly true that righteous zeal is unlikely to reduce ideological polarisation – where partisans move away from the centre. But the mere fact of such polarisation need not be detrimental to politics. Righteous zeal can combat a more worrying form of polarisation, affective polarisation – the refusal to engage with one’s opponents at all. And it is affective polarisation, not disagreement itself, that actually threatens political debate.
Perhaps in an ideal world, where everyone is equally included, and where everyone’s voices are heard, we wouldn’t need righteous, zealous partisans. But that is not the world we live in. Political life remains marked by deep inequalities of voice and standing. Insisting on politeness, moderation and reasonableness may make political debate more harmonious among those already fully included. Yet it simultaneously silences those on the margins – and bringing in a wider array of voices is precisely what is needed to improve political debate. Writing from the margins, Astell and Macaulay show us that righteous zeal is not a threat to politics, but rather a condition of genuine political inclusion and frank political debate.

War was supposed to crush Iran's 'Axis of Resistance.' Instead, it's bloodied but unbroken
