The unpopular populist: Why Nigel Farage’s Reform UK is losing support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:03:30 UTC
16:03:30 KST

Right-wing British populist Nigel Farage has returned to Parliament as planned, but the event can hardly be called a triumph. His Reform UK party, which until recently dreamed of definitively replacing the Conservatives, has faced falling poll numbers, investigations into suspicious donations, and its own institutional weakness. Now its leader must prove that his creation is not merely a temporary home for protest voters (or a one-man party built around a single scandal-prone politician), but a real political force.
Nigel Farage's the right-wing populist party, Reform UK, is at a make-or-break moment. It will either replace the Tories as the country's main political force on the right, or it will continue to be a marginal movement with no real hope of taking power. The populists face three fundamental barriers on the road to success: high unfavorable ratings outside their electoral base, an electoral platform that essentially promises to dismantle the government structures is seeks to lead, and a lack of “institutional depth” — i.e., a history, a developed organization, and a firm place in voters’ political memory.
What Reform UK does have in abundance, however, is dependence on its leader.
The Battle of Clowns in Clacton
Financing is often a weak spot for right-wing populists. Nigel Farage likes to talk about how he was given millions of pounds without being asked for anything in return, arguing that his finances are being investigated by British authorities only because the establishment cannot defeat him in a fair political fight. “Let ordinary voters judge me,” he said: “If I win, you win, because if I lose, they win.” This was the main message of Farage’s speech this past July 7, when he announced that he would stand again in an early election in his Clacton constituency. His slogan for that campaign: “The People versus the Establishment.”
The comedy began the very next day. All parties with any meaningful support – Labour, the Tories, the Liberal Democrats, the Greens, and Restore Britain (Farage’s rival on the right) – declined to field candidates. Thus, Farage’s main opponent was Count Binface (literally a man with a garbage bin on his head), along with three representatives of the Official Monster Raving Loony Party, several other novelty candidates, and a couple of dozen independents. A record 34 candidates in all joined the field.
Farage, of course, won. From the outset, around 70% of the constituency’s voters were ready to support him, compared with roughly 20% for Count Binface, and in the end the Reform UK head claimed 63% (then declined to attend the official announcement of the results). More importantly though, at the national level, 73% of Britons believe the investigation into Farage's finances should continue, no matter what the voters of Clacton may have said.
Political resilience
Farage is one of the most consistent and persistent politicians in modern Britain. For more than 30 years, he has built his political career around a single idea: I am on the side of the people in their struggle against a political class that betrays the will of ordinary Britons, and I will restore the country’s national sovereignty and control over its borders. The names and party labels change, but Farage and his basic message remain.
In 1989, Farage, still a Tory at the time, voted for the Green Party, reportedly because it was then seen as Euroskeptic. Three years later, in protest against the signing of the Maastricht Treaty (which created the European Union), he left the Conservative Party and joined the Anti-Federalist League, which soon became the United Kingdom Independence Party (UKIP). He led UKIP from 2006 to 2016 before taking over the newly established Brexit Party in 2019. In 2021, the party was renamed Reform UK, and Farage announced his retirement from politics. But ahead of the 2024 general election, he unexpectedly returned and, on his eighth attempt, was elected to the House of Commons.
Farage likes to portray himself as an outsider who can bring about the political revolution Britain so badly needs
Farage likes to portray himself as an outsider who can bring about a political revolution Britain supposedly so badly needs. The son of a trader, he attended a private school and then followed in his father's footsteps, becoming a trader in non-ferrous metals in the City of London. He made his way into politics thanks to an obvious talent for working with the media and a skillfully crafted political narrative that was very simple – and, therefore, persuasive.
The narrative works
Immigration and sovereignty remain at the core of Farage’s political program – in other words, his main political tool remains emotion. Farage's positions on “secondary” issues, especially economic ones, can change, sometimes radically, and his critics' charge that Farage offers slogans rather than plans are indeed consistent with reality. Unsurprisingly, 86% of Reform supporters consider immigration to be the country's most important political issue, compared with 42% of Britons overall. (The cost of living comes second, at 38%.)
In the worldview Farage offers, the topics of immigration, Brexit, economic problems, the declining quality of public services, and distrust in government institutions have become intertwined. The conclusion – that Britain is “broken” – is often expressed in forceful, militaristic rhetoric, with words such as “betrayal,” “war,” and “invasion.” The changes proposed are sometimes even given the names of military campaigns, such as “Operation Restore Justice.”
Channeling these emotions has proven effective. By summer 2026, 61% of Britons surveyed considered Reform to be one of the “major parties,” compared with just 19% two years earlier. In the 2025 and 2026 local elections, hundreds of the party’s candidates were elected as local councilors, and Reform now controls dozens of local authorities. It has become a real political force.
Something went wrong
Until early fall 2025, the average of the seven most recent polls conducted by different firms showed a steady rise in support for Reform, reaching around 32%. For comparison, Labour, now the governing party, won more than 400 of the 650 seats in 2024 with a comparable share of the vote.
But then came an equally steady decline. As of Aug. 5, support for Reform UK was back down to 24.0%, coming in behind Labour at 25.9%, with the Conservatives, Greens, and Liberal Democrats attracting 19.4%, 11.1%, and 10.7% support, respectively).
Reform’s growing prominence probably brought greater scrutiny of its plans, revealing that many people either saw the party’s proposals as eye-catching wish lists without realistic plans behind them (such as its call to invade France) or simply did not approve of them. For example, critics described as unfair and “un-British” the proposal to force people who had legally settled in Britain years or even decades ago to prove their right to remain all over again.
Another possible reason for Reform’s deteriorating position in the polls is the gradual recovery of the Conservative Party, which Farage has publicly vowed to displace. The Tories' current leader, Kemi Badenoch, has seen her popularity rise since September 2025.
Finally, a string of new scandals and reports of parliamentary and police investigations into the financial dealings of Farage and Reform, which began in spring 2026, may also have played a role. Not the main one, since Reform’s decline in the polls began long before the first reports of possible financial irregularities. Nevertheless, the allegations could ultimately cost Farage his seat in Parliament.
Is there life after Farage
The facts and suspicions described above – million-pound gifts, transfers sent through complicated channels, questions about financial disclosures, and ongoing investigations – look like a pattern of behavior when taken together, even if all of the allegations are yet to be proven. As a result, Farage's rhetoric of being with the people and against the elites is beginning to sound less convincing.
Traditionally, Farage is seen as the party’s main asset – he is still better than anyone else in Britain at using the media, and the loyalty of Reform UK supporters is centered on him. As many as 91% of those who back the party view him positively, with 49% viewing him very positively. Among the electorate as a whole, however, the picture is radically different. When More in Common asked Britons “Who do you trust more, the leader or the party?”, 7% chose Farage, while 17% chose Reform UK. Under the circumstances, breaking with Farage might actually benefit the party: while the leader once pulled the party upward, his high personal unfavorable ratings and financial scandals could now drag it down. For now, however, Reform UK is, in essence, Nigel Farage himself.
In the More in Common poll, when asked “Who do you trust more, the leader or the party?”, 7% chose Farage, while 17% chose Reform UK
Major internal party disagreements are usually resolved through Farage’s personal intervention. That was the case, for example, in June 2025, when party official Zia Yusuf announced his resignation. However, after speaking with Farage, who publicly said he had “forgiven” Yusuf, he returned 48 hours later. The same applies to tensions between Reform UK’s old core and the Conservatives who have joined the party – above all Robert Jenrick. For now, these tensions are largely being managed from above by Farage.
Or take the procedure for selecting parliamentary candidates. As of early August, the party’s Parliamentary candidates portal promised to “publish in due course” the rules for selecting them – this despite the fact that the party has existed for more than seven years, participated with some success in a general election two years ago, and intends to win a parliamentary majority in 2029. Somehow though, there are still no clear rules beyond the discretionary decisions of the party leadership.
The same story is playing out at the local level. In the absence of an established procedure, Reform UK can end up with candidates like Linden Kemkaran, who became leader of Kent County Council after the party won a majority there in 2025. So far, under her leadership, the local administration has been known largely for the advice its new leader gave to dissenting fellow party members: “fucking suck it up.”
That is precisely why bringing in experienced politicians and administrators is so important for Reform UK, as demonstrated by the example of North Northamptonshire Council, which is successfully led by a former Tory. Once in power, the rhetoric of revolution runs up against the mundane realities of everyday work like drawing up budgets and dealing with the rest of the administrative grind.
To become a successful, long-lived political force, Reform UK will have to develop mechanisms and procedures for the party’s internal life: how to resolve conflicts, how to constrain the leader’s arbitrary power, how to select high-quality candidates, and what a party member can do if they disagree with a decision. It is precisely the existence of such mechanisms that allows Labour and the Conservatives to survive instability at the top. With the “Faragists,” it is the other way around – stability at the very top and chaos below.
Obstacles from the right as well
In addition to internal professionalization, Reform UK’s future also depends on what happens to the Conservative Party over the next few years. The two right-of-center political groupings face different challenges. For Reform to win in the long run, it is not enough to be incrementally more popular; instead, it needs to prove that the Conservatives are finished as a serious electoral player.
This will not be easy. The growing personal popularity of Tory leader Kemi Badenoch represents a real threat to Reform UK. Among Reform supporters, 56% have a positive view of her, up from 37% a year earlier, and 40% say they would consider voting for her party. Among those who voted Conservative in 2024 but later switched to Reform, her net favorability rating has risen from +20 to +58, and 73% of this group say they could return to the Conservatives.
In short, the Conservatives are showing true signs of life. The results of the 2026 local elections were not as bad as expected, and they looked poor in part because they were being compared with unusually strong results in the previous electoral cycle. The Tories won the Aberdeen South parliamentary by-election with 49.5% of the vote, leaving Reform in third place with 8.6% – several times lower than its nationwide polling numbers. Moreover, this was the first Scottish by-election won by the Conservatives in half a century.
This was the first Scottish by-election won by the Conservatives in half a century
The Tories’ long-term prospects are impossible to predict. They may gradually recover under the firm hand of Badenoch, but it may also turn out that what we took for signs of life were merely bumps that made the corpse jolt.
Reform also has a more radical rival on the right – Restore Britain, founded by former Reform member Rupert Lowe. Like Reform, Restore too is “viciously attacked by the establishment.” It has also been publicly endorsed by Elon Musk and has already won 7–9% in several elections.
Lowe is popular among Reform supporters, particularly those who voted for the party in 2024 but do not see Farage as being radical enough. However, if Reform drifts to the right under the influence of this faction, it will ultimately lose the center, where elections are still won.
The electoral pen
Institutional weakness, an incomplete program, and high unfavorability ratings could trap Reform in a kind of electoral pen. Its outer boundary is made up of the many voters who find Farage and his party unacceptable, as even some people who are planning to vote for Reform sometimes say in focus groups that they will do so while holding their noses. Its inner boundary consists of the most radical supporters, who are ready to switch to Restore if Reform tries to become more moderate – for example, if it refuses to hold the referendum on restoring the death penalty as demanded by Lowe.
Institutional weakness could prevent Reform UK from convincing voters that it is capable of governing effectively. There is a gap between support for the party and perceptions of its readiness for exercising power — an Ipsos poll conducted in late June 2026 showed that support for Reform was significantly higher than the number of people prepared to trust it to form a government (and the latter figure fell from 29% last September to 21% earlier this summer). With Reform and Labour hovering around comparable polling numbers, 30% overall still preferred to see Andy Burnham as prime minister, while only 16% chose Farage.
Looking competent is especially important for a party that is deeply unpopular beyond outside its base of loyal supporters. This is a feature of the first-past-the-post system: whatever your overall polling numbers, what matters is beating your opponent by a single vote in a given constituency. As tactical voting becomes more popular, some voters cast their ballots for the party that can stop a candidate they dislike.
Here Reform is at a real disadvantage. A YouGov poll published in early July 2026 shows that around 62–63% of Britons have a negative view of Farage's party. When compared with the Conservative Party the overall figure for support is comparable, but 39% viewed the Tories “very negatively,” as opposed to 53% in the case of Reform – this a mere two years after the Tories suffered their worst electoral defeat in history.
Farage himself is doing no better. According to Pollcheck, as of Aug. 1 he ranked last among party leaders, with a net favorability rating of –22.3%, while his main rival on the right, the Conservatives' Badenoch, stood at +1.7%.
How the story ends
Forecasting at a point of bifurcation is a thankless task. Broadly speaking, two medium-term scenarios are emerging: Reform could replace the Tories as the main party on the right, or it could end up in its own electoral pen, expansive but with no way out.
For Farage’s party to succeed, it needs to halt its decline in the polls, become a professional political institution, and establish itself in the eyes of right-wing voters as the main means of removing Labour from power – and it needs to do so before investigations and internal infighting undermine voters' confidence in Farage and his movement. If Reform succeeds, it would attract not only tactical voters (for whom defeating the “left” is the overriding priority), but also higher-caliber candidates and staff.
Reform UK could replace the Tories as the main party on the right or end up in its own electoral pen, expansive but with no way out
But the opposite outcome is entirely possible: the party could retain its high unfavorable rating and remain unable to move beyond its current base, while also failing to professionalize. Meanwhile, the “revived” Conservatives could win back some of their erstwhile supporters who are currently holding their noses while voting for Reform.
In short, the populist tactics that enabled Reform to grow so quickly are now holding it back, making it harder to turn a “party of the aggrieved” into a party of government.
And of course, there is the separate question of what will happen with Farage himself. He has already shown that he can pursue his goal for decades and get back on his feet after defeats. But he has now set himself a new task – to create a party capable of crushing or absorbing one of the oldest political institutions in history. The Conservatives need only avoid losing, while Farage needs to win. The moment of truth is approaching for Farage and Reform UK.

An unenlightened traveller’s guide to Pride
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:01:21 UTC
16:01:21 KST

“But you aren’t gay?”
A family member said, raising her eyebrows, after I mentioned, between bites of a breakfast roll, that I was thinking about going to Copenhagen Pride.
She said it as if I’d be denied entry unless I could document my same-sex body count.
Later that week, I was in a bar with a friend drinking beers as if they were going to ask for them back.
“I’m thinking about going to Pride,” I said during my fifth beer.
He put down his glass but raised his eyebrows. “Is there something you want to tell me?”
According to the eyebrow raisers, Pride was for them, not for us. You had to be gay—or at least considering it—to think about going. I found that odd. Had I told them I was going to a food festival, nobody would have worried I’d quit my job to become a chef.
The concept of Pride began to gnaw inside of me. Were they right? Did I have to be gay? Could I pull off a netted vest? Would I trigger a gaydar? What is a gaydar?
It was settled; I would set out to be an unenlightened traveller. A goldfish being carried towards an unfamiliar aquarium in a plastic bag.
On P day, I donned my rainbow bucket hat and matching bracelets and burst out onto the streets, where I was immediately met with jeers from a group of lads in a passing car. When in a provincial town, this is the best indication that my outfit was spot on.
On the delayed train, an elderly man gestured to his wife. She glanced at me and whispered, as elderly people do, loudly.
“Pride.”
He tutted.
Stepping out of Copenhagen station, there was no doubt Pride had begun without me. Music reverberated through the busy streets. I dashed towards the thumping beat.
The parade had come to a halt, forcing the pink fairies, sequined cowboys and other colourful characters to wait like race car drivers for the green flag. Around them, soundboxes fought for supremacy with pop jams from every decade.
Kids chased confetti, gathering it in handfuls to toss back into the air over the paradees, who passed the wait with ecstatic dancing and euphoric kissing.
As the wheels of the parade started to turn, I snapped pictures with my camera and waved like a madman at anyone who looked in my direction.
The atmosphere was intoxicating. I needed to join in. When I saw an opening, I slipped into the parade’s ranks.
Feeling naughty, I went rigid, trying not to be detected, but as we progressed through the streets, my fellow paraders relaxed me. Soon I was moving to the tunes vibrating off the surrounding buildings. I caught the eye of a woman parading next to me who cheered me on, which spurred me into a full-on dance.
The route took us towards Rådhuspladsen. I jumped out of the parade and browsed the merchandise. If they can put a flag on it, they will.
Crowds flowed like a lazy river. I merged with one, allowing myself to drift with the current.
On route, I saw more leather than a shift manager at a tannery. And enough bulging abs to put most of the marble statues in Glyptoteket to shame.
Answering one of my questions, no, I most definitely couldn’t pull off a netted vest. I’d look like a Christmas ham, with the pork poking through the netting.
Sunlight was fading, and I was nowhere near to figuring out Pride. But I soon found that when the sun goes down, the volume of Pride cranks up.
That night, Copenhagen stood in stark contrast to the black night sky. I moved from street party to street party. Lights draped the old buildings in twinkling colours, refracted off the discoballs that spun over DJs banging out everything from Aqua, Cher and even Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas.”
At Slutterigade, the junction in front of the archway was clogged with people. With every step, I kicked glasses and shot tubes. When I reached the epicentre of the crowd, residue from hundreds of dropped drinks made my canvas sneakers stick to the cobbles. Even without the alcoholic glue, I couldn’t move. I was wedged amongst hundreds of people. I stood there and felt the crowd. Hundreds of people merged into one body, moving together to the greatest power women in music history. Every bump of a shoulder, every brush of bare, sweaty skin against my face seemed to connect me to it, and I realised I had become a small part of the party.
I’m not claiming Pride as my own. I can’t and probably never will understand the struggle of the majority of those on that street. But in that pulsating crowd on Slutterigade, I came to the realisation that the LGBTQ community were the hosts. I was a guest. And they seemed remarkably happy to let me dance in their living room.
There on the packed cobbles of Copenhagen, people expressed themselves and their love openly, turning the city into a bowl of pick ‘n’ mix where everyone was welcome to have a taste.
After unsticking my shoes from the pavement and bidding the hosts goodnight, I thought about all those eyebrow raisers who think Pride is just for the LGBTQ community. They are missing out on one hell of a party. I’d take power women and sweaty abs over standing on the outside tutting any day of the week.
Back at the station, my train was late again. And just as I thought Pride was coming to an end for me, there was one last surprise. The contrast between sky and street was broken as fireworks leapt into the black night sky, painting it with all the colours of a rainbow.
By then, feet were aching and my legs and shoes were sticky. But I found myself singing power woman Kylie Minogue’s “I Can’t Get You Out of My Head.”
And Pride, I’m sure you’ll be in there for some time.

Could the EU ban smoking? Commission to re-write rules for the next generation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:00:38 UTC
16:00:38 KST

The EU is pursuing its biggest overhaul of tobacco taxation in a decade. The proposed Tobacco Taxation Directive (TTD) raises taxes on cigarettes and introduces taxes on vapes, heated tobacco products, and nicotine pouches. After the Parliament rejected its position, Council negotiations continue.
As part of its Tobacco Control Framework Evaluation, the European Commission reviewed current tobacco laws and found that, while older rules successfully lowered traditional cigarette consumption, they are nowcompletely outdated and failing to stop a massive surge in digital marketing and novel nicotine products.
As a result, the Commission proposed a revision of the Tobacco Taxation Directive (TTD) to implement fresh rules and curb tobacco use. It remains under negotiation after the Parliament failed to adopt a formal position in June 2026, leaving the final decision to the Council of the European Union, where unanimous agreement among member states is required.
Roughly one in four Europeans still smoke or use tobacco regularly. And the problem is increasingly urgent among young people, with data showing that over 11 percent of teens aged 13 to 15 now regularly consume tobacco or trendy nicotine alternatives like flavoured disposable vapes.
“The EU continues to experience roughly 700.000 tobacco-related deaths annually. It remains a leading preventable cause of cancer and cardiovascular disease. From a public health perspective, lower taxes effectively subsidise consumption of a product that kills up to half of long-term users when used as intended”, Professor Martin McKee, Strategic Advisor at the European Public Health Association, told Euronews.
Does the EU have a cigarette problem?
300 billion cigarettes are sold annually in the EU; 24 percent of Europeans smoke, with higher rates among men than women. This massive consumer market is sustained internally, as European factories manufacture more than 220 billion cigarettes each year to meet demand.
Who smokes the most? Eurostat shows ranges from just 8 percent in Sweden up to 37 percent in Bulgaria. Regional disparities are particularly visible among males, with nearly half of the men in Bulgaria (49 percent) and Latvia (48 percent) smoking regularly, compared to less than 10 percent in Sweden.
For women, the highest use is in Greece at 32 percent, while Sweden again reports the minimum at 8 percent. Southern and Eastern European nations consistently report the highest tobacco use, with Croatia and Greece keeping overall smoking rates above 35 percent. Western and Northern European countries like the Netherlands and Denmark have driven their use down to 11 percent and 14 percent respectively.
Smoking poses huge pressures on health sectors. Chronic exposure to tobacco and nicotine results in millions of avoidable hospital admissions every year for respiratory failure, stroke, and ischaemic heart disease. Treating these long-term cardiovascular and chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases drains an estimated €25 billion annually directly from public healthcare budgets.
"Even a delay of a few years in major tobacco-control measures translates into millions of additional smokers, preventable diseases and deaths over time”, warned McKee.
The rise of vapes and IQOS
The peak of traditional tobacco consumption is among citizens aged 25 to 54. However, the market is shifting as younger generations pivot away from traditional cigarettes and towards other products.
These include e-cigarettes or vapes (which heat a liquid with nicotine and flavourings into an inhalable aerosol) and heated tobacco products, such as IQOS, which warm processed tobacco without burning it. Nicotine pouches deliver nicotine orally without containing tobacco leaf.
Health authorities consider these products less harmful than conventional cigarettes, but not risk-free. Studies by several health organisations identified potentially harmful substances, including formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein, while nicotine itself remains highly addictive. Public health experts also warn that nicotine exposure during adolescence can affect brain development and increase the risk of long-term dependence.
According to the World Health Organization, 11.6 percent of teens aged 13 to 15 in the European region use these products. "Marketing and product design are important drivers. Common features include flavours attractive to young consumers, heavy social-media promotion, lifestyle branding, claims that products are modern, cleaner or safer, and discreet designs that are easy to conceal”, said McKee.
The EU wants smokers to quit
The EU wants to create a “Tobacco-Free Generation” by 2040, where less than 5 percent of the population smokes. This is a cornerstone of Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan. But Brussels lacks the authority for a blanket ban on smoking, because health policy remains a sovereign right for states. Instead, the EU can use its fiscal and regulatory powers to dictate how tobacco is sold and promoted around the bloc.
Over the past decade, it implemented several landmark laws. The 2014 Tobacco Products Directive (TPD II) mandated graphic warnings covering 65 percent of packages and capped e-cigarette nicotine concentration at 20 mg/ml. The Tobacco Advertising Directive (2003) banned tobacco advertising, and the 2001/37/EC Directive completely banned misleading product descriptors like "light," "mild," or "low tar", forcing manufacturers to write bold, black-and-white health warnings on all cigarette packs.
The Tobacco Control Framework Evaluation found these measures successful at lowering traditional smoking rates, which fell from 28 percent to 24 percent among adults. However, it warns that these older laws left gaping loopholes that allowed high-tech nicotine alternatives, like novel products, to thrive unregulated.
The new directive
The Commission's proposed revision of the Tobacco Taxation Directive wants to make tobacco and nicotine products significantly more expensive by raising minimum duties across the EU. For example, it targets a dramatic 139 percent increase in minimum excise duties for standard cigarettes, instantly driving up the baseline retail price.
It also establishes mandatory EU-wide minimum excise taxes on vapes, heated tobacco, and nicotine pouches for the first time, and includes raw tobacco leaf in the EU's electronic tracking system to shut down underground black markets and cross-border tax evasion.
The Commission presented the proposal in July 2025. In June 2026, however, the European Parliament rejected its own advisory report on the file after political groups from across the spectrum voted against a heavily amended compromise text. Because tax legislation follows the EU's special legislative procedure, Parliament's opinion is not binding. The proposal therefore remains under discussion in the Council of the European Union, where unanimous approval from all 27 member states is required before it can become law.
"Many people think the European Parliament is deciding the future excise tax rates. We're not. We're giving an opinion that is not legally binding on the Council”, said Patriots for Europe MEP Tomas Kubin, the report’s rapporteur.
Although the Parliament failed to adopt a formal position, the legislative process continues because taxation is decided by the Council under the EU's consultation procedure.
In parallel, countries are implementing national bans within their own borders. Belgium became the first EU nation to outlaw the sale of disposable electronic cigarettes. France followed by passing its own single-usevape ban, alongside strict legislation that outlaws smoking in public parks, beaches, and school areas. The Netherlands has enforced one of Europe's toughest flavour bans by completely prohibiting every vape liquid except for basic tobacco profiles, while simultaneously drafting laws to raise the legal nicotine purchase age from 18 to 21.
What could change if the directive is adopted
If adopted, the revised directive would place huge pressure on tobacco companies by targeting their profits. The industry remains an economic giant in Europe, with total annual sales reaching approximately €130 billion across the bloc. Companies like Philip Morris International and British American Tobacco would face a direct threat to their business models as the EU introduces these new minimum taxes.
Logistically, manufacturers will no longer be able to use novel products as low-tax loopholes to offset declining traditional cigarette revenues. Furthermore, including raw tobacco into the EU's electronic tracking system will force companies to comply with strict supply chain audits, increasing their administrative and operational costs.
If the proposal is ultimately approved by all member states, European consumers would see significant changes in both the pricing and availability of nicotine products.
Public space restrictions are also tightening across several member states through separate national legislation. Belgium, France and the Netherlands have already introduced stricter rules on vaping and smoking in public places. If the revised TTD is eventually adopted, smokers across the EU would also face significantly higher prices for cigarettes and many alternative nicotine products.

====================================================================================================

Meta faces $200bn trial over child data and social media addiction by 29 states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:00:17 UTC
16:00:17 KST

More than half of the states in the US have joined together in an unprecedented lawsuit against Meta that goes to trial on Tuesday, accusing the parent company of Instagram and Facebook of deliberately designing addictive products that lured in young people and caused them harm.
The jury trial is taking place in federal court in Oakland, California, and is expected to last between six and eight weeks. The jury is expected to hear from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Instagram CEO Adam Mosseri and employee turned whistleblower Arturo Béjar.
“Meta designed a dangerous product for young users, knew it to be dangerous, and then lied to children, families and the community about how dangerous it was,” said Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general. The trial proceedings will be led by attorneys representing California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey, though the suit was filed by all 29 states in what is known as multidistrict litigation.
The 233-page lawsuit, first filed in October 2023, alleges that Meta regularly collects data on children under the age of 13 without parental permission in violation of federal and state laws. The lawmakers claim in court documents that Meta “refuses to abandon its use of known harmful features” and that its motives are based solely on profit to “maximize its financial gains”.
The sweeping legal proceedings could have profound consequences for the social media company. The attorneys general say that if Meta is found liable, damages could be as high as $200bn – an amount equivalent to the company’s 2025 annual revenue. The lawmakers are also asking that Meta be compelled to change the design of its products to make them safer for children, which may have longer-term effects than a fine.
Meta denies all allegations and says: “Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout.
“The State AGs may call this a landmark case, but their limited claims are unsubstantiated and their financial demands are vastly disproportionate,” the company said in a statement. “The AGs offer no proof anyone in their states was misled, claim benign features like having an additional Instagram account somehow harmed their residents, and attempt to penalize Meta for industry-wide challenges like age verification.”
The attorneys general also say Meta “developed and refined a set of psychologically manipulative” features designed to maximize people’s time on its apps. Those include an infinite scrolling recommendation algorithm, constant notification alerts, thumbs-up “likes”, and visual filters for altering one’s image.
The lawmakers say young people are especially vulnerable to falling prey to such features and that excessive time online can lead to increased depression, anxiety, eating disorders and other mental health issues.
Internal research conducted by Meta is expected to be presented at the trial, including, for instance, a survey of 2,500 teens conducted in 2019.
“Young people are acutely aware that Instagram can be bad for their mental health, yet are compelled to spend time on the app for fear of missing out on cultural and social trends,” the results read.
Mounting lawsuits
The federal trial comes just two weeks after a judge ordered Meta to pay $567m to New Mexico in a similar case brought by the state’s attorney general. This was the second court-ordered financial penalty for Meta in New Mexico, bringing the total it is responsible for paying the state to $942m. A state trial in Tennessee is now under way
Families, school districts and other attorneys general have brought thousands of lawsuits against Meta and other social media companies in recent years. The plaintiffs hope a death-by-a-thousand-cuts legal strategy will induce Meta to change its social networks for the better.
In California, thousands of coordinated cases have been filed in state court against Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap. Meta and YouTube lost the first of those cases to go to trial in February, being ordered to pay $6m to the young woman who brought the suit. (TikTok and Snap settled before the case went to trial.) Two more lawsuits slated to go to trial this summer, one federal and one in California state court, also settled for undisclosed sums.
The lawsuits have borrowed from the legal approach used against tobacco companies in the 1990s, which focused on cigarettes’ addictive qualities and the makers’ knowledge that their products caused harm and resulted in a $200bn in 1998 and enforced changes to cigarettes’ marketing.
Russell Coleman, the attorney general of Kentucky, said he and his colleagues are using that strategy and aim to show the jury that “Meta concealed what it knew about the harm its products cause young people”.
“AGs are in the perfect position to get this done,” he added. “We did it with the tobacco settlement in the 1990s. We did it with the companies behind the opioid crisis. We’ll do it again with Meta.”

Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson was convicted over three deaths. Now she’ll argue the court got it wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:00:17 UTC
16:00:17 KST

It was a Sunday lunch in a sleepy Australian town that was at the heart of one of the country’s most high-profile murder trials.
A central question fascinated people around the world: did Erin Patterson deliberately serve her in-laws poisoned beef wellingtons on 29 July 2023?
More than a year after a jury found Patterson had murdered her in-laws, an Australian court will consider whether her convictions should be quashed and if she should remain in prison for life without the possibility of parole.
On Wednesday, three judges of Victoria’s highest court will begin hearing two appeals – by Patterson herself and the state’s director of public prosecutions (DPP) – in the triple-murder case that attracted worldwide intrigue and intense media attention for months.
Patterson will appeal against her convictions, while the DPP will appeal against the sentence handed down to Patterson, arguing it is “manifestly inadequate”.
In September, Patterson was sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents – Don and Gail Patterson and his aunt, Heather Wilkinson. She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the lunch after spending weeks in hospital.
Patterson, who maintained her innocence throughout the 11-week trial last year, is not expected to attend court in person. The three court of appeal judges, who will consider the arguments, are expected to reserve their decision in both appeals. They will hand down their judgments at a later date.
Patterson to appeal on seven grounds
In November, Patterson, 51, filed an appeal against her convictions but did not appeal against her sentence.
The appeal is on seven grounds including the “fundamental irregularity” around sequestering the jury in the same hotel as police and media representatives, and that her cross-examination during the trial was “unfair and oppressive”.
While considering the verdict, the jury was sequestered in a hotel in a regional town where police and members of the media also stayed. According to media reports, the matter was raised with authorities by her lawyers at the time, but no concerns about the process were raised during the trial.
The appeal documents allege the sequestering issue “fatally undermined the integrity of the verdicts” and argue for the quashing of the convictions and the ordering of a re-trial.
Patterson is also appealing on the grounds that cell tower evidence – along with evidence of death cap mushroom sightings near her home – should not have been heard in the trial. The court last year heard that analysis of Patterson’s mobile phone records revealed she may have visited two locations soon after death cap mushroom sightings were reported.
She is also arguing evidence from her Facebook “friends”, who met Patterson through a true-crime group, should not have been allowed as it was not “relevant”. Patterson told a Facebook group chat that she wanted “nothing to do” with her parents-in-law, according to messages shown in court.
The other four grounds of appeal relate to Patterson’s cross-examination by prosecutors over five days, along with issues over other evidence, and the opening and closing addresses of the prosecution.
Patterson’s legal team is arguing the prosecution’s closing address caused a “substantial miscarriage of justice”. While the prosecution maintained there was no evidence of motive, Patterson’s legal team claims, this changed in the closing address to imply a motive for murder.
If Patterson is successful in her appeal, the court will quash her convictions and could order a retrial or acquit her.
Prosecution: sentence ‘manifestly inadequate’
Separately, the DPP is appealing against Patterson’s sentence, arguing that “the sentence imposed on Patterson is manifestly inadequate”, and that the trial judge erred in finding she was likely to spend “years to come” in solitary confinement when allowing for the possibility of parole.
During a pre-sentencing hearing last August, the DPP argued Patterson should not be granted a parole period because of the nature of her crimes, which the judge, Justice Christopher Beale, agreed were “horrendous”.
While the defence and prosecution agreed that Patterson should receive a life sentence for the murders, her then defence barrister, Colin Mandy SC, argued she should receive a non-parole period. Mandy argued Beale should consider the onerous conditions of her conditions in custody.
At the time of the pre-sentence hearing in August 2025, Patterson had effectively spent the past 15 months in solitary confinement, the court heard.
Beale found that Patterson would continue to be held in those conditions for years to come for her own protection due to the high-profile nature of her crimes.
If the DPP’s appeal is successful, Patterson’s non-parole period could be extended or she could be sentenced to life without parole, with no option for release.
No further documentation has been released to the media since the two appeals were lodged last year. This includes the written cases relating to the appeal.
During Patterson’s 11-week trial, the prosecution did not put forward an alleged motive but pointed to the deteriorating relationship between Patterson and her estranged husband, Simon, in the months leading up to the fatal lunch.
Patterson told the court she had accidentally served beef wellingtons containing death cap mushrooms to her lunch guests in July 2023. She raised the possibility that mushrooms she had foraged may have been in a Tupperware container which also contained store-bought dried mushrooms she said she had used in the beef wellington meal.
But the jury ultimately sided with the prosecution, finding Patterson had deliberately included death cap mushrooms in the infamous lunch meal with the intention of killing her four guests.

Here is the news from the US: Woke 1.0 is over. But what did progressives do wrong? | Nesrine Malik
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:00:16 UTC
16:00:16 KST

Every once in a while, the discourse gods send a tablet down to the people, announcing that a previous era is dead and a new age is upon us. Recently, it was the “vibe shift” – a post-pandemic change in culture that encompassed everything from fashion to politics. The vibe shift consolidated with Donald Trump’s second election, a harbinger of the end of fragility and of movements for racial and gender equality – a rejection of the long 2010s with their hashtags and pink pussy hats and women’s marches and protests. The vibe shift has recently been followed by a calling of time on what has come to be known as “Woke 1.0” – a term that represents what is now seen as a culture of hysterical overreach triggered by the momentary breakthrough of movements such as #MeToo and Black Lives Matter. “Woke 1 was crazy,” said Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez this month, quoting a New York City councilman. And there we have it, time to walk back some things said and done in the giddy heat of those moments. It was crazy!
This rush to the future away from what some perceive to be an embarrassing past groups together various disparate phenomena. But I’m afraid it’s not that simple. Woke 1.0 (or “peak wokeness” – I wish the gods would use less trivialising ways to refer to roiling social tides, but there we are) was about politics and culture and also about the behaviours and trends it triggered. It was about concrete problems: policing of minority communities, the right of women not to be sexually harassed or violated, the systemic racism and sexism that damaged both. And it was about reforming the cultural structures that created and perpetuated those systems; asking university curricula to expand and diversify intellectual sources, recognising the long shadow of glorified imperial histories, and updating institutions – from the media to the academy – in order to enfranchise change. None of this is “crazy”.
What did happen is that accompanying those movements was an adoption of postures and behaviours that signalled that one was on the right side. Some of it was performative, risible and low stakes; the black squares posted on social media and the taking of the knee in kente cloth. But some of it was more material in terms of tone, attitude and outcome. Some on social media made it their business to scold the language of others, others lost their jobs or reputations in cases that were questionable or even unjustified. A fixation on diversity and representation made a big song and dance about appointing minorities in high places, indulging the Joe Biden administration, reducing action to appearances.
A vast array of protagonists and platforms, all with different mechanics, are lumped into what is now being called an absolute “orthodoxy”. But what this part of the moment constituted was essentially two things. The first was a sort of mimetic fashion (rather than politics) that was adopted because that’s how trends work. The second was a storming-the-barricades sense that something that was too late to arrive, that was thought would never arrive, was finally upon us – an opportunity to make mainstream the sort of equalising politics that was consigned to the margins.
An altogether more serious – and shallow – allegation is that it was all “crazy” because this is what the left does. Given a chance, the left will waste capital by descending into infighting, radicalism and alienation. It is rarely acknowledged that this left never has political power, and so its energies become trapped in the realm of culture. This is not to excuse excesses, but to point out a mundane matter of physics. When a political movement is deprived of executive means, by way of democratic systems in which money and establishment interests are arrayed behind the right and the centre right, it becomes trapped outside policy and exercises its power in the only venues it can. It is a feature of weakness, not strength.
So powerful is the hold of this notion of a universally, monolithically persecuting left, that all sorts of wildly implausible ideas are being extrapolated from it. It is now being blamed for what has followed Woke 1.0: the resurgence of Donald Trump and Maga’s incursion into everything from the academy to the military in order to impose its agenda. Never mind that this “left” is a grab bag of remote, suggestible corporate liberals and online folk. In this lies the biggest logical flaw of our time – the assumption of an equivalence between social behaviours and state power. The left may have toppled a few statues. That left has not waged executive war on universities, sued and removed funding, or imprisoned students for political expression. It has not purged the military. It has not legally cracked down on protest, both in the UK and the US.
To talk about these violations as somehow the legacy of the left’s “McCarthyism” and cancel culture is to draw a staggeringly naive and motivated conclusion, one that posits that the right would simply never have had any of these ideas if it were not for wokeness.
Come on. I suspect that there is a little bit of the shame of loss here. Despite the rendering of the past few years as a time of giddy victory, the truth is that wokeness lost. It succumbed to a vicious backlash – one that is still playing out, and was grotesquely displayed in the hounding of Jason Arday. There is something embarrassing about ending up on the losing side of the battle. And so we must have just got it wrong, rather than been crushed by the media, allies and our inchoateness as a political movement far outside the halls of power.
Still, there are lessons to be learned. What follows (or, I’m sorry, “Woke 2.0”) is a time for understanding that cultural breakthrough is no guarantee of success, that the neoliberal body politic will find ways to pick up, and then discard, social justice the moment it is not profitable. There is no substitute for long-term political organisation on the grounds of policy that focuses on material concerns conjoined with solidarity with all those on the sharp end of discrimination because of their identity. But let’s not throw the baby out with the bathwater. Let us not trivialise and dismiss movements that resonated globally, and which had safety, dignity and equal opportunity at their heart. And let’s not succumb to suspect framings that are more quick to police and condemn efforts than they are to raise the alarm at powerful interests with state power. That would be crazy.
- 
  Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

Brown’s Cook Islands Party is on track to win a fifth consecutive term in government after securing 18 seats – up from its previous 12 – in last week’s election, according to preliminary results.

A defence and security declaration signed with New Zealand in April appeared to help ease those concerns, analysts said, allowing Brown to limit the political damage before last Wednesday’s election.

Why drugs are becoming more expensive to develop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Why drugs are becoming more expensive to develop
Drug development has always been expensive and risky, but now it’s measurably more so than a decade ago. Here are three reasons why.
When it comes to the pharma industry, US President Donald Trump has repeatedly accused European governments of “free-riding” on American spending, arguing that the profits generated from the US market help fund drug research and innovation that benefits the rest of the world. He has also argued that Europe should pay more for innovative medicines.
How true are his claims? Swissinfo is breaking down the figures to understand why developing new drugs are getting more expensive and where the innovation really comes from.
In 2024, the average cost of developing a new drug, from discovery to launch, reached $2.23 billion (CHF1.8 billion) for the world’s 20 biggest biopharma companies – a 65% jump from 2014, or around 25% once inflation is taken into account. The figure, published in Deloitte’s 2025 annual report on biopharma innovationExternal link, is calculated by dividing those companies’ total R&D spending by the number of drugs that made it to market, and it includes the cost of every candidate that failed. Twelve of those 20 companies experienced higher costs, suggesting the pressure is industrywide. So what’s driving the increase?
More
Drugmakers reassess Europe as Trump overhauls drug-pricing rules
More sophisticated medicines are raising development costs
Drug development has always been difficult, but the biology of today’s medicines makes it harder still, pushing up costs in research, lab work and manufacturing.
For decades the industry’s biggest sellers were simple chemical compounds taken as pills, from statins to painkillers.
“Now companies are increasingly moving into more complex areas: speciality drugs, gene therapies and highly specialised treatments for small patient populations,” Amanda Cole, a director at the UK-based non-profit Office of Health Economics, told Swissinfo.
These include monoclonal antibodies such as Keytruda, an immunotherapy used in cancer treatment. Other examples are RNA-based therapies such as the Covid-19 mRNA vaccines, and cell and gene therapies.
“These can offer real value for patients, but they also create difficult scientific and economic challenges,” Cole said. Traditionally, medicines targeted parts of the body that scientists understood well, but today’s drugs are more likely to go after biological mechanisms researchers are still piecing together – like the misfolded proteins behind Alzheimer’s, or the specific genetic mutations driving a rare cancer. That means longer research timelines and higher laboratory costs before a drug is ready to be tested in patients.
Many of the research efforts are now focused on biologics, drugs made from living cells or organisms rather than chemicals, such as insulin and many modern cancer treatments. Because these are fragile molecules, a small variation in temperature or a contamination can ruin a batch, so companies invest heavily in quality control at every step. Those higher production costs feed into the overall development bill.
Clinical trials have become more demanding and expensive
It is not only the medicines that have changed: trials themselves have got bigger, more data-heavy and harder to fill. The Tufts Center for the Study of Drug Development, a US research centre that has tracked the pharmaceutical industry for decades, estimatesExternal link that Phase 3 trials cost around $55,700 per day in direct running costs alone.
Trials today are much larger in scale and more data-heavy because they have to satisfy three audiences at once: regulators, who want more detailed evidence of safety and efficacy; insurers and national health systems, who want proof the drug delivers value worth paying for; and the doctors and patients who will ultimately prescribe and use it.
In 2025, a typical Phase 3 protocol – the master plan for the trial – included an average of 19 endpoints, the specific measurements used to judge whether the drug works. This is 30% more than in 2012, according to a studyExternal link by Tufts.
But the biggest jump is the volume of data each trial now collects. In 2012 the average Phase 3 trial gathered about 929,000 datapoints: measurements like blood-test results, scan readings, patient-reported symptoms and vital signs. But by 2025 that figure had risen to nearly six million. And each extra biopsy, MRI scan or country added to the trial requires more approvals and involves more logistics, monitoring and data-management work.
Running bigger trials is only half the challenge. Finding the right patients to participate has become harder than ever – and that, too, is pushing up costs.
As medicines have become more targeted, the pool of suitable participants has shrunk, but each one needs enough patients to produce statistically reliable results. This is especially visible in cancer and rare diseases, two areas where much of today’s R&D is concentrated.
According to IQVIAExternal link, oncology now accounts for 41% of all clinical trials, and 74% of those started in 2024 evaluated medicines for rare cancers. A new drug to treat lung cancer, for example, will not be tested on all lung cancer patients, but only on those with a specific tumour mutation, who are at a certain stage of the disease and with a specific biomarker profile.
Patient recruitment has become less efficient as a result. ResearchExternal link has found that 81% of people put forward to take part in rare-disease trials turn out to be ineligible, while more than half of those who pass initial screening still fail to be randomised into the trial. Companies therefore have to screen large numbers of patients – often using expensive tests such as biopsies, genetic sequencing and biomarker analysis – to find enough qualified participants.
When recruitment falls short, protocols are amended to relax eligibility criteria or add new sites, triggering costly resubmissions to regulators and delays.
More
The drug-pricing problem no one wants to talk about
Failure is costly – and the chances of success are falling
Success rates in drug development are falling, and each failure is enormously expensive. According to Deloitte’s 2025 report, the top 20 biopharma companies spent around $7.7 billion in 2024 alone on clinical trials for drugs that were ultimately abandoned.
According to an analysisExternal link of data from 2014 to 2023 by Citeline/Biomedtracker, the probability that a drug entering Phase 1 will eventually reach the market has fallen to 6.7%, an all-time low and down from 10.4% in Citeline’s widely cited 2014 estimate. The biggest bottleneck is Phase 2, where only 28% of trials are successful. Even in Phase 3, the longest and most expensive stage of testing, only 55% succeed.
This dynamic helps explain why the headline average cost is so high: each successful drug has to carry the expense of the many that failed along the way – and companies increasingly focus on areas where the biology is still poorly understood and thus diseases are harder to treat.
Roche’s gantenerumab, developed as a treatment for Alzheimer’s disease, shows how costly failure can be. The drug first failed a Phase 3 trial in 2014. Roche subsequently revived the programme, tested higher doses and launched two new global Phase 3 trialsExternal link, enrolling nearly 2,000 patients across 30 countries. In late 2022, both trials failed again. Roche never disclosed the full cost, but running two global trials of that size for that long almost certainly ran to several hundred million dollars – and all of it had to be written off.
The missing invoice
Even if the broad trend is clear, the development cost of any individual drug remains hard to audit, as pharmaceutical companies rarely disclose how much they spend to develop a specific medicine. Most industry estimates are averages, built from models that make very different assumptions about what should be counted: out-of-pocket spending, failed projects, or the cost of capital tied up for years in research.
This lack of transparency matters most when the conversation turns from cost to price. “It makes it impossible for regulators to check whether the price of a specific medicine can be justified by its investment,” said Patrick Durisch, health policy lead at Swiss NGO Public Eye.
Greater transparency would strengthen the hand of authorities in price negotiations, argues Severin Studer from Swiss insurer Helsana, even if Switzerland’s current pricing system does not formally use R&D costs as the basis for reimbursement decisions.
Drug developers have valid reasons for not publishing these figures: competitive sensitivity, legal exposure, and the difficulty of allocating shared costs across a portfolio. But the effect is that a debate of enormous public consequence – how far rising development costs justify increasing drug prices – is conducted without the product-level evidence needed to resolve it.

Japan seeks Australian ranges for long-range missile tests
Unknown

- Japan and Australia agreed to advance talks allowing Japan's Self-Defense Forces to use Australian ranges to test long-range missiles.
- Defense Minister Koizumi said it would be only the second such missile range arrangement Japan has secured with a foreign partner, after the United States.
Japan and Australia have agreed to begin discussions on allowing Japan’s Self-Defense Forces to use Australian test ranges for long-range missiles as Tokyo builds out its “counterstrike” capability, Nikkei reported, citing a joint press conference in Canberra between the two countries’ defense ministers.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi met with his Australian counterpart, Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles, on Tuesday. The two ministers said afterward they had agreed to advance talks on Japan’s use of Australian ranges to test its long-range strike weapons.
“We have agreed to progress a better and enhanced arrangement between Australia and Japan for Japan’s use of our missile ranges over the next decade across a range of missile capabilities,” Marles told reporters.
Koizumi said the arrangement would mark only the second time Japan has secured a missile range agreement with a foreign partner, after the United States.
“If the Japan Self Defence Forces are able to conduct test launches of stand-off missiles, such as hypersonic missiles in Australia, it would be a groundbreaking development,” Koizumi said.
Japan’s counterstrike capability refers to long-range missiles intended to strike enemy launch sites from outside their range, a posture Tokyo formally adopted as part of its 2022 national security strategy revision. Japan has been developing an upgraded, extended-range version of its Type 12 surface-to-ship missile as the centerpiece of that capability, alongside plans to acquire U.S.-made Tomahawk cruise missiles.
Japan is also developing a hypersonic weapon under its Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile program, which Koizumi’s comments suggest could be among the systems tested on Australian ranges.

Kanye ‘Ye’ West's 2026 European tour didn’t go so well, after multiple countries banned or cancelled his performances.
Now, it has been reported that the controversial US rapper will perform two high-profile stadium shows in St Petersburg in October, according to a post by the Telegram channel of Gazprom Arena - the stadium where the concerts are scheduled to take place.
If the concerts scheduled for 10 and 11 October go ahead, West would become the first major Western music star to perform in Russia since the country launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
These concerts would take place amid the ongoing controversy surrounding West, who has faced concert cancellations and performance bans this year due to his past antisemitic remarks, including praise for Adolf Hitler and the use of Nazi imagery.
Countries like England, France, Italy, Poland and Switzerland all pulled the plug on West, while the Netherlands and Turkey maintained his shows, sparking a debate on what constitutes freedom of speech in Europe.
It remains to be seen whether even these two Russian gigs will go ahead, as there has already been some criticism from conservative activists wishing to rid the country of any Western influence.
Conservative Russian lawmaker Vitaly Milonov released a video statement in which he suggested West should perform traditional Russian songs instead of his planned setlist. “Maybe after that he’ll stop his disgusting antics and become a normal person,” he said.
West’s anti-Semitic remarks began in 2022, when he made a series of offensive comments on social media which ended up getting him booted off both X and Instagram. The musician was dropped by his talent agency and fashion brands like Adidas and Balenciaga also distanced themselves from West.
West went on to post a picture of KKK robes, rescind his previous apology to the Jewish community, declare himself “a Nazi” and assert that he has“dominion over his wife”.

West apologised for his actions and took out a full-page ad in the Wall Street Journal earlier this year. He addressed his past antisemitic comments, reflecting on a "four-month-long manic episode of psychotic, paranoid and impulsive behaviour" and saying that he “lost touch with reality.”

10 new Russian bases for drones could threaten not only Ukraine - ISW
Kyiv • UNN
Russia is building new launch sites for attack drones along its border with Ukraine and Belarus, which could threaten not only Ukraine. ISW analysts warn of possible threat to NATO territory.
Russia's expansion of launch sites for Russian attack drones along the border with Ukraine and Belarus may threaten not only Ukraine, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said in a new report dated August 17, UNN reports.
Details
"Russia is expanding launch sites for its long-range attack drones along the border with Ukraine and Belarus, likely to intensify strikes against Ukraine and possibly NATO," the ISW report says.
On August 16, The Telegraph reported that Russia had built 59 new drone launch facilities at 10 different locations along its border with Ukraine and Belarus, and that each base could accommodate more than 1,000 drones. The Telegraph cited an analysis by a drone intelligence firm showing that around 20 of the new launch facilities are of significant length, indicating that Russian forces may use them to launch Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered attack drones, which can fly ranges of 450 to 850 kilometers and 950 to 1,000 kilometers, respectively.
"Russia is likely building these additional launch sites in western Russia to increase its ability to launch larger long-range drone salvos as part of Russia's regular strikes across Ukraine. Russia is also likely seeking to use Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones for deeper strikes in western Ukraine, using the drones' greater speed and survivability to penetrate Ukrainian air defenses," the ISW report says.
"Russia is also likely moving its drone launch sites to western Russia in an attempt to protect Russian drone infrastructure from Ukrainian drones," analysts noted.
As noted, "for example, Ukrainian forces successfully struck Russian drone launch sites near occupied Donetsk, so the creation of alternative launch sites farther inside Russia could improve their survivability."
"Russia may also be preparing to use its Rassvet satellite constellation (the Russian version of Starlink), using the new launch sites, which could allow Russian forces to conduct precision strikes against Ukraine's rear-area systems and air defense systems from different directions," the report states.
"The new Russian drone launch bases could also support future Russian strike packages against NATO if the Kremlin decides to do so, as the bases would allow for an increased volume of salvos, while the launch stations would provide the drones with operational range over NATO territory," ISW noted.

Brazilian restaurant adapts menus to climate challenges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
06:57:55 UTC
15:57:55 KST

One of the first restaurants in Latin America to earn three Michelin stars adapts its menus to seasonal produce, using practical, inventive solutions to cope with the growing climate volatility.
Built around a concept of seasonal cuisine, closely tied to rainfall and the natural rhythms of the climate, Tuju occupies a three-storey building in São Paulo, the Brazilian metropolis that is home to around 12 million people. Despite the city's size, meticulous attention to detail is the rule here.
The key ingredient on the menu is seasonality, which shapes every element of each dish. Here, it is the rain, or sometimes its absence, that dictates what is served.
"Here in São Paulo, there are times of year when, day after day, the weather brings us certain ingredients; there are transitional seasons, like the one we are in now; and then suddenly we have a time of year in São Paulo when 60 days go by without rain. Each of these patterns offers different products and possibilities," chef Ivan Ralston tells AFP.
The restaurant is run by chef Ivan Ralston and his partner, gastronomic researcher Katherina Cordas, who carefully think through every dish they serve. Cooking here is treated as an art, combined with improvisation and a strong capacity to adapt.
"By now, São Paulo should already be dry. Normally, July and August are dry months, but it still hasn't dried out. We've had occasional rain. This is linked to Super El Niño, which has given us a much longer mushroom season; it has lasted almost twice as long. So you always have to stay alert and adapt. In the end, it's not a fixed situation that will stay the same forever," the chef adds.
The establishment offers (source in Portuguese) tasting menus that change according to the weather conditions and rainfall patterns, which are becoming increasingly irregular in São Paulo because of global warming.
"For a 12-course tasting, our menus change every three months, so that each ingredient can be showcased at its absolute peak in terms of flavour, texture, provenance and environmental responsibility," the restaurant explains.
Three Michelin stars
In April, the restaurant secured its third Michelin star, alongside another São Paulo venue, Evvai, making the two establishments the first in Latin America to receive this culinary distinction.
The Michelin Guide (source in Portuguese) describes the venue as "a truly unique experience", and notes that the chef "draws on his experience to combine Brazilian seasonal products and flavours, particularly from São Paulo, with the most contemporary techniques".
Tuju offers four menus over the course of the year: "Humidity", "Rain", "Wind" and "Drought", which are not tied to fixed dates.
"Each season, with its distinctive climatic characteristics of humidity, rain, wind and drought, shapes an entirely new tasting menu!" the guide notes.
This award-winning gastronomic experience is not, however, within everyone's reach. Reservations must be made months in advance, and that is before mentioning the price: menus cost up to 1,650 reais, around 277 euros.
"It's a restaurant for celebrating. It's not the sort of place you come to every day just to eat and go home; it's for a special occasion," says co-owner Katherina Cordas, speaking to AFP.

Lukashenko: Domestic weapons are foundation of any army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
06:56:00 UTC
15:56:00 KST

MINSK, 18 August (BelTA) – Even in the era of drones and ballistic missiles, small arms are vital for any army, Belarusian President Aleksandr Lukashenko said during his visit to the country’s fully domestic small army manufacturing site in Minsk Oblast on 18 August, BelTA has learned.
“It is people, the soldiers, who determine the fate of a battle. And this is exactly what soldiers need. Having served as a soldier myself, I know firsthand the importance of small arms. We can do nothing without these weapons, regardless of whether we have drones, ballistic missiles, and the like,” the head of state said. Consequently, it was decided to establish domestic production in the country.
“We did it ourselves. Well done for achieving this. There can be no war, no national defense without it,” the Belarusian leader stressed. “In order to fight, you must have small arms. Therefore, this is vital. It is the foundation of any army.”
Aleksandr Lukashenko brought up the core task: “The instruction was to develop a combat weapon with 100% localization. So, there are zero imported parts?”
“Absolutely none,” Chairman of the State Authority for Military Industry Dmitry Pantus assured.
The president particularly emphasized that the domestic small arms are already in service. Defense Minister Viktor Khrenin confirmed the quality and high demand for these weapons.
“Indeed, it requires continuous refinement and polishing. However, the fact that it is entering service with the Belarusian Armed Forces proves its value. I always tell the minister when we develop the first prototypes: ‘Examine, criticize, and push it to its limits... We must refine it here, so we adopt a flawless product,’” the head of state stressed.
The president visited the Kidma Tech manufacturing facility, where he inspected a proprietary, fully localized serial production line for small arms and the first domestic model, the VSK-100B assault rifle.
Aleksandr Lukashenko examined the combat weapons and the technical production processes, offering high praise: “Great job! You did fantastic!”
However, the president urged the weapons manufacturers not to rest on their laurels: “We need to push ahead and stop fearing that something is beyond our reach. We can do anything. Yes, we need equipment, but we must know how to operate it. You have mastered this. No one should spare money for such projects. It is a monumental task, especially if it pays off through exports.”
The head of state received the very first Belarusian VSK-100B assault rifle as a gift. The inscription on the gift’s plaque reads: “Not for war... For confidence in peace!”
The president instructed to display a deactivated copy of the assault rifle at the Palace of Independence exhibition. “It was tough and challenging. Other nations, like the Russians, have spent centuries developing small arms. Under a democratic dictatorship, however, we succeeded in creating this in a very short span of time,” the Belarusian leader stressed.
Roman Golovchenko, Chairman of the National Bank’s Board and former chief of the State Authority for Military Industry, underscored that Belarus’ small arms manufacturing was built completely from the ground up, independent of any Soviet heritage or traditions. “There is no Soviet legacy here. This industry was built entirely in independent Belarus,” he stated.
Aleksandr Lukashenko recalled the early days of his presidency when he made a personal decision to halt the squandering of the nation’s military capabilities. At that time, tanks and other military hardware were being chopped up for scrap and exported. “I didn't become a dictator [as Western politicians see it] because I actually am one, but because I stopped that destruction,” the head of state said.
The president’s working visit to Minsk Oblast extended beyond defense industry matters. Seizing the opportunity, the head of state asked Governor Aleksei Kushnarenko on the status of the ongoing harvesting and winter crops planting campaigns, providing essential instructions.
Kidma Tech is a research and development company, affiliated with the State Authority for Military Industry. It focuses on the R&D, production, and sale of high-tech dual-use products, encompassing small arms, optical surveillance systems, body armor, and robotics.
Belarus launched its initiative to develop domestic manufacturing of small arms and related ammunition in 2018. This led to the creation of the VSK-100 series 7.62x39mm assault rifle, marking the first domestic weapon to enter service in early 2021. Production of the rifle originally kicked off in January 2020 utilizing semi-knocked-down assembly.
Kidma Tech has designed 5 models and 6 variants of combat small arms so far, with 4 models already entering service.
In late 2023, a presidential decree launched a project to set up a proprietary, fully localized serial production line for small arms in Belarus. This was followed by large-scale efforts to redesign and renovate existing facilities, completely upgrading engineering infrastructure to accommodate the required manufacturing equipment. The project also involved purchasing machinery, acquiring technologies, and training personnel.
Work on developing a fully localized version of the VSK-100B 7.62mm assault rifle, the country’s first domestic combat small arms model, is nearing completion.
Chambered for 7.62x39mm, the VSK-100B assault rifle is an advanced weapon utilizing an AK-based design. It supports the installation of optical and electro-optical targeting systems along with auxiliary equipment, including bipods, silencers, under-barrel grenade launchers, and knife bayonets. The design incorporates a folding adjustable stock, a storage-integrated grip, and comprises 141 individual parts.
The integration of a reinforced barrel and receiver into the VSK-100B design increases barrel durability and enhances both accuracy and shot grouping over comparable small arms. Additionally, the option for auxiliary attachments enables the assault rifle to dual-role as a light machine gun and a sniper rifle.
Beyond the VSK-100B assault rifle, the facility’s future production line is set to include the Stylet-type high-precision bolt-action rifle, the PP-919 submachine gun, and a PKM-type machine gun.
Consequently, a domestic small arms manufacturing industry has been built in Belarus virtually from the ground up. Delivering on these projects will enable the country to reach complete technological self-sufficiency in the small arms production sector over the medium term.
