A preacher and prominent conservative commentator has drawn backlash in Malaysia after questioning why a banner for a traditional Chinese festival was not written in Malay, the country’s national language.
Ridhuan Tee Abdullah, an ethnic Chinese Muslim convert known for provocative commentary on race and religion, was criticised by social media users and a Selangor politician for casting a routine notice about the Hungry Ghost Festival as an issue of language and national identity.
In a post on his social media account on Saturday, Tee questioned why the banner, which displayed information on the festival’s rites, was written in Chinese and asked whether the municipal council had monitored the organisers who put it up.
“Is this China? Where does our national language stand?” Tee wrote. “Religious freedom is assured but the national agenda must be respected.”
The Hungry Ghost Festival, also known as the Zhongyuan Festival, is celebrated by Chinese communities on the 15th day of the seventh lunar month, usually falling in August or September.

Another overnight drone attack on Moscow was the largest in the past two years, with 620 drones heading for the capital since Monday evening, according to Mayor Sergey Sobyanin.
Sobyanin said on Russian social media platform Max that 180 drones had been destroyed in the Moscow region between Monday evening and Tuesday until 5 am (0200 GMT).
“At the sites where debris fell, emergency services are working,” he said.

The latest attack also caused damage in parts of the Moscow region.

On March 11, 2025, Sobyanin described an attack as the most intensive at that time, saying 74 drones had been shot down on approach to Moscow and hundreds had been intercepted.

Instagram rolls out parental support alerts globally for teen safety
- Instagram now alerts parents globally if their teenager tries to search for suicide or self-harm terms repeatedly within a short time.
- Parents must link their accounts to their teen's via Instagram’s Family Centre to receive alerts through e-mail, text, WhatsApp, or app notifications.
- The feature was developed with expert advice and will expand to cover AI interactions related to suicide and self-harm in the future.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – Parents all over the world will be alerted if their teenager repeatedly tries to look up terms related to suicide or self-harm in a short period on Instagram, after the feature was made available globally on Aug 13.
The alerts, first announced on Feb 26, are designed to inform parents that their teen may need support while providing resources to help them manage the issue, said the social media platform, which is owned by Meta Platforms.
To receive the alerts, parents must link their account to their child’s through the supervision settings on Instagram’s Family Centre hub.
The alerts will be sent to parents via e-mail, text or WhatsApp – depending on the contact information they share with the platform – as well as through an in-app notification.
Teens under 16 need a parent’s permission to change their content settings to be less strict on Instagram, with an extra layer of monitoring that can be selected with the agreement of their child.

Russia Seeks to Lower Jet Fuel Standards Following Strikes on Oil Refineries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
06:01:54 UTC
15:01:54 KST

Russia wants to lower the standards for aviation fuel to increase its production following Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries, the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine reports.
The Ministry of Transport of the Russian Federation is proposing to allow the use of jet fuel with a freezing point of up to –50 °C instead of the current –60 °C.
There are also plans to allow the use of Russian anti-wear additives and heavier crude oil, as well as to increase a share of synthetic components.
Small and medium-sized businesses may be allowed to participate in fuel production. According to estimates by Russian officials, this could provide up to 1.8 million tons of jet fuel per year.
The intelligence report notes that at cruising altitude, temperatures outside the aircraft can drop below –50°C. If the jet fuel begins to crystallize, the resulting particles could clog the fuel system and cut off the fuel supply to the engine, potentially causing its failure.
“Russian officials are essentially proposing to cut costs by compromising the specifications of a product directly related to flight safety,” the agency said.
The intelligence added that the new additives and components still need to be tested. They may also accelerate wear and tear on parts.
Under sanctions, this means higher maintenance costs, parts shortages, and even more problems with aircraft repairs.
In early July, the Russian government imposed a ban on exports of kerosene and diesel amid shortages caused by Ukrainian attacks.
Russia planned to import jet fuel from Japan through a network of traders, using a South Korean port.
Later, Japan’s Minister of Economy, Trade, and Industry stated that Tokyo is prohibiting third countries from re-exporting its jet fuel to Russia under the sanctions regime.

As Europe’s challenges persist, where are its leaders unwinding this summer?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
06:00:56 UTC
15:00:56 KST

European leaders are trading their offices for coastlines and rural retreats. But with crises persisting across the continent, escapes are fraught with reputational risks.
Europe has slipped into its annual summer lull.
Brussels has emptied out, national parliaments are in recess, and politicians are looking to make the most of the rare opportunity to step away from the demands of public office.
But for Europe’s political class, switching off can be harder than it looks.
Europe’s crises haven’t disappeared. Russia’s continued bombardment of Ukraine, political tensions in the Middle East, economic uncertainty and wildfires that have ravaged several European countries continue to loom over governments, even as politicians seek to unwind.
Leaders find themselves measuring the length and extravagance of their escapes with particular care to avoid public fallout.
Here’s where some of Europe’s most notable leaders are spending their summer breaks.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen
The European Commission chief has not revealed where she is spending her summer break, but on 5 August wished her Instagram followers a good and restful holiday, sporting a pair of sunglasses.
A Commission spokesperson told Euronews that the President, “while currently spending some time with her family, remains in constant contact with her team in Brussels” as well as her team of Commissioners.
“While family time is important, she always follows all critical matters closely, remains fully engaged, and intervenes directly whenever needed,” the spokesperson added, explaining that the President already has official engagements scheduled for next week.
Von der Leyen is known to spend time away from official duties at her family home near Hanover, located on a farm where she keeps horses and has also spoken of raising hens and goats.
In August, she posted a video from the farm in which she introduces a hen named Chikeletta, asking her followers to suggest names for her two newly adopted chicks.
In the past, however, the Commission President’s choice of summer holidays have sparked controversy, with her August 2023 summer retreat at Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’ Cretan property sparking sharp criticism.
The EU’s top watchdog, the European Ombudsman, later said that the free-of-charge retreat revealed a “structural shortcoming” in EU ethics rules, and that the “incomprehensible” year-long delay in responding to complaints amounted to maladministration.
French President Emmanuel Macron
The French President is spending time at his official residence of Fort de Brégançon on the Côte d'Azur along with his wife, Brigitte Macron.
It’s the last summer for Macron as head of state, and the venue been the site of several high level visits during his presidency (he even hosted Russian President Vladimir Putin there back in 2019).

Yet Élysée officials are briefing French media that the President remains active politically despite his distance from Paris.
On Monday, Macron met mayors of the towns affected by the wildfires that have ravaged the Gironde region in recent weeks, while his Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has cut his holiday short to visit the affected area.
Macron has also been keeping up his telephone diplomacy while on his retreat, holding calls with Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, the Crown Prince of Saudi Arabia Mohammed bin Salman, as well as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi.
Spain’s Pedro Sánchez
Another European leader grappling with a crisis over the summer break is Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, whose government has been forced to deal with the mass entry of around 80,000 migrants to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in late July.
Since the outbreak of the crisis and his visit to the enclave on July 31, the Spanish Prime Minister has switched his Madrid office for his official residence of La Mareta on Lanzarote in the Canary Islands, and according to Spanish media has been conducting official duties from there since 1 August.

The government acknowledges that the situation in Ceuta is yet to return to normality, and estimates that around 8,000 migrants who crossed in late July remain in the enclave, with around 5,000 thought to be eligible to seek asylum or protection.
Sanchez’s critics, notably from the opposition Popular Party, have slammed the image of normality projected by the Prime Minister at a time of crisis.
Italy’s Giorgia Meloni

Isles of Scilly friendliest place in England, social division research finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
06:00:17 UTC
15:00:17 KST

The Isles of Scilly have been named as the friendliest place in England as part of a major study into social division across Britain.
All 296 local authority areas have been ranked in a new index using government data from the community life survey, measuring how often people chat to neighbours, feelings of loneliness and belonging, local pride, and levels of participation in civic life.
Scilly was followed by South Hams in south Devon, West Devon, Derbyshire Dales and Richmond upon Thames.
The area named the least friendly in England was Barking and Dagenham. The remaining areas in the bottom five were Stoke-on-Trent, Ashfield, Mansfield and Ipswich.
The index is intended to encourage people to share how their experience compares with the data, as part of the National Conversation, an engagement project that has already captured what thousands of British people think unites and divides us.
The views collected in the survey will inform a report later this year by the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion, which was set up to tackle what it describes as “the converging crises of social disconnection and division” in the UK.
Co-chaired by the former Tory home secretary Sajid Javid and the former Labour policy coordinator Jon Cruddas, the commission says its mission is to better understand the country’s state of connection and cohesion and create a shared vision for how we can live well together.
The foreword from its first report published last year said that “communal life in Britain is under threat” as a result of declining community infrastructure and institutions, weaker family units, growing inequality, dwindling trust in institutions and chronic neglect from policymakers.
The report also identifies current threats that are turning social disconnection into something more dangerous, including the mismanagement of immigration, cost of living pressures and social media-driven extremism.
The result, the commission says, is that the UK is “sitting on a tinderbox of disconnection and division”.
Cruddas, who used to be the MP for Dagenham, said: “This index is designed to get us talking. And I nearly choked on my cornflakes when my old area came rock bottom.
“I think government stats miss a lot of what really makes an area tick, including my old town. But that’s why we have developed it, to spark a conversation – because what we really want is your view on your area.”
The National Conversation survey is open until the end of August.

Burnham urged to intervene over ‘zero-hours’ custody officers in private prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
06:00:16 UTC
15:00:16 KST

Andy Burnham is under pressure to intervene in a privately run prison that is seeking to recruit custody officers on zero-hours contracts for the first time across England and Wales’ prison estate.
Managers at HMP Millsike, a category C prison for 1,500 prisoners near York operated by the outsourcing company Mitie, have signed off online adverts for £25-an-hour prisoner escort roles “on a flexible, task-based basis”.
Mitie has submitted a proposal to the Prison Service to employ people on a zero-hours contract which is “under consideration”, a government official confirmed on Monday night.
The £400m prison has about 350 empty cells because of a shortfall of staff, prison sources have confirmed. The POA, the prison officers’ union, has called on the prime minister to intervene in keeping with the government’s pledge to curb zero-hours contracts that undermine workers’ rights, security and stability.
Burnham has faced mounting pressure over the government’s early prisoner release scheme aimed at freeing up capacity, after it was revealed that the killers of the police officer Andy Harper would be freed. While the prime minister has pledged that Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers will remain in prison, he has been told he cannot exempt specific offenders from early release without also keeping about 500 other offenders who have also been convicted of manslaughter locked up.
The deputy general secretary of the POA, Mick Pimblett, said: “At a time when the government is releasing prisoners because of a chronic lack of cell space, Mitie is unable to fulfil its contractual obligations because they cannot recruit enough officers to safely staff the jail. Now they are trying to introduce zero-hours contracts by another name.
“The POA rejects this attempt to bring casualised labour into the prison system. Prison officers are committed professionals working in a highly pressured, often hostile environment. Treating them in the same way as zero-hours contractors is disgraceful.”
HMP Millsike, a training prison with up-to-date facilities, started taking prisoners in March 2025. A recent report expressed “serious concerns” over the jail, where violence levels were so high that members of the watchdog the Independent Monitoring Boards (IMB) said they only felt safe if they walked around in pairs.
Adverts placed by the Sangfroid Group on behalf of Mitie say the new prison custody officers at Millsike will escort prisoners between prisons, courts and medical appointments – tasks currently performed by full-time prison officers.
The advert reads: “Prison Custody Officer – Escort Duties, £25 per hour. Are you a former member of the UK Armed Forces, Blue Light Services, or Prison Service looking for flexible, meaningful work that fits around your existing commitments?”
It continues: “Sangfroid Group is proud to be partnering with Mitie Care & Custody, the operator of HMP Millsike, to deliver an innovative and pioneering operational support model within the UK prison estate.”
The role is to support “prisoner escort duties in locations near to the prison” and successful applicants will be given seven weeks of training, the advert says.
“If you’re looking for more routine, predictable hours, we can offer regular rotational work. This would typically involve working up to 2-3 weeks each month on a rotation basis, with deployments of up to five consecutive days at a time. Alternatively, if you prefer greater flexibility, you can join our contingent workforce, supporting ad hoc operational requirements.”
State-run prisons already recruit operation support-grade officers who staff gates and let visitors into reception. However, they are not supposed to escort, guard, handcuff or interact with prisoners, unlike Millsike’s new prison custody officers referred to in the advert.
Mitie, which is paid about £33m a year to run the prison, has faced intense criticism over its management since it opened 17 months ago.
In January, IMB said that during staff visits they noticed “inconsistent gate security”, with “doors and gates being left open”. A month later, Mitie replaced the director, who moved to a strategic role.
There were more than 1,600 vacancies for prison officers in England and Wales in June, compared with 22,000 or so currently working, according to data. While 248 prison officers joined that month, another 256 left.
According to Acas, the definition of a zero-hours contract is one where the employer does not give minimum working hours and the employee does not have to take any work offered.
Mitie said it did not offer “zero-hours” contracts to Millsike employees, pointing out that Sangfroid Group provided “contingent workers” and was responsible for the terms and conditions of staff recruited through the advert.
A Mitie spokesperson said: “HMP Millsike continues to operate in line with the ramp-up plans agreed with the Ministry of Justice, with staffing and recruitment aligned to the prison’s phased population buildup. We remain focused on maintaining a safe, secure and supportive environment for prisoners and colleagues.”
A government spokesperson said: “Our dedicated prison officers work around the clock to keep our prisons running and the public safe, and prison officer contracts will always be compliant with employment law.
“We inherited a prison capacity crisis after places increased by just 500 in 14 years, and are pulling every lever possible to fix this – building 14,000 new places with 3,200 already delivered.”
Sangfroid Group has been approached for comment.

Student bank accounts: don’t be swayed by the freebies, freshers told
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
06:00:16 UTC
15:00:16 KST

In the scramble to sort out university accommodation, join freshers group chats and work out how a student loan payment is meant to stretch across a whole term, there is one big decision that is easy to put off but worth getting right: which student bank account to open.
Student accounts work like any other current account but come with two extras that don’t apply to the general public: an interest-free overdraft, and a lot of perks designed to hook you in as a customer for life.
However, while it is tempting to choose an account on the strength of the free cash, vouchers or other goodies, personal finance experts advise you not to be swayed by the extras.
“An interest-free overdraft could provide greater value over the course of a degree than a one-off freebie,” says Caitlyn Eastell at Moneyfactscompare.co.uk.
The ranking of the best student bank accounts for 2026-27 by the website Save the Student also places an emphasis on the size of the interest-free overdraft. “Maintenance loans now fall short of living costs by an average of £502 per month,” says Tom Allingham, the site’s student banking expert.
Its top picks for this year are the NatWest/Royal Bank of Scotland (RBS) student account, Nationwide FlexStudent and the Santander Edge student account.
To help you make your own mind up, here’s what’s on offer.
Santander Edge student current account
Freebies: a free four-year 16-25 Railcard, which is good for a third off most rail fares in Great Britain, as well as discounts on the tube when linked to an Oyster card. For students who travel home regularly, it is one of the more valuable perks on the market, potentially saving hundreds of pounds a year.
Interest-free overdraft: £1,500 in years one to three, but up to £2,000 in year five (if relevant).
Anything else? A prize draw: everyone who opens an account between 14 July and 16 October and makes a debit card purchase by the end of December is guaranteed at least £20, with one lucky student walking away with £100,000. Further prizes of £10,000, £1,000 and £100 are also on offer.
NatWest/RBS student account
Freebies: £100 cash, plus a four-year Tastecard subscription, which gets you money off at thousands of restaurants and cafes across the UK. NatWest says the Tastecard is worth £79.99 a year, although at the time of writing it was on sale for £39.99.
Interest-free overdraft: up to £2,000 from the second term of the first year (up to £500 available from day one), rising to up to £3,250 from year three onwards – one of the largest on the market.
Anything else? RBS is running an identical offer to NatWest for students in Scotland.
Nationwide FlexStudent
Freebies: £100 cash plus £120 in Just Eat vouchers, paid as £10 a month for a year. To unlock the offer, students need to pay in £500 and make five debit card payments by 11 December.
Interest-free overdraft: up to £1,000 in year one, up to £2,000 in year two and up to £3,000 in year three. (Your limit stays at £3,000 if your course is longer.)
Anything else? You could get a “Fairer Share” payment: each year since 2023, Nationwide has paid £100 to eligible members with a qualifying current account and savings or mortgage. Also, there are no fees for using the debit card abroad.
Lloyds/Bank of Scotland student account
Freebies: £100 to anyone who opens (or switches to) the account and pays in at least £500 by 30 October, plus up to £120 in Deliveroo vouchers – paid as £20 a month for six months to those making 20 or more debit card payments each month between November and April.
Interest-free overdraft: up to £1,500 in years one to three, rising to £2,000 for those studying on courses of four years or more.
Anything else? Both let you earn up to 15% cashback on everyday spending with selected retailers. Lloyds is also offering a prize draw in which five students will each win £9,790 – equivalent of a year’s maximum tuition fees in England.
HSBC Student bank account
Freebies: none at the time of writing.
Interest-free overdraft: up to £1,000 from day one, then up to £2,000 in year two, and up to £3,000 in year three.
Anything else? Access to HSBC’s 5% regular saver account, and to discounts via its home&Away offers programme.
Barclays Student Additions account
Freebies: none at the time of writing.
Interest-free overdraft: up to £500 from day one, rising to £1,000 in year one, and then up to £1,500 in year two and beyond.
Anything else? Not much to shout about this year.
TSB student bank account
Freebies: none at the time of writing, but the account pays a generous 5% (variable) interest on balances up to £500 – worth up to £25 a year.
Interest-free overdraft: up to £500 during the first six months, then up to £1,000 from months seven to nine, then up to £1,500 from month 10 onwards.
Anything else? Nothing of note.
Whichever account you choose, remember that the overdraft is not free money forever: once you graduate, most accounts convert into a graduate account that gradually withdraws the interest-free borrowing over a year or two, after which unpaid balances start accruing interest like any other loan.

Transylvania beyond the spooky castles: a family adventure in Romania’s mountains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
06:00:16 UTC
15:00:16 KST

As the sun disappears behind the high tree line, our campfire spits and crackles. Four plump trout are sizzling on a flame-heated slab of rock, a cooking technique used by people in the Gurghiu mountains, part of Transylvania’s Eastern Carpathians, for centuries. Apart from gentle birdsong, it’s the only sound up here, 1,550 metres above sea level and far from any town or village.
“This area is very wild,” says Samir Teslovan, who drove us up through the densely forested peaks from his guesthouse in Toplița. “When I come here to the mountains, I charge my battery, charge my soul. I feel free, like the wind.”
Sitting on the edge of a fragrant forest of spruce, fir, beech and pine, our view stretches over the valley to misty mountains receding in layers to the horizon. Samir points to a far-off peak in the east, a pyramid on a ragged ridge. “That’s Ukraine, maybe 200km,” he tells us. Then, pointing west: “That way, 400km, is Hungary.” The forest is still home to bears, wolves and lynx, but it’s the solitude that brings him here. “I prefer wild zones, where no one goes,” he says. “There are places here that nobody knows.”
Across the vast forests and mountains of Harghita County in central Romania, there are many places that nobody knows. In fact, the whole region has flown under the radar of international travellers – 85% of visitors come from Romania itself, which feels bizarre when you discover the wonders here, as we did on a 12-day family road trip, staying at self-catering lodges and cabins along the way.
A holiday here costs a fraction of what it would in the Dolomites or the French or Swiss Alps. Even better, it’s remarkably uncrowded, which makes for a more authentic-feeling adventure.
The region previously belonged to the Austro-Hungarian empire, but Transylvania, including Harghita, was awarded to Romania after the first world war. The local population remains largely of Hungarian descent (about 85%), with most people identifying as Székelys (Szeklers), a distinct, Hungarian-speaking cultural group. And the Hungarian influence can be seen in the region’s food, from goulash to kürtőskalács (chimney cakes), and in the ornately carved székelykapu (wooden gates) outside houses.
We pick up a hire car in Brașov and drive north, in the opposite direction to Bran Castle and all the vampiric hoopla. Soon, we’re enjoying wide, open countryside, sharing the road with farmers on horse-drawn carts and passing churches with silvery spires and white storks nesting on top of electricity poles.
Our first base is Sâncrăieni, staying in Organicle Lodge, a lovely, quiet cabin with an upstairs spruce bedroom, spacious lounge and kitchen. While our four-year-old son races around the garden with the owners’ cats and French bulldog, we rest on our wooden deck, drinking Harghita beer, looking over a paddock, where a brown horse and white pony gambol and graze, and out towards the Harghita mountains. In the evenings, swifts flit about and white storks glide across pink skies.
We spend time at nearby Lacul Sfânta Ana (Saint Anne Lake), the only volcanic lake in Romania, wandering first through Mohoş Peat Bog, where the trees and curious plant life make it feel like stepping back into the ice age, then take a boat trip on the sparkling lake, surrounded on all sides by shades of forest green. In the evening, we head to Medveles Székelyföld observatory, where we watch four bears feeding on corn that’s laid out for them; Harghita has one of the highest bear population densities in Europe. The best sighting of our trip, though, comes during our drive to the lake, when we spot a mother and cub ambling through the forest and sniffing the air by the roadside.
Heading farther north, we spend a couple of days at Vila Adela, near Lacu Roșu (Red Lake), an orange house decorated with red geraniums, with fairy houses, windmills, animal statues, see-saw and slide in the garden. Our bedroom looks out on to the majestic limestone massif Suhardul Mic.
Later, we drive through Bicaz Gorge, gazing up at massive rock walls and structures, dominated by Piatra Altarului (Altar Rock), the summit marked with a metal cross. Stopping to climb the tower of medieval manor house Lázár Castle en route, we reach Toplița at the far north of the county, staying at Casa Samir, where Samir and his son David run wildlife photography and nature tours.
After a steep and bumpy afternoon drive, we go hiking in the serene Gurghiu mountains. Golden sunlight winks through the trees as David points out the tracks of wild animals as we walk to where his father has parked and started a campfire. Along with trout, Samir serves a homemade salty sheep’s cheese, called burduf, and lamb sausage, both from his farm, and a bottle of palinka, a warming plum brandy. “I’ve been coming here all my life,” he tells us. “My grandfather and great-grandfather came here. I listen to the silence and the sounds of the forest, the birds and wild animals.”
Looping back around through the county, we make one final stop at Turul Guesthouse, a row of neat, two-storey, wooden lodges with hot tubs and a big trampoline. We wander among detailed models of Transylvanian castles, palaces, and churches, including Bran Castle, at Mini Transylvania Park and large-scale, moving models of ants, butterflies and the like at neighbouring Insect Park.
One morning, we hike up to the top of Harghita Mădăraș, at 1,801m (5,909ft) the highest peak in the Harghita mountains. Thunder rumbles and rain drenches us, as we reach the gold, white and blue Székely flag, the reportedly magnificent views blocked out by cloud that gives a sombre, funereal atmosphere to the cairns, flags, crosses and other memorials clustered around the summit.
We watch more bears at a tucked-away forest hide outside the Băile Homorod resort, including two mighty females who look as if they might clash over the feeding area, and spend one of our last afternoons at Zetea lake, where we take out a kayak. “It’s really a beautiful experience to be on the water,” Előd Tímár, co-owner of KayaKing, tells us. “Bears sometimes come to drink on the shore.”
Paddling south towards a forested peninsula, we’re surrounded on all sides by swaying trees. We pause in the vast expanse of open water and put down the paddles to float and drift for a while, and there it is again: a glorious, battery-charging feeling of peace, nature and being free, like the wind.
The trip was provided by Visit Harghita. Graeme stayed at Organicle Lodge (from £75 a night), Vila Adela (£50), Casa Samir (£43 B&B) which offers mountain adventures from £94 per person, and Turul Guesthouse (£87). Bear-watching at Medveles Székelyföld £35pp and at Băile Homorod £25pp. Kayaking with KayaKing from £6.50 per hour

Clamping down: China tightens exit rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
06:00:11 UTC
15:00:11 KST

Clamping down: China tightens exit rules
The Chinese government announced new border regulations in late July in a move seen as expanding state control over its citizens. The new rules, which come into effect on September 15, tighten checks on travellers and provide new grounds for restricting Chinese citizens from leaving the country, including exit bans of up to three years in some cases.
In a document published on July 31, China's State Council announced that, in order to “preserve national sovereignty and interests”, border control officials could require travellers to provide additional information and documents about their reasons for travelling.
Those who provide false documents or statements could be prohibited from entering or leaving the country. Chinese nationals who have “acquired travel documents by deceit” or have been involved in “exiting or entering the country illegally” could face an exit ban of between six months and three years in addition to existing punishments, according to the new rules.
The ban can also apply to citizens who have “participated in illegal activities” or “threatened national security and interests” while abroad.
The new articles also state that Chinese citizens can be prohibited from leaving the country if they “violate” regulations on the import and export of technology, and if these violations endanger China’s “industrial or technological security”.
In March, Beijing imposed a travel ban on two co-founders of Manus, a Chinese AI company that Meta had planned to acquire for $2 billion.
China blocked the acquisition plan in April, and the Financial Times reported that the ban is soon to be lifted.
In a country where overseas travel is already heavily scrutinised, and where some civil servants are required to surrender their passports to their employers, the new rules have prompted intense discussion on social media. Some Chinese netizens have questioned whether they will still be able to travel abroad freely once the regulations come into force.
Meanwhile, analysts have warned that the regulations could formalise and expand existing exit restrictions.
'Leave while you still can'
In a post on X that was widely quoted by Chinese-language media, Henry Gao, a law professor at Singapore Management University, called for people in China to "leave while you still can".
"These regulations represent another major step in transforming the right to leave China into a privilege granted at the discretion of the state," he wrote.
In an interview with FRANCE 24, Gao said that while the new border rules do not significantly expand formal state power, they consolidate and codify existing regulations and “long-standing enforcement practices that already contained significant ambiguity and room for discretion".
"What the regulations mainly do is give enforcement agencies an explicit basis in written rules for what they were already doing," China legal expert Christopher Nye and policy analyst Charles Sun of the Jamestown Foundation said in an emailed response.
"What changes is the level of specificity," they said, adding that border officers now have "express authority" to review whether a traveller's stated purpose for leaving the country is "truthful".
"Standardisation of this kind lowers the cost of routine enforcement, and officials no longer need case-by-case approval from above to keep a citizen in the country."
For individuals barred from leaving, the practical avenues for challenging the decision may be limited.
Citing Article 6, Gao said authorities can prohibit individuals from leaving the country on national security grounds without providing detailed reasons, making such decisions difficult to challenge.
"Such measures are often insulated from robust judicial review, leaving affected individuals with few realistic remedies beyond administrative channels that rarely provide transparent reasoning or independent oversight," he said.
While the regulations call for anyone facing an exit ban to be notified and outline the channels for appeal, in some cases authorities can decline to notify the individual in question where doing so could affect national security or a criminal investigation.
As a result, individuals may not learn they are subject to an exit ban until they attempt to leave the country.
"The US State Department [notes in an] advisory ... that people usually discover an exit ban only when they try to leave, with no way to learn how long it will last," Nye and Sun wrote, adding that cases related to national security are rarely tried in Chinese courts.
“The person has nothing to appeal against and no record that the state ever acted.”
Beyond China's borders
While the new regulations are primarily aimed at controlling who can enter and leave China, experts say they could also strengthen Beijing's ability to exert pressure on Chinese nationals over activities carried out abroad.
Watch more'China Targets': New investigation explores how Beijing extends its repression worldwide
“China has long asserted personal jurisdiction over certain offences committed abroad by its nationals, but historically this was more clearly associated with more serious crimes,” Gao said.
The new rules "broaden the practical reach of enforcement by extending consequences – such as post-sentence exit bans – to a wider range of offences, including those that may be vaguely framed".
Noting the potential for human rights abuses, Nye and Sun warned that individuals participating in advocacy activities abroad, where those activities are legal, could nevertheless face sanction when they return to China, as could their families.
"The effect is to project the party-state's standards onto Chinese nationals everywhere and to hold those standards over them as a standing threat against the ordinary exercise of freedoms abroad."
According to a 2024 report published by Safeguard Defenders, a human rights NGO, the Chinese Communist Party has been steadily expanding its use of exit bans. Beijing is increasingly barring human rights activists and journalists from leaving the country, or using restrictions on their family members to pressure them to return to China.
"This is less a dramatic expansion of legal jurisdiction in principle than a notable expansion of enforcement leverage and extraterritorial pressure in practice," Gao said.
"Beijing has spent the past decade extending the reach of its own law in order to extend its influence and protect party-state interests, and this is one more concrete instance of the long-arm jurisdiction it has been testing," Nye and Sun noted.
Foreign nationals
The regulations also contain provisions affecting foreign nationals, although the risks for them are different from those facing Chinese citizens.
Article 5 states that foreign nationals could be barred from entering China for between one and five years if they provide false information or statements when applying for a visa or seeking entry at the border.
Analysts say those who face particular risks include foreign nationals who were formerly Chinese citizens, as Beijing does not recognise dual nationality.
US seismologist Chen Youlin, a naturalised US citizen, is facing espionage charges after travelling to Beijing to visit family in November 2024.
Watch moreFamily of detained US scientist breaks silence after quiet diplomacy stalls
Taiwanese nationals, meanwhile, may also face increased risks, as Beijing does not view them as foreign nationals.
Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council (MAC), the official body responsible for cross-strait affairs, has warned of heightened risks for Taiwanese travelling to China.
"China is not a country governed by the rule of law, the rules are abstract and open to interpretation," MAC Minister Chiu Chui-cheng told a press conference earlier this month.
"If they (the Chinese government) ban you from leaving, then you're not leaving."
According to MAC figures, as of August 14, a total of 416 Taiwanese citizens remain stuck in China, including 226 who have been detained, 156 who are missing and 34 who are being questioned.
Growing distrust
China's new border rules reflect a broader contradiction within the country, some analysts say. As China's economic and military power has grown, so too has the government's concern over security and control.
Gao said the new rules were notable not simply because they give border officials greater discretion, but because they apply that discretion to Chinese citizens seeking to leave the country.
While border authorities in many countries have powers to restrict entry, he noted, restrictions on citizens leaving their own country are generally reserved for specific legal circumstances and are typically accompanied by clearer grounds and avenues for judicial review.
Li Shaomin, a sociologist and professor at Old Dominion University, noted in a post on X that during the Mao era, travelling abroad was largely reserved for people trusted by the state. Today the situation has been reversed, with those closest to the regime often facing the greatest restrictions on their ability to travel.
“Not only is there a lack of trust in the general public, but there is an even greater lack of trust in its own [party] officials – in the very people it has promoted,” he wrote.
Beijing does not want to return to the complete isolation of the Mao era but instead seeks a more selective form of openness, according to Li: “An open economy but with people under heavy control.”
The new entry and exit regulations are not an isolated measure but reflect a broader tension between an increasingly powerful country and a government that is increasingly insecure about its own stability.
“Under a one-party dictatorship, this is a contradiction that cannot be resolved,” Li said.

Want to block gambling ads? Soon, this is how you will do it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:59:31 UTC
14:59:31 KST

How and when the proposed gambling advertising opt-out register will work
The government is moving to make opting out of gambling ads online as easy as paying a bill.
It is part of a deal with the Coalition to pass gambling ad reform through parliament, legislation that would also include changes to how gambling companies can induce people to place bets, and an ad blackout either side of live sports games.
The government is warning the opt-out mechanism will be complicated to build, and could take a long time to implement.
But in essence, the goal is to allow families and individuals to tell companies and platforms they do not want to see gambling ads when they log in online.
Critics of the government's proposed reform say it goes nowhere near far enough to address real gambling harm, pointing to the vast majority of recommendations from the government's own 'You Win Some, You Lose More' report from 2023 that are not being adopted.
The Greens have gone so far as to suggest the gambling overhaul is purposely convoluted, and have doubted the communications watchdog's ability to manage the opt-out register.
Here is what we know.
How would I opt out of gambling ads?
The details are slim at this stage, but the ABC understands people would be able to opt out by submitting details, such as their email and the platform they hold an account with, to the register.
It is not yet clear whether the register would then pass that information to the platforms, or if they would be required to check their lists against the opt-out register proactively.
Ultimately, the idea is that the online platforms would be required to stop showing gambling ads to anyone on the register.
In parliament on Monday, Communications Minister Anika Wells described it as a "one-stop shop" for Australians.
"It is expected that the government's reforms will respond to these concerns by introducing new restrictions on inducement-based marketing and establishing the wagering advertising opt-out register, which will provide Australians with a one-stop shop to opt out of seeing wagering advertising on online platforms," she said.
Doesn't opt-out already exist?
Yes, on some platforms.
For example, SBS has an option to opt-out on gambling ads on its streaming platform.
But the Senate inquiry that looked at the proposed changes to gambling ads heard that only 1 per cent of SBS viewers chose to opt out.
It is likely that, in part, that is because people either did not know it was an option, or found it too hard to figure out how to click the right button.
Already, the government's proposal includes what is called a "triple-lock" mechanism.
It would force social media and streaming companies to turn off gambling ads to users 18 and under, and give adults the option to opt out.
That has been criticised as too onerous for the user, with some advocates calling for an opt-in mechanism instead, an idea the prime minister has firmly rejected.
A centralised register, like the one being considered in this deal, would help to make it easier for people who want to turn off gambling ads across all their online accounts in one fell swoop.
The "triple lock" would also remain for people to manually opt out from a specific platform.
There is also BetStop, a scheme administered by the federal government, for people who want to be stopped from gambling altogether.
BetStop is the national self-exclusion register and allows users to prohibit themselves from engaging in online and phone gambling for a minimum of three months, up to a lifetime.
Gambling companies are also barred from sending marketing messages and offering inducements once someone has self-identified on BetStop.
Who will be in charge of the opt-out register?
The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) would be in charge of building, administering and monitoring the scheme.
The government has introduced legislation that would require betting companies to pay for it, as they do with BetStop, via a levy.
Initially, ACMA said they had not received extra resourcing to implement the changes coming with whatever version of the bill passes parliament.
But the government has since clarified the regulator will get extra help to regulate the new laws.
What don't we know yet?
Quite a lot.
The full details of the deal have not been made public, but we know the Coalition will be asking for more amendments beyond the opt-out register in exchange for their support.
We do not know a whole lot about how the government plans to make the one-stop opt-out shop happen, noting the difficulty of sharing data and matching emails across multiple platforms and services.
The broader changes to gambling ads are expected to take effect from July 1 next year, but it is clear the opt-out register would not be ready by then.

Einstein’s biggest “mistake” came back — and changed cosmology forever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:58:07 UTC
14:58:07 KST

Einstein’s biggest “mistake” came back — and changed cosmology forever
- Date:
- August 18, 2026
- Source:
- Universe Today
- Summary:
- Einstein’s abandoned cosmological constant made a spectacular comeback when astronomers discovered that the universe’s expansion is accelerating. It now sits at the heart of our best cosmological model—a model that works extraordinarily well, yet may still be wrong.
- Share:
A little more than a century ago, Albert Einstein turned his attention from gravity itself to the fate of the entire universe. In 1917, shortly after developing his general theory of relativity, he began applying his new equations to cosmology. General relativity had transformed our understanding of gravity, so it made sense to ask what those same equations said about the universe on the largest possible scales.
Gravity was the natural place to start. On average, the universe is electrically neutral, which means electromagnetism does not dominate its large-scale behavior. Einstein also knew nothing about the strong and weak nuclear forces (to be fair, nobody did), but those interactions only operate over very short distances.
Einstein's Unexpected Dynamic Universe
For cosmology, gravity determines how matter behaves across enormous distances. If you imagine a collection of matter representing "a universe," Einstein's equations can tell you how that collection should evolve.
What Einstein found surprised him. General relativity did not naturally describe a universe that remained unchanged forever. Instead, the equations pointed toward a dynamic cosmos that would either expand or contract. That conclusion conflicted with the prevailing view at the time, which held that the universe was static and had remained essentially the same throughout cosmic history.
Einstein responded by adding a "cosmological constant" to his equations, represented by the Greek letter Lambda. General relativity already allowed such a term. In simple terms, it acts like a gravitational influence built into spacetime itself, one that can exist even in otherwise empty space. Depending on its value, that effect can produce either attraction or repulsion. Einstein selected a value that counteracted the gravitational pull of matter, allowing the universe to remain stable.
That solution did not last long.
An Expanding Universe Changes Everything
Within a few years, Edwin Hubble would discover that the universe is expanding. Meanwhile, theorists such as Russian cosmologist Alexander Friedmann took Einstein's equations more literally and developed the theoretical foundation that would help support the Big Bang theory.
Einstein eventually abandoned the cosmological constant. He would later tell friends that introducing it had been his "greatest blunder."
Then came another major surprise.
Fast forward to 1998. Two teams of astronomers were trying to resolve a long-running disagreement over how much matter the universe contained. Different observations had produced very different estimates, with some suggesting there was relatively little matter and others indicating much more.
Astronomers already knew that the universe was expanding. Because matter produces gravity, however, that matter should have been gradually slowing the expansion. By measuring how strongly the expansion was decelerating, researchers hoped to determine how much matter was actually out there.
Instead, they discovered the opposite.
The Universe Was Speeding Up
The expansion of the universe was not slowing. It was accelerating.
The observations still indicated that the universe contained relatively little matter, but even that matter was not enough to explain what astronomers were seeing. Something appeared to be pushing cosmic expansion to proceed faster over time.
The simplest explanation was a familiar one: Einstein's cosmological constant. A constant background effect that produces cosmic repulsion could account for the observed acceleration. Decades after Einstein had discarded the idea, his supposed mistake returned as the leading explanation for the new data.
Dark Energy Reshapes Modern Cosmology
During the 1980s and 1990s, cosmologists had developed an increasingly sophisticated framework that became known as the Standard Model of Cosmology (physicists have a penchant for calling cohesive, collaborative, consensus models "Standard"). But the discovery that cosmic expansion was accelerating meant that model could no longer stand in its existing form.
Its replacement became our current best description of how the universe has evolved since the Big Bang: LCDM cosmology.
The Lambda refers to the cosmological constant, which is also known as dark energy. CDM stands for cold dark matter, the type of matter believed to account for most of the mass in nearly every galaxy. Cold dark matter is a story of its own. Here, the focus is Lambda.
A Remarkably Successful Model With a Problem
LCDM has been extraordinarily successful. It is also surprisingly simple, relying on only a handful of adjustable parameters and a small number of assumptions within the framework of general relativity.
Despite that simplicity, the model can account for an enormous range of observations. It describes the expansion history of the universe, the appearance of background radiation, the BAO feature, the growth of galaxies, the development of large-scale cosmic structure, and much more.
LCDM has become one of the most thoroughly studied and extensively tested theories in ALL of science.
And it is almost certainly wrong.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Universe Today. Original written by Paul Sutter. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

====================================================================================================

A 'huge' trade-off: One Nation's pitch for cheaper cigarettes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:57:06 UTC
14:57:06 KST

In brief
- One Nation has proposed slashing the tobacco tax by 75 per cent to address the surge in black market activity.
- Experts are divided on whether cheaper cigarettes would weaken organised crime networks or undermine decades of tobacco control efforts.
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has vowed to slash the tax on tobacco by 75 per cent and dramatically reduce the price of legal cigarettes, arguing the move would curb the booming black market.
Illicit tobacco trade in Australia has expanded rapidly since 2020. The value of illicit tobacco attempting to enter the market has soared from $1.74 billion in 2018-19 to more than $6.4 billion in 2023-24, according to Australian Taxation Office estimates.
Meanwhile, government revenue from the tobacco excise — the tax applied to legal tobacco products — has plummeted and is forecast to continue declining.
"Labor has not only lost the revenue, it has lost control of the black market in illegal tobacco," Hanson said in her announcement on Tuesday.
Hanson said her party would also pause indexation on the excise for three years, saying the policy, if passed through in full, would reduce the price of a $46.50 legal packet of cigarettes to around $21 to $22.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Tobacco is subject to a high excise to keep prices high and discourage smoking. Currently, excise duty rates increase by 5 per cent each year, in addition to routine indexation.
"This is not about encouraging smoking. It is about restoring the rule of law and breaking the black market," Hanson said.
Labor has previously resisted calls to cut the excise. On Tuesday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government was not considering a cut and its focus was on compliance.
What could a policy like this accomplish? Experts have mixed views on how it would impact crime, public health and government revenue from the excise.
The public health perspective
The use of illicit tobacco has surged in recent years, raising alarm bells for public health experts despite an overall decline in smoking rates.
Laura Hunter, CEO of the Australian Council on Smoking and Health, told SBS News making cigarettes cheaper would have "huge ramifications for the health of Australians".
"Australia now has the lowest smoking rates that we've ever recorded, and that's the result of decades of policies that are designed to make cigarettes less affordable, less available in the community, and less normalised," she said.
Hunter rejected the idea that legal tobacco prices were the primary driver of the black market, arguing its growth was being fuelled by international organised crime networks mass producing illicit tobacco.
"Our tobacco laws in Australia were never designed to combat sophisticated organised crime groups," she said.
She said crackdown measures across the country, including efforts to strengthen tobacco laws and enhance on-the-ground enforcement, were starting to turn the tide, and urged state and territory governments to continue tightening legislation.
She also disputed the argument that lowering the excise would hinder the illegal market's price advantage.
"You can't price match criminals," she said.
Last year, the Australian Medical Association's president said calls to reduce the excise were "misguided" and backed by big tobacco.
"There's absolutely no evidence to support the idea that reducing excise will impact illegal tobacco — in fact the evidence says the opposite," Danielle McMullen said.
"Jurisdictions that have reduced the excise [are] seeing a horrible combination of increased smoking rates and no tangible impact on the illegal tobacco trade."
Tobacco use carries serious health risks and is a leading cause of preventable illness and death.
How could it impact revenue?
Legal cigarettes now cost upwards of $40 a pack, with the excise accounting for the bulk of the price.
The revenue from the excise increased steadily until 2020, when it began to fall from a high of $16.3 billion to $7.8 billion in the 2024-25 financial year.
Analysis last year from the e61 Institute, which describes itself as a not-for-profit, non-partisan economic research institute, found cutting the tobacco excise might not be enough to draw smokers back to legal products, and could worsen government revenue declines.
Even if legal cigarettes fell to around $21 a pack under One Nation's proposal, they would still be substantially more expensive than many illicit products.
Fei Gao, a taxation lecturer in the University of Sydney's School of Accounting, Governance and Regulation, told SBS News it's "too late" to cut the excise, and any such move would have needed to occur several years ago.
"I don't think it's going to be an incentive for people to switch back to the legal product," she said. "When the customers are gone, they're gone. They will only go back if you can beat the price."
Gao said the likely result would be an even faster decline in government tobacco excise revenue.
Australia, a world leader in smoking reduction measures, introduced graphic health warnings in 2006 and pioneered plain packaging laws.
Gao noted that legal tobacco manufacturers face costs that illicit operators do not, making it difficult to compete on price with black-market products.
A criminologist's view
James Martin, associate professor in criminology at Deakin University, studies the illicit tobacco trade. He argued the growth of Australia's black market was primarily driven by tobacco excise increases.
He said organised crime groups had captured a growing share of the market by offering much cheaper products, while government efforts to tackle the trade through enforcement have yielded limited results.
"We've seen massive investment in law enforcement over the last few years, and it's been accompanied by record arrests, record seizures," he told SBS News.
"But the actual impacts on the market have been negligible."
Martin said reducing the excise could shrink the illegal market and lure consumers back into regulated channels, arguing that criminal groups would be unable to compete with the efficiency of legal manufacturers.
While public health advocates warn cheaper cigarettes could increase smoking rates, Martin notes that illicit tobacco is already widely available at low prices across Australia.
He said enforcement would remain important, but would not be effective until a "critical mass of consumers" could be diverted back to the legal market.

Fear grips children after deadly earthquake in eastern Indonesia leaves thousands displaced

Fear grips children after deadly earthquake in eastern Indonesia leaves thousands displaced
LAMBA LEDA, Indonesia (AP) — Thousands of people remained displaced on the Indonesian island of Flores on Tuesday, three days after a powerful earthquake killed at least 70 people, injured nearly 1,200 others and damaged thousands of homes. The disaster left many children struggling with fear and trauma.
More than 40,000 people were sheltering in tents, evacuation centers and makeshift camps after the earthquake struck off Flores, a remote island in East Nusa Tenggara province, early Saturday, damaging at least 11,925 homes, according to the National Disaster Management Agency.
The quake caused widespread destruction across the island, damaging 172 health facilities, 658 schools, 187 offices and 172 places of worship, the local disaster agency said.
At crowded evacuation camps across Flores on Tuesday, children played under tarpaulin shelters while aid workers and volunteers provided psychosocial support alongside food and medical assistance.
The quake occurred at a depth of 10 kilometers (6 miles) shortly before 6 a.m. Saturday, according to the U.S. Geological Survey, and residents fled in panic as tsunami warnings were issued but later lifted. Authorities recorded more than 2,100 aftershocks into Tuesday, though only 70 were felt by residents.
Fear and painful memories haunt survivors
An aftershock that struck during an interview Tuesday prompted Vincentius Rano and his wife to instinctively duck and cover their heads. Nearby, their daughter began crying, a reminder of the fear that continues to haunt many survivors.
Rano is a resident of Lamba Leda, one of the hardest-hit villages in the lush hills of East Manggarai regency, where widespread damage was reported, with at least 50 homes shattered and trees toppled over. He recalled the terrifying moment the earthquake struck Saturday just after he and his wife had woken up.
“Suddenly, we felt a tremor that kept getting stronger,” said Rano, the father of a 5-year-old girl. The couple rushed to grab their sleeping daughter, but before they could escape, part of the house came down, causing injuries to his back and shoulder.
“We didn’t have time to get outside. Everything happened so fast. The roof collapsed on us, and all I could do was shield my wife and child with my back,” Rano said, gesturing toward his flattened home, a modest house, built of timber rather than concrete.
Children in shelters treated for trauma
Psychosocial support programs, which combine mental health treatment and social care, are being rolled out across the region hit by the earthquake. Children have been encouraged to read books and join counselors for games, educational activities and group activities designed to help them cope with fear and anxiety.
“For many survivors, especially children, the psychological impact has lingered long after the shaking stopped,” said local police chief Yudhi Franata, who organized trauma-healing sessions for children displaced by the disaster in Ende regency.
Parents at an evacuation center said many children were afraid to return indoors and woke up frightened whenever aftershocks rattled the island, he said.
Mieke Suharni, a police officer who was among 30 personnel deployed to Lamba Leda, said much of their work is focused on helping children cope with the disaster’s emotional aftermath. She said officers have organized trauma-healing activities at several evacuation camps, but emotional distress remained widespread among survivors.
Earlier Tuesday, she comforted a woman who was visibly shaken by memories of the quake and used a psychological support method known as Universal Spiritual Emotional Freedom Technique, which she learned during a police training.
“We are trying to help people manage their fear step by step,” Suharni said. “Some survivors continue to experience anxiety and excessive fear. Our goal is to help calm that trauma so they can begin to recover.”
Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic eruptions because of its location on the Pacific Ring of Fire. Flores experienced one of the country’s deadliest disasters in 1992, when an earthquake and an ensuing tsunami killed about 2,500 people.

Scientists recommend not swimming in bog pools to help retain biodiversity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:51:00 UTC
14:51:00 KST

Scientists recommend not swimming in bog pools to help retain biodiversity
Bog pools are sensitive to large numbers of visitors and frequent swimming alters their ecosystems. To preserve biodiversity, scientists recommend swimming in other bodies of water.
People often go swimming in Estonia's many pristine bogs, but this has caused some problems.
"As a result of swimming, the water in the main swimming pool has become thoroughly mixed. This means that both the surface layer and the deeper bottom layers are practically the same temperature. We also studied the vegetation along the edges and at pools used for swimming there was clearly an abundance of grasses, while dwarf shrubs had receded," said Imre Arro, a nature tourism guide and tour organizer.
Sunscreen and other cosmetics entering the water have also been a concern.
"It is certain that they remain in the water and you can also see a layer of them there, but their impact definitely needs to be measured," said Marika Kose, senior lecturer in nature tourism at the Estonian University of Life Sciences.
The extent of the changes depends, among other things, on how often and in what ways people use the same bog area.
"Our research shows that when a lot of people walk in one place, small local changes do occur. If there are a great many of these small changes in one place — for example, in very popular wetlands such as Viru Bog, Kakerdaja Bog or Kõnnu Wetland where many people walk both on and off the trails — then perhaps these wetlands are no longer doing so well," Kose said.
To preserve biodiversity in bog pools, scientists recommend keeping visits brief or going elsewhere instead.
"We certainly can't say that people can't or mustn't touch the water there. But it may be worth considering whether you really need to go swimming there. Perhaps you can go in, have your swim, experience the water and what it feels like and then get back out without leaving additional traces or putting additional pressure on the area, so to speak. A larger lake with infrastructure for swimming may be more suitable, as may lakes, rivers and beaches that are actually intended for swimming," Kose said.

South Korea president calls for military independence in wake of Trump call to cut joint drills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:50:33 UTC
14:50:33 KST

South Korea’s president has renewed his push to regain independent control of the military from the US in the event of war and urged faster progress in acquiring nuclear-powered submarines after Donald Trump’s order to cut joint drills.
On Sunday night, Trump instructed the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” this week’s joint military exercises with South Korea, saying the nuclear-armed North “has been unthreatening and respectful” and that the US president had a “very good relationship with Kim Jong-un”.
Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday that Seoul should proceed without disruption with the planned transfer, during his term, of wartime operational control, or Opcon, of South Korean forces from the US – a goal he and the government have long held.
“A strong alliance makes the foundation of security stronger, and strengthening our own capabilities increases our value and necessity as an ally,” Lee said in a cabinet meeting, describing the US-South Korea alliance and independent defence as mutually reinforcing.
The issue dates back to the Korean war, which ended in an armistice rather than a formal peace treaty in 1953, meaning the two Koreas remain technically at war. US troops have been stationed in South Korea ever since, and the country now hosts Camp Humphreys, the largest American military base outside the US. The two militaries train and operate together closely, including through large-scale annual exercises such as this week’s.
Wartime Opcon, the authority to direct South Korean forces if fighting resumes, has rested with the US since the war began, exercised through the head of the allies’ Combined Forces Command, a position that has always been held by an American four-star general.
Seoul regained peacetime control of its own military in 1994, but the wartime authority has become a potent symbol of national sovereignty, and reclaiming it has been one of South Korea’s foremost security goals for more than two decades, repeatedly delayed under successive governments.
This week’s now-curtailed drills were meant to help certify South Korea’s readiness to finally take it over, a process Lee has pushed to accelerate since taking office.
Lee also called for faster progress on South Korea’s nuclear-powered submarine programme and on developing officers capable of integrated operations for future conflicts.
The renewed push follows Trump’s call to make cuts to the planned 10 days of drills that started on Monday under the name Ulchi Freedom Shield, one of two main annual exercises held by South Korea and the US.
They were expected to involve about 18,000 South Korean troops, alongside US forces and personnel from 11 of the 18 member states of the United Nations Command (UNC), the multinational body that oversees the 1953 armistice that halted hostilities of the Korean war.
During questioning in the Oval Office on Monday, Trump claimed North Korean leader Kim had responded to his order to the Pentagon but did not provide details. When asked what stage the conversations with Kim were at, Trump said “it’s very positive” but provided no further detail.
Trump doubled down on his praise for Kim, saying their ties had reduced tensions. “You see, I’m actually making it much safer. Kim Jong-un has always treated me with great respect,” he said. “I understand him. He understands me.”
Trump has previously suspended major US-South Korean military exercises in pursuit of diplomacy with Kim. After his first summit with the North Korean leader in 2018, that year’s Ulchi Freedom Guardian exercise was cancelled, while other drills were suspended or scaled back. The exercises were redesigned and resumed in modified form with changed names.
The US president acted despite warnings from US and South Korean military officials that Kim’s regime is learning new battlefield tactics from sending North Korean troops to the Ukraine war. Last week, South Korean and US military officials said Ulchi Freedom Shield drills would incorporate aspects such as the North Koreans’ experience with drones on the battlefield.
North Korea has deepened military ties with Russia since they signed a comprehensive strategic partnership pact in June 2024. Pyongyang is providing troops, artillery ammunition and ballistic missiles to support Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
“They’ve taken those lessons they learned there and brought them back to North Korea, that changes the DPRK capability,” said Col Ryan Donald, the public affairs director for the US-led commands in South Korea.
“Our training accounts for that threat, that is why the exercise looks different [from previous exercises], and over the last five years it’s continually evolved.”
On Tuesday, Seoul’s presidential office said the drills did not reflect “any intention to attack North Korea or escalate tensions on the Korean peninsula”.
Lee’s office reiterated that their fundamental purpose was “not to treat a specific entity as an adversary, but to safeguard the safe and peaceful daily lives of the people”.

Hong Kong aiming to revamp heat-stress warning system by end of this month
Labour minister Chris Sun says authorities adjusting system after it failed to trigger higher alert during record-breaking temperatures
2-MIN READ2-MIN
4
 Listen
Hong Kong authorities aim to complete a revamp of the city’s heat-stress warning system by the end of this month, the labour minister has said, following criticism that the alert level was not increased during record-breaking temperatures.
Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said on Tuesday that changes to the Heat Stress at Work Warning system would require thorough preparatory work at several levels.
This would include setting the system’s activation thresholds and determining how alerts would be triggered to ensure seamless operation, he said.
Sun added that any adjustments to optimise the system must address the challenges posed by climate change in Hong Kong.
“Our current goal is to complete this work as quickly as possible, make any necessary adjustments promptly and put them into practice,” he said.
“I have discussed this with the Labour Department and the Hong Kong Observatory, asking them to spare no effort so that we can present the optimised plan to everyone by the end of August.”
The Labour Department recently came under criticism after its warning system remained at the lowest level despite a peak temperature of 36.9 degrees Celsius (103 Fahrenheit) being recorded at the Observatory’s headquarters in Tsim Sha Tsui on August 9 – the highest such reading since records began in 1884.

The USS Benfold, an Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer, was left without power for four days in the South China Sea last month following an engineering failure.
"On July 24, 2026, while conducting routine operations in the Indo-Pacific, Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Benfold (DDG 65) reported an engineering casualty involving its generators, causing a loss of power," Cmdr Matthew Comer, spokesperson for the US 7th Fleet, told USNI News in a statement.
"There were no injuries to the crew, who demonstrated resilience, grit, professionalism and unwavering steadiness in their response," Comer said.

The George Washington Carrier Strike Group, with which the Benfold had been sailing, supported the destroyer during the incident. USS Robert Smalls, a cruiser attached to the strike group, helped provide meals for the crew, Comer said.
An investigation is ongoing into the cause of the incident.

Over 2,400 school building projects implemented in a year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-18
05:47:21 UTC
14:47:21 KST

Over 2,400 school building projects implemented in a year
TEHRAN - The Organization for the Renovation of Schools announced that 2,407 school construction projects were completed last year (March 2025-2026), and plans are in place to build over 2,300 classrooms this year.
Hamidreza Khan-Mohammadi, the head of the organization, also spoke about the development of solar power plants in schools, stating that the implementation of a solar power project with a total capacity of 1,260 megawatts has begun across 12,000 schools, Mehr reported.
"So far, work has been carried out on approximately 2,500 power plants, and equipment for another 5,000—out of a total of 12,000—has been procured and prepared," he added.
 
  
 
 Regarding the commitments made by school-building benefactors, he stated: "Last year, the total value of pledges by benefactors stood at 286 trillion rials (around 155 million dollars), and to date, new commitments amounting to 97 trillion rials (around 52 million dollars) have been registered."
Benefactors contribute to building half of schools
In February 2025, the government spokesperson, Fatemeh Mohajerani, said some 51 percent of the schools in the country are constructed with the help of benefactors.
“The participation of school-building benefactors has significantly increased in recent years so that about 48 to 51 percent of the schools are built thanks to their financial assistance,” IRIB quoted Mohajerani as saying.
Benefactors’ participation in constructing schools shows their commitment and will to improve educational opportunities and develop educational infrastructure; their efforts can have positive, profound impacts on the education, students, and the future of the country, she noted.
The official went on to say that the current administration focuses on expanding educational infrastructure and building new schools, to replace the prefabricated ones, with the help of benefactors, even in areas where there are only one or two students.
“Education, educational equity, and the elimination of educational deprivation are among the top priorities of the current administration,” she highlighted.
Solar-powered schools
A national plan to equip around 12,000 schools across the country with solar power plants began in June with the installation of a 5-kilowatt system in a technical-vocational school in Tehran.
Schools affected by war, boarding schools, schools in border areas, and in underprivileged regions are given priority. Donors have taken responsibility for covering costs, and the Clean Energy Organization is providing the required equipment to the selected schools. Also, the provincial officials and electricity departments are participating in the preparation and installation process, IRNA reported.
So far, 12 out of 31 provinces have announced their readiness, and the goal is to equip all 12,000 schools with 5-kilowatt systems by mid-September. There are about 100,000 public schools in the country, more than 60 percent of which have the capacity to install solar panels.
In November 2025, Majid Parsa, head of the Tehran Education Department, announced that 1,200 schools across Tehran province were set to be equipped with rooftop solar panel systems by the end of the past Iranian calendar year (20 March 2026). The initiative followed an agreement with the Tehran Governor’s Office to install five-kilowatt systems on each participating school.
Parsa noted that the project would initially be implemented on a trial basis to assess performance, maintenance and grid integration. “The Education Department has already equipped five schools with pilot solar systems, which have shown promising results,” he said at the time. He added that solar-powered schools could play a vital role in energy conservation, providing clean electricity for their own use and potentially supplying surplus power to the national grid.
